p10-1.q: Middleware is a piece of code in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline that handles an HttpContext: it can do work before the next component runs, call the next one, do work after it returns, or stop the request (short-circuit). The pipeline is just a chain of these components, executed in the exact order they are registered in Program.cs.
i: How it works: each middleware is a `RequestDelegate` (`Task Invoke(HttpContext)`). At startup the `IApplicationBuilder` composes them in reverse into one delegate, so at runtime a request flows in through every layer and the response flows back out in reverse order.

Four verbs: `Use` adds a component that can call `next`; `Run` adds a terminal one that never calls next; `Map` branches by path prefix; `MapWhen`/`UseWhen` branch on a predicate (UseWhen rejoins the main pipeline, MapWhen does not).

Order is behaviour: exception handler first so it catches everything; `UseRouting` before CORS, authentication and authorization; `UseAuthentication` before `UseAuthorization`; endpoints last. WebApplication adds UseRouting and UseEndpoints for you if you do not call them.

Short-circuiting: static files, CORS preflight, auth failures (401/403) and rate limiting (429) end the request early, so later middleware and your controller never run. That is also a performance win.

Middleware vs filters: middleware sees every request and knows nothing about MVC actions or model binding; filters run only around controller actions and see ActionArguments and results. Cross-cutting HTTP concerns go in middleware.

In IRT: our pipeline has [a correlation-id middleware] at the top that reads or creates `X-Correlation-ID`, pushes it into the logging scope and echoes it in the response, plus global exception handling returning ProblemDetails, so every log line in CloudWatch can be traced across services.
Pitfall: you cannot change status code or headers once the response has started streaming (`Response.HasStarted`); set headers before calling next or use `Response.OnStarting`.
f: What is a RequestDelegate?
A delegate `Task (HttpContext context)`; the whole pipeline compiles down to one of them.
What happens if UseAuthorization comes before UseAuthentication?
HttpContext.User is still anonymous when policies are checked, so protected endpoints return 401 even with a valid token.
Is middleware a singleton?
Convention-based middleware is created once at startup (effectively singleton); IMiddleware is resolved per request from DI.
p10-1.y: Middleware is a piece of code that sits in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. Every request passes through the middleware in the order I register them, and each one can do some work, call the next one, and then do more work on the way back, or stop the request early. Authentication, routing, CORS and exception handling are all middleware. In my project, I wrote a correlation-id middleware so we could trace every request across [4] services.
p10-1.k: middleware, request pipeline, request delegate, use, next, http pipeline

p10-2.q: There are three ways: an inline lambda with `app.Use`, a convention-based class (constructor takes `RequestDelegate next`, public `InvokeAsync(HttpContext)` method), or a class implementing `IMiddleware` that DI creates per request. Each one does its work before `await next(context)`, after it, or both, and is registered in Program.cs at the right place in the order.
i: Convention rules: the class needs a public constructor with `RequestDelegate` and a public method named `Invoke` or `InvokeAsync` returning Task whose first parameter is HttpContext. No interface is required; ASP.NET Core finds the method by reflection once at startup.
Extra InvokeAsync parameters are resolved from DI per request. That is the correct place for scoped services such as DbContext or an audit service.

Package it as an extension method (`public static IApplicationBuilder UseCorrelationId(this IApplicationBuilder app) => app.UseMiddleware<CorrelationIdMiddleware>();`) so Program.cs reads like a story.
Always `await next(context)`; never fire-and-forget it, and do not call it twice. To short-circuit, set the status code, write the response and simply return without calling next.
Pass CancellationToken from `context.RequestAborted` to downstream calls, and use `ILogger` scopes rather than static state; the class is shared by all requests, so it must be thread-safe.

In IRT: [the correlation-id middleware and a request-audit middleware] that records user, route, status code and duration for regulated endpoints, writing through a scoped audit service injected into InvokeAsync.
Testing: unit-test by constructing it with a fake `next` delegate and a `DefaultHttpContext`; integration-test through WebApplicationFactory.
f: Why use Response.OnStarting for the header?
Headers must be set before the body starts streaming; OnStarting runs at exactly that moment, even if a later component writes the response.
How do you unit-test middleware?
new DefaultHttpContext(), a next delegate that records it was called, then assert headers, status and logs.
Inline lambda or class?
Lambda for two lines; a class for anything with dependencies, logic or tests.
p10-2.y: To write custom middleware, I create a class with a constructor that takes the next RequestDelegate and an InvokeAsync method that takes HttpContext. Inside, I do my work, await next, and then do any work after the response. Then I register it in Program.cs with app.UseMiddleware, at the right position. Our correlation-id middleware reads or creates an id, adds it to the response header and the logging scope, and then calls next.
p10-2.k: custom middleware, invokeasync, requestdelegate, usemiddleware, httpcontext

p10-3.q: Convention-based middleware is created once at startup, so anything in its constructor lives as long as the app; scoped services must be taken as `InvokeAsync` parameters instead. IMiddleware-based middleware is resolved from DI by `IMiddlewareFactory` on every request, so it can use constructor injection with any lifetime, but you must register it in DI yourself.
i: Captive dependency: a scoped DbContext captured in a singleton is shared across concurrent requests (DbContext is not thread-safe) and never disposed. With `ValidateScopes` (on in Development) you get "Cannot resolve scoped service from root provider".

IMiddleware signature: `Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, RequestDelegate next)`; registration `builder.Services.AddScoped<AuditMiddleware>();` then `app.UseMiddleware<AuditMiddleware>();`. Forgetting registration throws at the first request.
Trade-off: IMiddleware gives strong typing and normal constructor DI at the cost of one resolve per request (tiny); convention-based is slightly faster and is what the framework itself uses.
You cannot pass extra constructor arguments to IMiddleware through UseMiddleware(args); configuration should come from IOptions.
In IRT I used IMiddleware for [the request-audit middleware], because it depends on a scoped audit repository and the current-user service, and constructor injection keeps it clean and testable.
f: How does ASP.NET Core know which style you used?
UseMiddleware checks if the type implements IMiddleware; if so it uses IMiddlewareFactory, otherwise it activates the class once by convention.
Which is better?
Convention-based for simple, stateless middleware; IMiddleware when you want constructor injection of scoped services.
p10-3.y: Convention-based middleware is created once at startup, so it is effectively a singleton, and scoped services must be passed as parameters to InvokeAsync, not the constructor. Factory-based middleware implements IMiddleware and is created from DI for each request, so constructor injection of scoped services is fine, but I must register it in the container. The pitfall is injecting a scoped service like DbContext into a convention middleware's constructor, which captures it forever.
p10-3.k: imiddleware, convention-based middleware, factory-based middleware, scoped service, captive dependency

p10-4.q: Situation: in [2024] support tickets about failed shipment updates took [about an hour] to triage, because one request crossed [4] services and we matched CloudWatch logs by timestamp. Task: make every request traceable end to end. Action: I added a correlation-id middleware to our shared service template, propagated the id downstream, and added it to every log line. Result: one query now shows the whole journey, and triage dropped to [a few minutes].
i: Middleware: reads `X-Correlation-ID` or creates one, sets `TraceIdentifier`, opens a logger scope and echoes the header in the response, so the UI and vendors can quote it in tickets.

Outbound HTTP: a `DelegatingHandler` registered with `AddHttpMessageHandler` copies the id onto every HttpClient call; for RabbitMQ and Kafka the publisher adds it as a message header and consumers open the same logging scope.
Logging: structured JSON logs to CloudWatch, so Logs Insights can filter `CorrelationId = "..."` across all log groups at once.
Audit: a separate IMiddleware writes user, route, status and duration for regulated endpoints; it reuses the correlation id so audit rows link to logs.
Lesson: today I would align it with W3C `traceparent` and OpenTelemetry (Activity.TraceId) so it also feeds distributed tracing in X-Ray or Grafana Tempo, rather than a custom header only.
Pitfall avoided: never trust a client id blindly; we limit its length and characters before logging to prevent log injection.
f: Why not just use Activity / OpenTelemetry?
That is the better long-term answer; the custom header came first because vendors and the UI needed an id they could see and quote.
How do you stop log injection through the header?
Validate format and length (for example 64 characters, letters, digits and dashes) and generate a new id otherwise.
w: I look for the root cause of slow support work, not just the ticket in front of me.
I build small shared pieces that help every service and every team.
p10-4.y: In [2024], tracing a failed shipment update across [4] services took [about an hour], because we matched logs by timestamp. I added a correlation-id middleware to our shared service template. It reads the id from the request header or creates one, returns it in the response, puts it in the logging scope, and passes it to downstream HTTP calls and messages. Now one log query shows the whole journey, and triage takes [a few minutes].
p10-4.k: correlation id, audit logging, middleware, story, tracing, logging scope

p10-5.q: Filters run inside the MVC action pipeline, after routing has selected a controller action. The order is authorization, resource, (model binding), action, the action method, exception (on errors) and result filters; each can run code before and after the next stage or short-circuit by setting a result.
i: Authorization filters run first and can short-circuit with 401/403; resource filters wrap model binding (good for caching or turning off binding); action filters see `ActionArguments` and the `IActionResult`; result filters wrap result execution; exception filters catch exceptions from model binding, action filters and the action, but not from result execution.
Scope and order: global, controller, then action; within the same scope the `Order` property decides. Before-code runs outside-in, after-code inside-out.
DI: attributes cannot take constructor services, so use `[ServiceFilter(typeof(AuditFilter))]` (filter registered in DI) or `[TypeFilter]` (activated with DI arguments).
`[ApiController]` adds an automatic model-validation filter that returns 400 ProblemDetails before your action runs.
Minimal APIs use endpoint filters (`IEndpointFilter`, `AddEndpointFilter`) instead, with a similar before/after model.
In IRT I used [an action filter that rejects changes to a locked study] by checking the study id in ActionArguments, so every write endpoint got the rule from one attribute.
f: Filter or middleware for global exception handling?
Middleware (UseExceptionHandler / IExceptionHandler), because exception filters miss errors outside MVC, such as in other middleware or result execution.
ServiceFilter vs TypeFilter?
ServiceFilter resolves the filter itself from DI (must be registered); TypeFilter creates it with ActivatorUtilities, so it does not need registration and can take extra arguments.
p10-5.y: MVC filters run around controller actions, in this order: authorization filters, resource filters, action filters around the action, exception filters for errors, and result filters around the response. To write a custom action filter, I implement IAsyncActionFilter, do my check before calling next and my work after, then apply it as an attribute or globally. For example, an audit filter that records which user changed which study.
p10-5.k: filters, action filter, authorization filter, resource filter, exception filter, result filter, iasyncactionfilter

p10-6.q: All three give you strongly typed configuration bound from appsettings, environment variables or secrets. `IOptions<T>` is computed once and never changes; `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is recomputed once per request (scoped); `IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton that always returns the latest value and can notify you on change.
i: Binding: `builder.Services.AddOptions<SftpOptions>().Bind(config.GetSection("Sftp")).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart();` so a missing host or key fails at startup, not at 2 a.m. on the first transfer.
.NET 8 adds a source-generated validator (`[OptionsValidator]`) and the configuration binding source generator, which removes reflection and supports native AOT.
Reload: values change at runtime only when the provider reloads (appsettings.json with reloadOnChange, Azure App Configuration, a custom provider); environment variables do not reload.
Named options: `Get("DepotA")` on Monitor or Snapshot lets one class hold settings per vendor, which fits per-vendor SFTP settings.
Pitfall: injecting IOptionsSnapshot into a singleton throws (scoped into root); in singletons and BackgroundServices use IOptionsMonitor.

In IRT our SFTP component uses [named options per vendor] (host, port, provider, host key fingerprint) with validation on start, so a bad config blocks the deployment health check instead of failing a live transfer.
f: Why not inject IConfiguration everywhere?
Magic strings, no types, no validation and harder tests; options give typed, validated, testable settings.
How do you test code that uses IOptions?
Options.Create(new SftpOptions { ... }) builds an IOptions<T> instance without any DI.
p10-6.y: IOptions reads configuration once and never changes, so it is good for settings that are fixed. IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, so it picks up changes for each new request. IOptionsMonitor is a singleton that always gives the current value and can notify me when the file changes, so it is the one to use inside singletons and background services. Most of our settings use IOptions with validation at startup.
p10-6.k: ioptions, ioptionssnapshot, ioptionsmonitor, options pattern, configuration reload

p10-7.q: A hosted service is a class the .NET Generic Host starts when the application starts and stops on graceful shutdown, by calling `StartAsync` and `StopAsync`. `BackgroundService` is the convenient base class for a long-running loop: you override `ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)` and keep working until the token is cancelled.
i: Lifetime: hosted services are singletons. To use DbContext or other scoped services, inject `IServiceScopeFactory` and create a scope per unit of work (per message or per loop iteration).

Shutdown: on SIGTERM (ECS task stop, Kubernetes) the host cancels the stoppingToken and waits `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` (30 seconds by default in .NET 6+) for StopAsync; finish or checkpoint the current item inside that time.
Errors: since .NET 6 an unhandled exception in ExecuteAsync stops the whole host by default (`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost`), so wrap each iteration in try/catch and log.

Startup: before .NET 10 the synchronous part of ExecuteAsync up to the first await blocked startup; .NET 10 runs the whole of ExecuteAsync on a background task. .NET 8 added `IHostedLifecycleService` (StartingAsync, StartedAsync...) and concurrent start options.
Timers: use `PeriodicTimer` (`await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)`) instead of Task.Delay loops or System.Threading.Timer callbacks that can overlap.
Scaling: with several instances, every instance runs the service; for single-run jobs use a lock (database or Redis) or a queue so work is not duplicated.
In IRT: [the SFTP polling worker] that checks vendor folders every [5 minutes], and RabbitMQ consumers that run as BackgroundServices in worker containers on ECS.
f: Hosted service vs Hangfire or Quartz?
Hosted services suit simple loops and consumers; Hangfire/Quartz add persistence, retries, cron schedules and dashboards for many scheduled jobs.
Why not do this work inside an API request?
Requests should be short; background work needs its own lifetime, retries and graceful shutdown.
p10-7.y: A hosted service is a class that starts and stops with the application. BackgroundService is the base class for long-running work: I override ExecuteAsync with a loop that runs until the stopping token is cancelled. Because it is a singleton, I create a scope for each piece of work to use DbContext. Our SFTP poller is a BackgroundService that checks vendor folders [every 5 minutes].
p10-7.k: hosted service, backgroundservice, ihostedservice, executeasync, worker

p10-8.q: `ILogger<T>` is the logging abstraction from Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, injected by DI; the type parameter becomes the category, so you can turn levels up or down per namespace in configuration. Structured logging means writing message templates such as `"Shipment {ShipmentId} moved to {Status}"`, so the values are kept as named properties that you can query, not baked into a string.
i: Never interpolate: `$"Shipment {id}"` loses the fields and always allocates the string, even when the level is disabled. Use templates, and for hot paths the `[LoggerMessage]` source generator that creates zero-allocation, strongly typed log methods.
Scopes: `BeginScope` attaches properties (CorrelationId, StudyId) to every log inside it; providers such as Serilog or the JSON console formatter include them.
Levels: Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical; set them in `Logging:LogLevel` (for example Microsoft.AspNetCore at Warning) to cut noise and cost.
Providers: console JSON formatter in containers is enough for CloudWatch; Serilog adds enrichers and sinks; OpenTelemetry logs link logs to traces.
Never log secrets, tokens or patient data; in GxP logs are operational data, the audit trail is separate.
In IRT: JSON logs from ECS tasks go to CloudWatch, and Logs Insights queries by CorrelationId or ShipmentId; [an alert] fires on Error-level counts per service in Grafana.
f: ILogger vs ILogger<T>?
ILogger<T> fixes the category to T's name; inject ILoggerFactory only when you need dynamic categories.
Why is string interpolation bad in logs?
It allocates even when the level is off and turns fields into plain text, so you cannot filter by them.
p10-8.y: ILogger of T is the built-in logging interface, where T sets the category, usually the class name. Structured logging means I write a message template with named placeholders, like Shipment {ShipmentId} updated, instead of joining strings. The values are stored as separate fields, so in CloudWatch I can filter by ShipmentId directly. With our correlation id in the scope, I can follow one request through every service.
p10-8.k: ilogger, structured logging, logging, message template, serilog, log levels

p10-9.q: Rate limiting protects an API from abuse and overload by limiting how many requests a caller may make in a time window; extra requests are rejected with 429 Too Many Requests or queued. Since .NET 7 ASP.NET Core ships rate-limiting middleware (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting`) with four algorithms that you can partition per user, IP, client id or tenant.
i: Algorithms: fixed window (simple, bursty at window edges), sliding window (smoother), token bucket (allows controlled bursts, refills over time), concurrency (limits in-flight requests, good for expensive endpoints like CSV import).
Partitioning: `PartitionedRateLimiter.Create` keyed on `User.Identity.Name` or API key; never only on IP behind a load balancer unless you trust X-Forwarded-For through ForwardedHeaders.
Gotcha: the default rejection status is 503; set `RejectionStatusCode = 429` and add a `Retry-After` header in OnRejected.
It is per instance and in memory: with [3] ECS tasks each one counts separately. For a global limit use API Gateway usage plans or throttling, AWS WAF rate rules, or a Redis-based limiter.
Place UseRateLimiter after UseRouting (for endpoint-specific policies) and after authentication if you partition by user.
In IRT: [a concurrency limit of 2 per user on the CSV import endpoint] and token-bucket limits on vendor-facing APIs, plus API Gateway throttling at the edge.
f: Where else can you rate-limit?
At the edge: API Gateway throttling and usage plans, AWS WAF rate-based rules, or an API management layer; app-level limits are a second line.
Token bucket vs fixed window?
Token bucket allows short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing an average rate; fixed window can let 2x the limit through around a window boundary.
p10-9.y: Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make in a time window, to protect the API from overload and abuse. Since .NET 7 it is built in: I add AddRateLimiter with a policy like fixed window, sliding window, token bucket or concurrency, call UseRateLimiter, and attach the policy to endpoints. Rejected requests get a 429. We used a concurrency limit of [2 imports per user] for the CSV upload.
p10-9.k: rate limiting, throttling, 429, token bucket, fixed window, sliding window, addratelimiter

p10-10.q: A minimal API maps HTTP routes directly to handlers, such as `app.MapGet("/shipments/{id}", handler)`, without controllers, action filters or MVC conventions. It was introduced in .NET 6 and has grown into a full option: parameter binding from route, query, body and DI, route groups, endpoint filters, typed results, OpenAPI and native AOT.
i: Binding is inferred: simple types from route or query, complex types from the JSON body, registered services from DI, plus `HttpContext`, `CancellationToken` and `[AsParameters]` to bundle many parameters into a record.
`TypedResults.Ok(dto)` / `Results<Ok<T>, NotFound>` make return types explicit, which improves OpenAPI documentation and unit testing.
Organise with `MapGroup("/api/shipments").RequireAuthorization().WithTags("Shipments")` and one static extension method per feature, so Program.cs stays short.
Cross-cutting: endpoint filters (`AddEndpointFilter`) replace action filters; .NET 10 adds built-in DataAnnotations validation with `builder.Services.AddValidation()`.
Performance: less overhead than MVC, and the Request Delegate Generator makes it AOT-friendly; good for small services and Lambda functions.
When I still choose controllers: big APIs with many filters, conventions, and teams used to MVC structure, which is the case for most IRT services.
f: Are minimal APIs only for demos?
No; they are production-ready, fast and support auth, validation, OpenAPI and filters.
How do you test them?
Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory, or unit-test the handler as a static method returning TypedResults.
p10-10.y: A minimal API is a way to build HTTP endpoints with very little code, by mapping a route to a lambda in Program.cs, like app.MapGet. Parameters come from the route, query, body or DI automatically. They support validation, filters, OpenAPI and authorization, and they are a bit faster than controllers. I use them for small services and internal endpoints, and route groups keep them organised.
p10-10.k: minimal api, mapget, mappost, route groups, endpoints

p10-11.q: Exception-handling middleware sits at the very start of the pipeline and catches any unhandled exception from everything after it, turning it into a clean error response instead of a crash page. In .NET 8 the recommended way is `IExceptionHandler`: classes whose `TryHandleAsync` decides whether they handle an exception and writes a ProblemDetails response.
i: Registration: `builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<DomainExceptionHandler>(); builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();` then `app.UseExceptionHandler();`. Several handlers run in registration order until one returns true.
Map types to status: ValidationException 400, NotFoundException 404, ConcurrencyException 409, everything else 500 with a generic message.
ProblemDetails (RFC 9457) gives `type, title, status, detail, instance`; add `traceId` or correlation id so support can find the logs.
Security: never return stack traces or SQL errors to clients in production; log them with full detail instead.
What it cannot catch: exceptions after the response has started streaming, and exceptions in background threads; those must be handled where they happen.
Alternatives: the developer exception page in Development, custom middleware with try/catch (older style), exception filters (MVC only, miss non-MVC errors).
In IRT we map [domain exceptions such as StudyLockedException to 409] and all responses carry the correlation id, which support asks users to quote.
f: Exceptions or Result types for validation?
Expected outcomes (validation, not found) are often cleaner as results; exceptions for truly exceptional cases. The handler is the safety net either way.
Why must the exception handler be first?
Middleware only catches exceptions from components registered after it.
p10-11.y: Exception middleware catches any unhandled exception in the pipeline, so it must be registered first. In .NET 8, I call UseExceptionHandler and register a class that implements IExceptionHandler. It logs the error with the correlation id and writes a ProblemDetails response, mapping known exceptions to the right status, like 404 or 409, and everything else to 500 without leaking details. This gives every service the same error format.
p10-11.k: exception middleware, iexceptionhandler, problemdetails, useexceptionhandler, error handling, .net 8

p10-12.q: `IHttpClientFactory` creates HttpClient instances whose underlying handlers (connections) are pooled and recycled, solving two classic bugs: socket exhaustion from `new HttpClient()` per call, and stale DNS from one static client living forever. It also centralises configuration (base address, headers, timeouts, retries) through named or typed clients.
i: Socket exhaustion: disposing HttpClient closes the connection, but the socket stays in TIME_WAIT for minutes; under load you run out of ports.
Handler rotation: the factory reuses handlers for `HandlerLifetime` (2 minutes by default) then creates new ones, so DNS changes (blue/green, failover) are picked up.
Typed clients: `AddHttpClient<DepotApiClient>(c => c.BaseAddress = ...)` injects a configured HttpClient into your class; they are transient, so do not capture them in singletons.
Outgoing middleware: `DelegatingHandler`s for correlation ids, auth tokens and logging, added with `AddHttpMessageHandler<T>()`.

Resilience in .NET 8: `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` with `AddStandardResilienceHandler()` adds rate limiting, total timeout, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker and per-attempt timeout.
Alternative for singletons/console apps: one long-lived HttpClient with `SocketsHttpHandler { PooledConnectionLifetime = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2) }`.
In IRT: [typed clients for the depot and courier APIs], each with the standard resilience handler and the correlation-id handler.
f: Named vs typed clients?
Named: CreateClient("depot") with string keys; typed: a class receiving a configured HttpClient, strongly typed and easier to test.
How do you unit-test code that uses HttpClient?
Pass an HttpClient built on a fake HttpMessageHandler that returns canned responses, or use a mock server such as WireMock.Net.
p10-12.y: IHttpClientFactory creates HttpClient instances for me and manages the underlying connections. If I create new HttpClient for every call, sockets can run out, and if I keep one forever, it may miss DNS changes. The factory pools and recycles handlers to solve both. It also lets me configure typed clients with base address, headers and resilience policies in one place, which is how we call vendor and internal APIs.
p10-12.k: ihttpclientfactory, httpclient, socket exhaustion, typed client, dns

p10-13.q: `Span<T>` is a lightweight view (pointer plus length) over a contiguous region of memory, such as part of an array, a stackalloc buffer or native memory, that lets you read, write and slice it without allocating or copying. It is a `ref struct`, so it lives only on the stack; `Memory<T>` is the equivalent that can be stored on the heap and used across `await`.
i: Why it matters: parsing and formatting without creating substrings or temporary arrays cuts allocations and GC pressure; much of .NET's performance gains (System.Text.Json, Kestrel, int.Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>)) is built on spans.

Rules: cannot be boxed, captured in lambdas, stored in class fields or used as a generic type argument in most places; C# 13 relaxed this so ref structs can be locals in async methods and iterators as long as they are not used across an await or yield.
`ReadOnlySpan<char>` from `"text".AsSpan()` replaces Substring in hot paths; `stackalloc byte[256]` for small temporary buffers; `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` for larger rented buffers.
`Memory<T>` / `ReadOnlyMemory<T>`: store in fields, pass to async APIs (Stream.ReadAsync(Memory<byte>)), and call `.Span` when you process synchronously.
When to use: hot paths you have measured (parsers, protocol handling); not needed in normal business code where readability wins.
In my work: [parsing fixed-width fields in vendor files] with ReadOnlySpan<char> slices instead of Substring, which reduced allocations in the import loop; measured with BenchmarkDotNet.
f: Why can't Span<T> be used across await?
The method's state is moved to the heap at an await, and a span may point to stack memory that no longer exists.
Span vs ArraySegment?
ArraySegment works only over arrays and is a normal struct; Span works over any contiguous memory and is faster but stack-only.
p10-13.y: Span of T is a view over a block of memory, like part of an array or a string, without copying it. So I can slice and parse data with no extra allocations. It lives only on the stack, so it can't be used in async methods. Memory of T is the version that can be stored on the heap and used across awaits. They are useful in hot paths like parsing large CSV files.
p10-13.k: span, memory, performance, allocations, stackalloc, parsing

p10-14.q: `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` represents a sequence whose items arrive asynchronously, such as rows from a database or pages from an API. You produce it with an `async` iterator method (`await` plus `yield return`) and consume it with `await foreach`, handling each item as soon as it is ready instead of loading everything into a list first.
i: Memory: streaming [100,000] audit rows one by one keeps memory flat, compared with ToListAsync which materialises all of them.
Cancellation: add `[EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct` to the iterator and call `.WithCancellation(ct)` when consuming.
EF Core: `query.AsAsyncEnumerable()` streams rows; keep the DbContext alive for the whole enumeration and do not run other queries on the same context meanwhile.
ASP.NET Core: returning IAsyncEnumerable<T> from an action streams the JSON array to the client as items are produced (System.Text.Json, .NET 6+).
System.Linq.Async adds LINQ operators (WhereAwait, SelectAwait); .NET 10 includes `System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable` in the framework.
Use case in IRT: [exporting audit trail reports] by streaming rows from SQL Server straight into a CSV stream, so large studies do not spike memory.
f: IAsyncEnumerable vs Task<List<T>>?
The list waits for everything and holds it in memory; the async stream yields items as they come.
IAsyncEnumerable vs Channels?
IAsyncEnumerable is pull-based for one consumer; channels decouple producers and consumers with buffering and backpressure.
p10-14.y: IAsyncEnumerable lets me return items one by one as they become available, and the caller uses await foreach to consume them. So I don't need to load everything into memory before starting. For example, streaming rows from the database or reading a large file line by line. ASP.NET Core can also stream it directly as a JSON response.
p10-14.k: iasyncenumerable, async streams, await foreach, streaming

p10-15.q: They cache at different levels. Response caching is HTTP-header driven (Cache-Control, Vary) and mostly benefits browsers and proxies; output caching stores the generated response on the server under policies you control; IMemoryCache, IDistributedCache and HybridCache cache data objects inside your code.
i: Response caching middleware obeys client headers, so a client sending `Cache-Control: no-cache` bypasses it; it only caches GET/HEAD 200 responses without Authorization headers.

Output caching: `AddOutputCache` + `[OutputCache(Duration = 60, Tags = ["studies"])]` or `.CacheOutput()`; evict with `IOutputCacheStore.EvictByTagAsync("studies")` when data changes; storage can be Redis (.NET 8) for multiple instances.
IMemoryCache: per instance, fast, lost on restart, set size limits and expirations; IDistributedCache (Redis/ElastiCache) shares across instances but needs serialisation.
HybridCache (.NET 9): L1 memory + L2 distributed, stampede protection (one caller computes, others wait), tags; API `GetOrCreateAsync(key, factory)`.
Pitfalls: caching user-specific or authorised data under a shared key, no invalidation strategy, cache stampede at expiry; add jitter and invalidate on write events.
In IRT: [reference data such as countries, depots and study configuration] in IMemoryCache with ElastiCache behind it; never randomisation or kit allocation data.
f: What is a cache stampede?
Many requests miss an expired key together and all hit the database; prevent with locking (HybridCache does this), early refresh or jittered expirations.
What should never be cached?
Security-sensitive or highly consistent data, such as permissions mid-change or kit allocation.
p10-15.y: Response caching uses HTTP cache headers so browsers and proxies can cache responses. Output caching, added in .NET 7, stores the response on the server and gives me control to expire it. IMemoryCache caches any data in the memory of one server. HybridCache combines memory and a distributed cache like Redis, and it prevents many requests rebuilding the same item at once. We cache reference data like countries and depots this way.
p10-15.k: caching, response caching, output caching, imemorycache, hybridcache, redis, distributed cache

p10-16.q: `UseAuthentication` asks the default scheme's handler to authenticate every request; for JWT bearer that means reading the `Authorization: Bearer` header, validating the token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and turning its claims into `HttpContext.User`. `UseAuthorization` then checks the policies on the matched endpoint and returns 401 if the user is not authenticated or 403 if authenticated but not allowed.
i: Keys: with `Authority` set, the handler downloads OpenID configuration and signing keys (JWKS) and caches them, refreshing on unknown key ids, so key rotation works without redeploying.
Lifetime: default `ClockSkew` is 5 minutes, so a 15-minute token is really valid for about 20; set it lower if you need tight logout.
.NET 8 switched to the faster `JsonWebTokenHandler` by default; claim mapping (`MapInboundClaims`) can rename claims such as sub to the long XML names, so set it false for clean claim names.
Revocation: JWTs are valid until expiry; combine short lifetimes, refresh-token revocation and a jti denylist checked in `OnTokenValidated` (our logout fix used [ElastiCache]).

Policies: `AddAuthorizationBuilder().AddPolicy("StudyManager", p => p.RequireRole("StudyManager").RequireClaim("study_access"))`; resource-based checks with `IAuthorizationService` for "this user, this study".
Events (`OnAuthenticationFailed`, `OnChallenge`) help debugging; never log the token itself.
f: 401 means we do not know who you are (missing or invalid token); 403 means we know you but you are not allowed.
Where are tokens validated in microservices?
Every service validates locally with cached keys; the gateway may also check, but services do not trust the network.
p10-16.y: The client sends the JWT in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. The authentication middleware validates it: the signature using the identity provider's public key, the issuer, the audience and the expiry. If it is valid, it creates the user with claims, and the authorization middleware checks policies and roles for the endpoint. If it fails, we return 401, and if the user lacks permission, 403.
p10-16.k: jwt, bearer authentication, token validation, authentication middleware, claims, 401, 403

p10-17.q: Keyed services, added in .NET 8, let you register multiple implementations of the same interface under a key and ask DI for a specific one. You register with `AddKeyedScoped/Singleton/Transient<TService, TImpl>(key)` and resolve with the `[FromKeyedServices(key)]` attribute or `IServiceProvider.GetRequiredKeyedService<T>(key)`.
i: Before .NET 8 the options were a custom factory, `IEnumerable<T>` and picking by a property, or a third-party container (Autofac keyed registrations).
Works with constructor injection, minimal API parameters and `IKeyedServiceProvider`; keys can be any object, often strings or enums.
Good for the Strategy pattern where the choice comes from configuration at runtime, such as provider per vendor.
Pitfall: resolving by key from IServiceProvider inside business code is service location; keep it inside one factory class.

In my SFTP component the factory resolved [the provider by the vendor's configured name]; with keyed services it becomes `sp.GetRequiredKeyedService<ISftpClient>(options.Provider)`, removing a switch statement.
f: Keyed services vs IEnumerable<T>?
IEnumerable gives all implementations (good for pipelines of handlers); keyed gives exactly one by name.
Does the built-in container support decorators?
Not directly; use Scrutor or manual registration to decorate.
p10-17.y: Keyed services, added in .NET 8, let me register several implementations of the same interface with a key, and then ask for a specific one with the FromKeyedServices attribute. Before that, I needed a factory or a list of all implementations. We use it for SFTP clients: each vendor's configuration says which library key to use, like Rebex or SSH.NET.
p10-17.k: keyed services, dependency injection, fromkeyedservices, .net 8, multiple implementations

p10-18.q: `System.Threading.Channels` provides fast, async, thread-safe in-memory queues for producer/consumer scenarios. Producers write to `channel.Writer`, consumers read with `await foreach (var item in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct))`, and a bounded channel applies backpressure when it is full.
i: Bounded vs unbounded: always prefer bounded in services; `BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait` makes producers wait, DropOldest/DropNewest/DropWrite discard data deliberately.
Options `SingleReader`/`SingleWriter` enable faster internal implementations when true.
Completion: `Writer.Complete()` lets consumers finish the remaining items and exit cleanly at shutdown.
Versus BlockingCollection: channels are async-first and do not block threads; versus a broker (RabbitMQ): channels are in-process only, lost on crash, no persistence.
Pattern: API endpoint writes a work item and returns 202; a BackgroundService drains the channel with limited parallelism.
In my work: [the MCP server's log-summarisation queue], where tool calls enqueue log fetch jobs and one worker processes them so Azure DevOps Server is not flooded.
f: When not to use channels?
When work must survive a crash or be shared by several instances; use a durable queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) instead.
What is backpressure?
Slowing producers when consumers fall behind, instead of growing memory without limit.
p10-18.y: Channels are a fast, thread-safe queue for passing data between producers and consumers in the same process, and they work with async. A bounded channel has a size limit, so producers wait when it is full, which gives back-pressure. I use them with a BackgroundService: the API writes work into the channel and the background worker processes it, so the request returns quickly.
p10-18.k: channels, producer consumer, queue, back-pressure, backgroundservice

p10-19.q: `TimeProvider` is a .NET 8 abstract class that represents "now" and timers. You inject it instead of calling `DateTime.Now` or `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` directly, using `TimeProvider.System` in production and `FakeTimeProvider` (Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing) in tests, where you can set and advance time.
i: API: `GetUtcNow()`, `GetLocalNow()` with `LocalTimeZone`, `GetTimestamp()`/`GetElapsedTime()` for durations, `CreateTimer()`.

Integrations: `Task.Delay(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)`, `new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)`, Polly v8 and the resilience libraries accept it, so retry delays are testable without waiting.
Replaces home-made `IClock` interfaces with a standard type every library understands.
Always store and compare UTC (`DateTimeOffset`), convert to local time zones only for display.
In my work: after [the time-zone bug in the shipment report in 2023] I moved date logic to TimeProvider and wrote tests for midnight UTC across [IST and US] time zones with FakeTimeProvider.
f: Why not DateTime.Now?
It is local server time, hidden global state and untestable; UTC from an injected clock is explicit and testable.
DateTime vs DateTimeOffset?
DateTimeOffset carries the UTC offset, so the instant is unambiguous; prefer it for stored timestamps.
p10-19.y: TimeProvider, added in .NET 8, is an abstraction for the current time and timers. Instead of calling DateTime.UtcNow directly, I inject TimeProvider, so in tests I can use a fake time provider and move time forward. That makes things like token expiry, retry delays and scheduled jobs easy to test without waiting.

p10-20.q: Polly is the standard .NET resilience library; version 8 composes strategies (retry, circuit breaker, timeout, rate limiter, fallback, hedging) into a `ResiliencePipeline`. In .NET 8, `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` wires Polly into IHttpClientFactory, and `AddStandardResilienceHandler()` gives a recommended stack in one line.
i: Standard handler order (outer to inner): rate limiter, total request timeout (30 seconds), retry (3 attempts, exponential backoff with jitter), circuit breaker, per-attempt timeout (10 seconds). All values are configurable.
Retry only transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, 408, 429) and idempotent operations; respect `Retry-After`; never retry 400/401/403.
Circuit breaker: after a failure ratio within a sampling window it opens and fails fast, giving the dependency time to recover, then half-opens to test.
Hedging (`AddStandardHedgingHandler`) sends a parallel request after a delay to cut tail latency, only for safe reads.
Polly also works outside HTTP: `ResiliencePipelineBuilder` around SFTP, database or SDK calls; inject `TimeProvider` to test delays.
Telemetry: Polly v8 emits metrics and logs for retries and circuit state; alert when the breaker opens.
In IRT: the SFTP base class retries [3 times with backoff and jitter] on timeouts and connection resets, and typed HttpClients to vendor APIs use the standard handler.
f: Why jitter?
Without randomness all clients retry at the same moment and create synchronised spikes (thundering herd).
Circuit breaker vs retry?
Retry handles short blips; the breaker stops calling a dependency that is clearly down, protecting both sides.
p10-20.y: In .NET 8, I add resilience to HTTP calls with the Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience package, which is built on Polly. AddStandardResilienceHandler gives sensible defaults in one line: a total timeout, retries with backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker and a per-attempt timeout. I can also build custom pipelines. We use it for vendor API calls so temporary failures recover on their own.
p10-20.k: resilience, polly, retry, circuit breaker, timeout, addstandardresiliencehandler, .net 8

p1-1.q: .NET Framework is the original Windows-only runtime (last version 4.8.1, maintenance only). .NET Core was the cross-platform, open-source rewrite, and from .NET 5 it is simply ".NET": even-numbered releases (.NET 6, 8, 10) are LTS with 3 years of support, odd ones are STS with 2 years (since .NET 9).
i: Runtime model: .NET Framework is installed machine-wide and tied to Windows and IIS; modern .NET can be self-contained per app, runs on Linux containers and is side-by-side versioned.
Missing in modern .NET: WCF server (use CoreWCF or gRPC), Web Forms, AppDomains, .NET Remoting; that is why migrations need redesign in places.
Performance: every release brings big runtime and JIT wins (tiered compilation, Dynamic PGO on by default in .NET 8, faster GC); upgrading is often the cheapest performance fix.
Support dates: .NET 8 support ends November 2026, .NET 10 (November 2025) is supported until November 2028; in a GxP product staying on a supported runtime is a compliance requirement.
My experience: SharePoint and .NET Framework at DXC, ASP.NET Core on .NET 6 and 8 at IQVIA, and I upgraded [3] IRT services to .NET 10.
c:
<!-- the upgrade itself is mostly this line, plus packages and Docker images -->
<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
f: What is .NET Standard?
A shared API contract for libraries targeting both .NET Framework and .NET Core; for new libraries target net8.0 or net10.0 directly.
LTS vs STS?
LTS gets 3 years of support, STS 2 years (from .NET 9); regulated products stick to LTS.
p1-1.y: .NET Framework is the old Windows-only version, and it now only gets fixes. .NET Core started as the cross-platform, open-source rewrite, and from .NET 5 onwards it is simply called .NET. Versions like .NET 6, 8 and 10 are long-term support releases with three years of support. In my project I moved our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10 so we stay on a supported runtime and get the performance gains.

p1-2.q: Value types (struct, enum, int, DateTime) hold their data directly and are copied on assignment; reference types (class, string, arrays, delegates) hold a reference to an object on the managed heap, so copies share the same object. Where they live depends on context: locals of value type usually sit on the stack, but a value-type field of a class lives inside that object on the heap.
i: Boxing: converting a value type to object or an interface allocates a heap copy; avoid in hot paths (non-generic collections, string.Format with ints in old code).

Equality: value types compare field by field (ValueType.Equals uses reflection unless overridden, so implement IEquatable<T>); reference types compare identity unless overridden; records give value equality for classes.
Nullability: value types need Nullable<T> (int?) to be null; reference types can be null, and nullable reference types (C# 8) warn you at compile time.
Passing: both are passed by value by default, but for a reference type the reference is copied, so the method can mutate the same object; ref/out/in pass by reference.
Guideline: make structs small (16 bytes or so) and immutable (readonly struct), otherwise copies cost more than allocations.
f: Is string a value type?
No, it is a reference type with value-like behaviour: immutable and compared by value with ==.
Are value types always on the stack?
No; that is a common myth. They live wherever their container lives, e.g. inside a class on the heap.
p1-2.y: A value type holds its data directly, like int, bool or a struct, and it is copied when you assign it. A reference type, like a class or string, holds a reference to an object on the heap, so two variables can point to the same object. Value types are good for small, short-lived data. I use structs for small immutable values and classes for business objects.

p1-3.q: The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. At each await on an unfinished task it saves the method's state, returns an incomplete Task to the caller and frees the thread; when the awaited operation completes, a continuation resumes the method from where it stopped, possibly on another thread.
i: Nothing is "running" during I/O: an async database or HTTP call holds no thread while waiting; that is why async scales ASP.NET Core under load.
The awaiter pattern: await works on anything with GetAwaiter() (IsCompleted, OnCompleted, GetResult); if the task already completed, execution continues synchronously without a context switch.
Context: in UI apps the continuation returns to the captured SynchronizationContext; ASP.NET Core has none, so ConfigureAwait(false) matters mainly in libraries.
Exceptions are stored in the Task and re-thrown at await; async void methods cannot be awaited and crash the process on exceptions, so only use them for event handlers.
Pitfalls: .Result or .Wait() (sync-over-async) blocks a thread and can deadlock with a context; CPU-bound work does not become faster with async, use Task.Run only to offload from a UI thread.
In IRT every API call to SQL Server, SFTP and RabbitMQ is async with CancellationToken from HttpContext.RequestAborted, so abandoned requests stop work early.
f: Does async make code faster?
Not a single request; it improves throughput and scalability because threads are not blocked during I/O.
What does the state machine contain?
The method's locals, the current state number and the awaiters, stored in a struct that is boxed to the heap only if the method actually suspends.
p1-3.y: When I await a task, the method does not block the thread. The compiler turns the method into a state machine, the thread goes back to the pool, and when the work finishes the method continues from where it stopped. This lets one server handle many more requests. In our APIs every database and HTTP call is async, so threads are free while we wait for SQL Server.
p1-3.k: state machine, thread pool, non-blocking, task

p1-4.q: A Thread is an OS thread you manage directly; a Task is a promise of a future result that usually runs on thread-pool threads or represents pure I/O with no thread at all. ValueTask<T> is a struct alternative to Task<T> that avoids an allocation when the result is often available synchronously.
i: Prefer Task for almost everything; create raw threads only for special long-running, dedicated work (or use TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning).
Task.Run queues CPU work to the thread pool; never use it to "make" I/O async in ASP.NET Core, it just burns a pool thread.

ValueTask rules: await it only once, never await it concurrently, never call .Result before it completes; convert with .AsTask() if you need more. Use it for hot paths that are usually synchronous (cache hits).
Task.WhenAll for parallel independent I/O; Parallel.ForEachAsync (.NET 6) for bounded parallel loops with MaxDegreeOfParallelism.
Thread-pool starvation shows as rising latency with low CPU; causes are sync-over-async and blocking calls.
c:
public ValueTask<StudyConfig> GetConfigAsync(Guid id) =>
    _cache.TryGetValue(id, out StudyConfig? c) ? ValueTask.FromResult(c!) : new(LoadAndCacheAsync(id));
f: When would you use a dedicated Thread?
Rarely: e.g. a long-running loop that must not occupy a pool thread, or code needing a specific apartment state; BackgroundService covers most cases.
Task.WhenAll vs awaiting in a loop?
WhenAll starts all operations together and waits once; a loop awaits them one by one.
p1-4.y: A Thread is an actual operating system thread, which is expensive. A Task represents work that will finish in future, usually running on the thread pool, and it is what we use with async and await. ValueTask is a lighter version for methods that often finish immediately, like a cache hit, to avoid allocations. In my day-to-day code I use Task, and ValueTask only in hot paths.
p1-4.k: thread pool, valuetask, task parallel library

p1-5.q: IEnumerable<T> is an in-memory, forward-only sequence evaluated with LINQ-to-Objects in your process; IQueryable<T> holds an expression tree that a provider such as EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; List<T> is a concrete, materialised collection already in memory.
i: The crucial difference: filtering an IQueryable adds a WHERE to SQL, while filtering after converting to IEnumerable (AsEnumerable or ToList) pulls every row into memory first.
IQueryable methods take Expression<Func<T,bool>>; IEnumerable methods take Func<T,bool> delegates, so custom C# methods work there but not in SQL.
Return types: repositories returning IQueryable leak query logic to callers; returning IEnumerable from a materialised list hides the cost; returning IReadOnlyList<T> is explicit.
Multiple enumeration: an IEnumerable from a query or yield runs again each time you enumerate it; materialise once with ToList when you need it twice.
In IRT the shipment list query stays IQueryable until paging and projection, so SQL Server returns only [50] rows of the DTO columns.
c:
IQueryable<Shipment> q = _db.Shipments.Where(s => s.StudyId == id);   // nothing executed yet
var page = await q.OrderBy(s => s.ShipmentDate).Skip(0).Take(50)
                  .Select(s => new ShipmentRow(s.Id, s.Status)).ToListAsync(ct); // one SQL query
var bad = _db.Shipments.AsEnumerable().Where(s => s.StudyId == id);   // loads the whole table!
f: What is an expression tree?
Code represented as data (Expression<T>) that a provider can inspect and translate, e.g. into SQL.
IEnumerable vs ICollection vs IList?
IEnumerable only iterates; ICollection adds Count/Add/Remove; IList adds index access.
p1-5.y: IEnumerable works on data in memory and filters it in C#. IQueryable builds an expression that the provider, like EF Core, turns into SQL, so filtering happens in the database. List is a concrete in-memory collection that is already loaded. So I keep queries as IQueryable until I have added filters and paging, and only then call ToListAsync, which avoids pulling whole tables into memory.
p1-5.k: linq, deferred execution, ef core, list

p1-6.q: An abstract class is a partially implemented base type that can hold state, constructors and shared code, and a class can inherit only one; an interface is a contract that a class or struct can implement many of. Since C# 8 interfaces can have default implementations and static members, but still no instance fields or constructors.
i: Use an interface for capabilities and seams for DI and testing (ISftpClient, IClock); use an abstract class to share real code and enforce a template (SftpClientBase with retry and logging).
Template Method pattern: the abstract base defines the algorithm and calls abstract or virtual steps; that is how our SFTP base class wraps every provider call with retry, logging and error mapping.
Versioning: adding a member to an interface breaks implementers unless it has a default implementation; adding a virtual method to a base class does not.
Combine them: interface for consumers, abstract base for implementers (ISftpClient + SftpClientBase).
Static abstract interface members (C# 11) enable generic math and factory patterns.
f: Can an abstract class implement an interface?
Yes, and it may leave members abstract for subclasses to implement.
When do default interface methods make sense?
Evolving a public interface without breaking existing implementers.
p1-6.y: An interface is a contract that says what a class can do, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class can hold shared code and state, but a class can inherit only one. I use interfaces for dependencies, so I can swap implementations and mock them in tests. For example, all our SFTP libraries sit behind one ISftpClient interface, and I used an abstract base class for the shared retry logic.

p1-7.q: SOLID is five design principles that keep code easy to change: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation and Dependency inversion. I can show each one in my SFTP integration and CSV import work.
i: S: the CSV import is split into parser, validator and importer classes, so a new validation rule never touches parsing code and each piece has focused unit tests.
O: adding Rebex meant one new ISftpClient class plus configuration; no caller or switch statement changed.

L: every provider honours the same contract (same exceptions mapped to SftpException, same behaviour on missing files), so swapping one for another cannot break callers; violating it would be a provider that silently ignores overwrite flags.
I: reporting code depends on a small IShipmentReader, not a large repository with write methods, so read services cannot write by accident.
D: high-level services depend on abstractions registered in ASP.NET Core DI; tests inject fakes and Moq mocks.
Balance: SOLID is a tool, not a goal; I avoid interfaces with exactly one implementation unless they are a test seam or a boundary.
f: Which principle is broken most often?
Single responsibility: services grow into god classes; I split by reason to change.
What is the difference between DI and DIP?
DIP is the design principle (depend on abstractions); DI is the technique that supplies those abstractions at runtime.
p1-7.y: SOLID is five principles that keep code easy to change. Single responsibility means one reason to change, open-closed means extend without editing, Liskov means a child class must work wherever the parent works, interface segregation means small focused interfaces, and dependency inversion means depending on abstractions. In my SFTP integration, each vendor library implements one interface, so adding a new library did not touch the business code.
p1-7.k: single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion, design principles

p1-8.q: In production I have used Strategy and Adapter (SFTP providers behind one interface), Factory (choosing a provider by configuration), Decorator (adding retry and logging around clients), Repository/Unit of Work over EF Core in some services, Options and Singleton through DI, Observer/pub-sub via Kafka and RabbitMQ, plus Outbox and Retry for messaging.
i: Strategy: the algorithm (SFTP provider) is chosen at runtime; Adapter: each provider wraps a third-party API (Rebex, SSH.NET) into our ISftpClient.
Factory: SftpClientFactory reads the vendor's configured provider; with .NET 8 keyed services this is a one-liner.
Decorator: wrap an interface to add behaviour without changing it, e.g. a caching or retry decorator registered with Scrutor's Decorate.
Mediator (MediatR) and CQRS: separate commands and queries in larger services; useful but I avoid it in small ones to keep code simple.
Outbox: save the business change and the event in one transaction, then publish, so events are never lost when the broker is down.
I name patterns only when they clarify intent; the goal is simpler code, not pattern count.
f: Strategy vs Factory?
Strategy is the interchangeable behaviour; the factory decides which strategy instance to create.
A pattern you regret using?
Generic repositories on top of EF Core: they hid useful EF features and added code without value.
p1-8.y: In production I have used Strategy and Adapter to put different SFTP libraries behind one interface, and a Factory to pick the library from configuration. I used Decorator to add retry and logging around clients without changing them. With messaging I used the Outbox pattern so events are not lost, and publish-subscribe with Kafka and RabbitMQ. I pick a pattern only when it solves a real problem.
p1-8.k: design patterns, strategy, adapter, factory, decorator, outbox, singleton, repository

p1-9.q: .NET uses a generational, compacting, tracing garbage collector: it finds objects no longer reachable from roots (statics, stack, registers, handles), frees them and compacts the heap. New objects go into generation 0, survivors are promoted to 1 and 2, and large objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the Large Object Heap.
i: Generations work because most objects die young; gen 0 collections are cheap, gen 2 (full) collections are expensive.
Server GC (default in ASP.NET Core) uses a heap and GC thread per core for throughput; workstation GC suits desktop; concurrent/background GC reduces pauses.
LOH is not compacted by default, so repeated large allocations fragment memory; rent buffers from ArrayPool<T> instead.
Containers: the GC respects container memory limits; .NET 8 adds DATAS (dynamic adaptation of server GC heaps, default in .NET 9) for lower memory in small containers.
Finalizers delay collection by a cycle; implement IDisposable for deterministic cleanup and use SafeHandle instead of finalizers.
Diagnose with dotnet-counters (gc-heap-size, gen-2 count, % time in GC) and dotnet-gcdump; I used them for [a memory growth issue caused by an unbounded static cache].
f: What causes memory leaks in .NET?
Objects kept reachable: static collections, event handlers not unsubscribed, caches without limits, captured closures.
Should you call GC.Collect()?
Almost never; it disrupts the GC's tuning. Fix the allocation pattern instead.
p1-9.y: The garbage collector frees memory for objects that are no longer used. It divides objects into generations: new objects are in generation 0 and cleaned up often, while long-lived objects move to generation 1 and 2 and are checked less often. Large objects go on a separate heap. Most of the time I don't touch it, but I dispose resources properly, and once I fixed a memory leak caused by event handlers holding objects alive.
p1-9.k: gc, memory, generations, dispose, large object heap

p1-10.q: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method; Func<> and Action<> are built-in generic delegates (Func returns a value, Action returns void); a lambda is concise syntax for creating a delegate or an expression tree; an event is a delegate wrapped so outsiders can only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=), not invoke or overwrite it.
i: Multicast: delegates can hold several methods; invoking runs them in order, and only the last return value is kept.
Closures: lambdas capture variables, not values; capturing a loop variable or a large object can surprise you or keep it alive longer.
Lambdas become Expression<Func<...>> when the target type asks for it; that is how EF Core reads your Where clause.
Event pattern: EventHandler<TEventArgs>, raise with `Handler?.Invoke(this, args)`; unsubscribe to avoid leaks when the publisher outlives the subscriber.
In ASP.NET Core, middleware is literally a chain of RequestDelegate instances, and Polly policies take Func<CancellationToken, Task> delegates.
f: Why use events instead of public delegates?
Events stop outside code from invoking the delegate or replacing all subscribers with =.
Func vs Predicate?
Predicate<T> is an older delegate equal to Func<T,bool>; LINQ uses Func.
p1-10.y: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. Func and Action are built-in delegates: Func returns a value and Action returns nothing. A lambda is a short way to write the method inline, and an event is a delegate that others can subscribe to but only the owner can raise. I use lambdas every day in LINQ and in minimal API endpoints.
p1-10.k: delegate, func, action, lambda, event, callback

p1-11.q: LINQ queries are not executed when you write them, only when you enumerate them (foreach, ToList, Count, First). The query is a recipe; each enumeration runs it again against the current data.
i: Deferred operators: Where, Select, OrderBy, Skip, Take; immediate operators: ToList, ToArray, Count, Sum, First, Any.
For IQueryable the whole chain is translated to one SQL statement at enumeration, so you can compose filters conditionally before executing.
Multiple enumeration pitfall: enumerating twice runs the database query or the yield iterator twice; analyzers warn about it.
Captured variables are read at execution time, not when the query was defined.
Exceptions inside the query appear at enumeration time, which can be far from the line that built it.
I use this for dynamic filters in IRT list endpoints: add Where clauses only for the parameters the user supplied, then page and execute once.
f: How do you force execution?
Call ToList/ToArray (or an aggregate) to materialise the results once.
Is deferred execution good or bad?
Good for composition and efficiency; risky when it causes repeated or late execution.
p1-11.y: Deferred execution means a LINQ query does not run when you write it. It runs only when you loop over it or call something like ToList or Count. The good part is you can keep adding filters before it runs. The risk is running the same query twice by accident, so when I need the result more than once, I call ToList once and reuse it.

p1-12.q: Code is thread-safe when concurrent callers cannot corrupt shared state. The best way is to avoid shared mutable state (immutability, local variables, scoped services); when sharing is needed, use the right primitive: lock, SemaphoreSlim for async code, Interlocked for counters, and concurrent collections.
i: lock (Monitor) for short synchronous critical sections; you cannot await inside a lock, so use SemaphoreSlim(1,1) with WaitAsync for async sections.
Interlocked.Increment and CompareExchange for lock-free counters and flags.
ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd can run the factory more than once; wrap the value in Lazy<T> if the factory must run exactly once.
Immutable records and ImmutableArray make sharing safe by design; .NET 8 adds FrozenDictionary for fast read-only lookups.
DI: singletons are shared by all requests, so they must be thread-safe; DbContext is not thread-safe, so never share it across concurrent tasks.
Across instances (several ECS tasks) in-process locks do nothing; use database locks, optimistic concurrency or a distributed lock. Our study transfer guard uses a lock row inside a transaction.
f: lock vs Monitor vs Mutex?
lock is syntax for Monitor (in-process, fast); Mutex can be cross-process and is slower. .NET 9 adds System.Threading.Lock as a dedicated lock type.
What is a race condition?
The result depends on timing between threads, e.g. two requests reading and writing the same counter.
p1-12.y: To make code thread-safe, first I avoid shared state where possible, by keeping services stateless and using immutable objects. When sharing is needed, I use concurrent collections like ConcurrentDictionary, the lock statement for small critical sections, and SemaphoreSlim for async code because you cannot await inside a lock. For example, our CSV import used a lock row in the database so two users could not import the same study at once.
p1-12.k: thread safety, lock, concurrency, race condition, semaphoreslim, concurrentdictionary

p1-13.q: A class is a reference type with identity; a struct is a value type copied by value; a record is a type (record class by default, or record struct) with compiler-generated value-based equality, ToString, deconstruction and non-destructive mutation through `with`.
i: Records are ideal for DTOs, messages and value objects: two ShipmentCreated events with the same data are equal.
Positional records (`record Kit(string Number, int SiteId)`) create init-only properties; `with` makes a copy with changes.
Equality includes the runtime type (EqualityContract), so a derived record never equals its base record.
record struct (C# 10) gives value-type records; readonly record struct makes them immutable.
EF Core entities should usually be classes with identity, not records, because value equality confuses change tracking.
Structs: small, short-lived, immutable values (coordinates, money); large or mutable structs cause copying bugs and costs.
f: Are records immutable?
Positional records have init-only properties, but you can add mutable properties, and referenced objects (lists) can still change.
Why not records for EF entities?
Entities need stable identity and tracked mutation; value equality and with-copies fight that.
p1-13.y: A class is a reference type with identity, so two objects with the same values are still different. A record is mainly for data: it compares by value, is easy to make immutable, and has a nice ToString and the with-expression for copies. A struct is a value type that is copied, best for small values. I use records for DTOs and events, and classes for services and entities.
p1-13.k: record, class, struct, immutable, value equality, dto

p1-14.q: Catch exceptions only where you can handle them meaningfully, let the rest bubble to one global handler that logs and returns ProblemDetails, and never swallow them silently. Use specific exception types, preserve stack traces with `throw;`, and do not use exceptions for normal control flow.
i: `throw;` keeps the original stack trace, `throw ex;` resets it; wrap with an inner exception when adding context.
Exception filters (`catch (SqlException ex) when (ex.Number == 1205)`) catch only matching cases without unwinding the stack first, which helps debugging.
Use finally or using/await using for cleanup; IAsyncDisposable for async resources.
Expected outcomes (validation, not found) are often clearer as results or specific domain exceptions mapped to 400/404/409 centrally.
Cancellation: let OperationCanceledException flow when the request is aborted; do not log it as an error.
Logging: log once, at the boundary, with structured context (ids), not at every layer; never expose stack traces to clients.
f: Why not catch (Exception) everywhere?
It hides bugs and leaves state inconsistent; only boundaries (global handler, background loops) should catch everything.
Exceptions vs error codes?
Exceptions for exceptional failures; results for expected business outcomes.
p1-14.y: My rules are simple: catch an exception only where I can actually handle it, otherwise let it bubble up to one global handler. I never swallow exceptions, I log them once with context, and I return a clean ProblemDetails response without exposing stack traces. I use specific exception types and avoid using exceptions for normal flow. In our APIs, one exception handler converts all errors into consistent responses.
p1-14.k: exception handling, try catch, problemdetails, global error handler, logging

p1-15.q: Generics let you write type-safe, reusable code parameterised by type, such as List<T> or Result<T>, without casting or boxing. Constraints (`where T : class, new(), IEntity`) tell the compiler what T can do, so you can call members on it safely.
i: Performance: generics over value types get specialised code, so List<int> does not box like ArrayList.
Constraints: class, struct, notnull, unmanaged, new(), base class, interface, and in C# 11 static abstract interface members for generic math.
Variance: `out T` (covariance) on IEnumerable<out T> lets IEnumerable<string> be used as IEnumerable<object>; `in T` (contravariance) on Action<in T>.
Generic methods with inference keep call sites clean: `Map<TSource, TDest>()`.
Open generic DI registration: `services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));`.
Used in IRT for [a Result<T> type returned by validation services and a generic paged response PagedResult<T>].
f: What is covariance?
Using a more derived type argument where a less derived one is expected, allowed for out-only positions.
Generics in C# vs Java?
C# generics are reified at runtime (real types per instantiation); Java uses type erasure.
p1-15.y: Generics let me write code once and use it with any type while keeping type safety, so no casting and no boxing. Constraints like where T is a class or has a parameterless constructor tell the compiler what the type can do. For example, I wrote a generic paged result type and a generic repository method, so every list API returns pages in the same way.
p1-15.k: generics, constraints, type safety, where t

p1-16.q: For backend services, .NET 8 (LTS) brought big performance gains, native AOT for ASP.NET Core, TimeProvider, keyed DI services, IExceptionHandler, built-in Identity API endpoints, better metrics and the resilience libraries. .NET 10 (LTS, November 2025) adds C# 14, further JIT and GC improvements, built-in minimal API validation, OpenAPI 3.1 and more AOT work.
i: Performance: Dynamic PGO on by default in .NET 8, faster JSON, Kestrel and LINQ; most services get faster just by upgrading.
Native AOT: small, fast-starting binaries for minimal APIs and Lambda; limits on reflection and EF Core.
Developer productivity: primary constructors (C# 12), collection expressions, keyed services, FrozenDictionary, TimeProvider for testable time.
Observability: built-in metrics with System.Diagnostics.Metrics and OpenTelemetry-friendly meters; .NET Aspire for local orchestration and dashboards.
.NET 9 (STS) in between: HybridCache, built-in OpenAPI document generation (Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi), DATAS GC by default.
In IRT we moved from .NET 8 to 10 before .NET 8 support ends (November 2026) and saw [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency.
f: Which C# 14 feature do you like?
Extension members (extension properties and static extension members) and the field keyword for properties.
Why stay on LTS?
Longer support and fewer upgrades, which matters when every upgrade needs validation in a regulated product.
p1-16.y: For backend services, .NET 8 brought Native AOT for APIs, keyed services in dependency injection, TimeProvider for testable time, built-in resilience handlers, and IExceptionHandler. .NET 10 is the next LTS with C# 14 and more performance improvements. When I upgraded [3] services to .NET 10 in [early 2026], we saw about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency without code changes.
p1-16.k: .net 8, .net 10, new features, keyed services, native aot, timeprovider, c# 14

p1-17.q: The pipeline is the ordered chain of middleware that every HTTP request passes through in ASP.NET Core: Kestrel receives the request, builds an HttpContext, and each middleware can act before and after calling the next one until an endpoint produces the response, which then flows back out in reverse. See Part 10 for standalone deep answers on middleware and custom middleware.
i: Recommended order: exception handler, HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, custom middleware (rate limiting, correlation id), endpoints.
Routing is split in two: UseRouting selects the endpoint early so later middleware (CORS, auth) can read its metadata; the endpoint executes at the end.
Branching: Map (by path), MapWhen (by predicate, separate branch), UseWhen (conditional middleware that rejoins).
Short-circuit: any middleware can end the request; .NET 8 adds `.ShortCircuit()` on endpoints such as /health to skip the rest of the pipeline.
Cost: every middleware runs for every request, so keep them fast and async.
In IRT the order is exception handler, correlation id, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, controllers.
f: Where does Kestrel fit?
Kestrel is the server underneath; it accepts connections and hands each request to the pipeline.
What does app.Run do at the end of Program.cs?
Starts the host and blocks until shutdown; Run(delegate) in the pipeline is different: a terminal middleware.
p1-17.y: The middleware pipeline is a chain of components that every HTTP request passes through, in the order they are registered in Program.cs. Each middleware can do something before calling the next one and something after, or stop the request early. The order matters a lot: exception handling first, then HTTPS, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, and finally the endpoints. In my project I added a correlation-id middleware so every log line could be traced across services.
p1-17.k: middleware, request pipeline, request delegate, use, run, ordering

p1-18.q: DI lifetimes define how long a service instance lives: Singleton is one instance for the whole application, Scoped is one per request (per DI scope), Transient is a new instance every time it is resolved. Choose by state and thread safety: stateless or thread-safe shared things as singletons, per-request things like DbContext as scoped, lightweight stateless helpers as transient.
i: Captive dependency: a singleton must not depend on scoped or transient services that hold state, or it keeps them forever; ValidateScopes catches this in Development.
Background code has no request scope: create one with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() (or CreateAsyncScope) per unit of work.
Disposal: the container disposes services it created when their scope ends; do not dispose injected services yourself.
Transient IDisposable services resolved from the root provider are kept until app shutdown, a hidden leak.
.NET 8 keyed services let one interface have several named registrations.
In IRT: DbContext scoped, HttpClient typed clients transient via IHttpClientFactory, SFTP provider factory and caches singleton.
f: What is ValidateOnBuild?
It checks at startup that every registered service can be constructed, catching missing registrations early.
Is HttpClient a singleton?
Use IHttpClientFactory or one long-lived client with PooledConnectionLifetime, not new HttpClient per call.
p1-18.y: Singleton means one instance for the whole application. Scoped means one instance per HTTP request, which is right for DbContext. Transient means a new instance every time it is asked for. The key rule is that a longer-lived service must not depend on a shorter-lived one, for example a singleton holding a scoped DbContext, because that causes threading bugs. In our services, DbContext and repositories are scoped and stateless helpers are singletons.
p1-18.k: di, dependency injection, lifetimes, singleton, scoped, transient, captive dependency

p1-19.q: Controllers group actions in classes with attributes, filters, model binding conventions and [ApiController] behaviour; Minimal APIs map routes directly to lambdas or methods with less ceremony and slightly better performance. Both share routing, DI, auth and OpenAPI, so the choice is about structure and team preference.
i: Controllers: mature conventions, action filters, model validation automatically, great for large APIs and teams used to MVC.
Minimal APIs: route groups, endpoint filters, TypedResults, native AOT support; ideal for small services, Lambda and new code.
Validation: automatic in controllers with [ApiController]; .NET 10 adds built-in validation to minimal APIs (AddValidation).
Testing: both via WebApplicationFactory; minimal handlers can be unit-tested as static methods.
Mixing is fine: one app can have controllers and minimal endpoints.
IRT uses controllers; for [the Node log summariser's .NET replacement prototype] I would use minimal APIs.
f: Which is faster?
Minimal APIs have less overhead, but the difference rarely matters compared with database calls.
How do you organise many minimal endpoints?
MapGroup per feature and one extension method per feature file.
p1-19.y: Controllers are the classic MVC way: classes with actions, filters and attribute routing, good for large APIs. Minimal APIs map endpoints directly in Program.cs with lambdas, with less ceremony and slightly better performance. Both share the same routing, DI and middleware.
