I use controllers for our larger domain APIs and minimal APIs for small services and health or internal endpoints.
p1-19.k: minimal api, controllers, mvc, endpoints, routing

p1-20.q: Program.cs builds and runs the app with the minimal hosting model: WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up configuration (appsettings, environment variables, secrets), logging and the DI container; you register services; builder.Build() creates the app; then you configure the middleware pipeline and endpoints; app.Run() starts Kestrel and blocks until shutdown.
i: Configuration sources load in order, later ones override: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development), environment variables, command line.
Services must be registered before Build(); after Build the container is read-only.
Hosted services start before Kestrel starts listening (in registration order); .NET 8 adds IHostedLifecycleService hooks.
Startup validation: ValidateOnStart for options and ValidateOnBuild for DI make misconfiguration fail fast at deployment.
Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM triggers IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping, then hosted services' StopAsync within ShutdownTimeout.
Startup.cs (ConfigureServices/Configure) still works but is no longer the template.
f: Where would you put startup tasks like migrations?
Not in app startup for regulated releases; we run migration scripts as a controlled release step.
What happens if configuration is invalid?
With ValidateOnStart the app fails to start and the health check fails the deployment instead of failing at runtime.
p1-20.y: In Program.cs, first the builder is created, which loads configuration from appsettings, environment variables and secrets, and sets up logging. Then I register services in the DI container. Then app is built, and I add middleware in the right order and map the endpoints. Finally app.Run starts the Kestrel server. Since .NET 6 there is no separate Startup class, everything is in this one file.
p1-20.k: program.cs, startup, host, builder, configuration, kestrel

p1-21.q: Middleware runs for every request at the HTTP level and knows nothing about MVC; filters run only inside the MVC (or endpoint) pipeline around a selected action, so they can see action arguments, model state and the action result. Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns and filters for action-specific concerns.
i: Middleware examples: exception handling, correlation id, CORS, authentication, rate limiting, response compression.
Filter examples: validation, auditing an action's arguments, a "study not locked" rule, caching a result, transforming results.
Ordering: middleware order is Program.cs order; filters run authorization, resource, action, exception, result, ordered by scope and Order.
Global exception handling belongs in middleware, because exception filters miss errors from other middleware and result execution.
Minimal APIs use endpoint filters, the filter equivalent.
Detailed filter answer and code: see Part 10 "MVC filter types".
f: Can middleware read the selected endpoint?
Yes, after UseRouting via context.GetEndpoint(), including its metadata (attributes).
Can a filter short-circuit?
Yes, by setting context.Result in an authorization, resource or action filter.
p1-21.y: Middleware runs for every request, early in the pipeline, and only knows about the HTTP context. Filters run inside MVC, around a specific controller action, so they know which action is being called and can see the model binding results. So I use middleware for cross-cutting things like correlation ids, logging and exception handling, and filters for action-specific things like validation or an audit attribute on certain endpoints.
p1-21.k: filters, middleware, action filter, mvc pipeline, cross-cutting

p1-22.q: Model binding converts HTTP data (route values, query string, headers, form, JSON body) into action parameters and objects; validation then checks them against rules (DataAnnotations or FluentValidation) and fills ModelState. With [ApiController], invalid models automatically return a 400 ValidationProblemDetails before your action runs.
i: Sources: [FromRoute], [FromQuery], [FromBody] (one per action, read by System.Text.Json input formatter), [FromHeader], [FromForm], [FromServices]; [ApiController] infers most of them.
Complex types from the body are deserialised once; the body stream is not rewindable by default (EnableBuffering if middleware must read it).
Validation attributes: [Required], [Range], [StringLength], [RegularExpression]; IValidatableObject for cross-field rules; FluentValidation for complex rules and better testability.
Over-posting: bind to request DTOs, never directly to EF entities.
Custom binders (IModelBinder) for special formats; TypeConverter or TryParse for simple custom types in minimal APIs.
In IRT request DTOs validate format, while business rules (site active, depot valid) run in the service layer and return 409/422.
f: Why is required validation on a non-nullable value type tricky?
A missing Guid binds to Guid.Empty; use Guid? with [Required] or validate explicitly.
FluentValidation vs DataAnnotations?
FluentValidation keeps rules in testable classes and handles complex conditional rules better.
p1-22.y: Model binding takes data from the route, query string, headers and body and converts it into my action parameters. Then validation runs using data annotations or FluentValidation. With the ApiController attribute, if the model is invalid, ASP.NET Core automatically returns a 400 with the errors. In our CSV import API, I validated each row and returned errors with row and column numbers so users could fix the file easily.
p1-22.k: model binding, validation, data annotations, fluentvalidation, apicontroller, 400

p1-23.q: Global exception handling catches every unhandled exception in one place, logs it with context, and returns a consistent error response (ProblemDetails) instead of leaking stack traces. In .NET 8 I use UseExceptionHandler with IExceptionHandler implementations and AddProblemDetails; Part 10 has the detailed IExceptionHandler answer with code.
i: Map exception types to status codes centrally: validation 400, not found 404, conflict 409, everything else 500.
Include a traceId or correlation id in the response so users can quote it to support.
Register the handler first in the pipeline; it only catches exceptions from later components.
Development shows the developer exception page; production shows a generic message.
Background services and message consumers need their own try/catch, the HTTP handler does not cover them.
Exceptions after the response has started cannot change the status code; the connection is aborted instead.
f: Why not try/catch in every controller?
Duplication and inconsistency; one handler gives one format and one logging policy.
How do you test it?
Integration test an endpoint that throws and assert the status and ProblemDetails body.
p1-23.y: I handle exceptions globally in one place instead of try-catch in every controller. In .NET 8 I use UseExceptionHandler with an IExceptionHandler class that logs the error with the correlation id and returns a standard ProblemDetails response. Known errors, like not found or validation, map to the right status code, and unknown errors return a 500 without internal details. This keeps every service's errors consistent.
p1-23.k: global exception handling, iexceptionhandler, problemdetails, useexceptionhandler, error handling

p1-24.q: REST models the API as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with standard HTTP methods, stateless requests and representations such as JSON. GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST and PATCH are not (by default).
i: Idempotent means repeating the same request leaves the server in the same state; safe means no state change at all (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created with Location, 202 Accepted for async jobs, 204 No Content, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 Conflict, 422, 429, 500, 503.
Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key header stored with the result.
Resource naming: plural nouns (/studies/{id}/sites), no verbs, filtering and paging with query parameters.
HATEOAS and Richardson maturity level 3 are rarely used in practice; consistent conventions and OpenAPI matter more.
Concurrency: ETags with If-Match return 412 on conflicting updates.
f: PUT vs PATCH?
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes some fields (JSON Patch or merge patch).
Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?
Yes; the state is the same (resource gone), even though the response differs.
p1-24.y: REST means treating things as resources with URLs and using HTTP verbs for actions: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to update part, and DELETE to remove. Idempotent means calling it many times gives the same result: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not. For POSTs that must not repeat, like creating a shipment, we use an idempotency key so a retry does not create duplicates.
p1-24.k: rest, http verbs, idempotency, get, post, put, patch, delete

p1-25.q: API versioning lets you evolve an API without breaking existing clients. Common approaches are URL segment (/api/v2/...), query string (?api-version=2.0), header (api-version or a media type); in ASP.NET Core the Asp.Versioning package handles routing, reporting and deprecation.
i: Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields) so most changes need no new version.
Breaking changes (renamed fields, changed semantics, removed endpoints) get a new major version, with the old one supported for an agreed period.
Report supported and deprecated versions in response headers (api-supported-versions) and announce sunset dates.
Keep versions in OpenAPI documents per version so clients see exactly what they get.
Version message contracts too (events on Kafka) with a schema version field.
In IRT vendor-facing APIs use URL versions because vendors' tools handle them easily.
f: Which approach do you prefer?
URL versioning for external clients (visible, cache-friendly); headers for internal APIs if the team prefers clean URLs.
How long do you keep old versions?
As long as agreed with clients, with usage metrics to see when traffic drops to zero.
p1-25.y: I version APIs so existing clients don't break when the contract changes. The common options are a version in the URL like /v1, a query string, or a header. I prefer URL versioning because it is clear and easy to test. Mostly I avoid new versions by making only backward-compatible changes, like adding optional fields, and I create v2 only for breaking changes, with a deprecation period for v1.
p1-25.k: api versioning, v1, v2, backward compatibility, breaking change

p1-26.q: ASP.NET Core configuration merges key-value pairs from providers (appsettings.json, environment-specific files, environment variables, user secrets, command line, Azure App Configuration, AWS Parameter Store) with later sources overriding earlier ones. The Options pattern binds sections to typed classes (IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T>, IOptionsMonitor<T>) with validation; Part 10 compares the three in depth.
i: Hierarchical keys use ":" in JSON and "__" in environment variables (Sftp__Vendors__DepotA__Host).
Secrets: user secrets locally, AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store in deployed environments; never commit them.
Validate with ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart so bad config stops the deployment.
Reloading works only with providers that support it (JSON files with reloadOnChange, App Configuration); use IOptionsMonitor to react.
Keep configuration per environment in IaC or variable groups, so environments differ by data, not by code.
f: Why bind to classes instead of IConfiguration["key"]?
Types, validation, IntelliSense and easy testing, with no magic strings scattered around.
How does ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT affect config?
It selects appsettings.{Environment}.json and enables Development-only features such as user secrets.
p1-26.y: Configuration in ASP.NET Core comes from layers: appsettings.json, environment-specific files, environment variables and secret stores, where later sources override earlier ones. The Options pattern binds a section to a strongly typed class, so I inject IOptions of that class instead of reading strings. I also validate options at startup, so a missing setting fails the deployment immediately instead of failing later in production.
p1-26.k: configuration, options pattern, ioptions, appsettings, environment variables, validateonstart

p1-27.q: I log with ILogger<T> using structured message templates, enrich every entry with a correlation id through logging scopes, and send JSON logs to a central store (CloudWatch Logs); for tracing I propagate the id (or W3C traceparent) across HTTP and messages so one request can be followed across services. Part 10 covers ILogger and structured logging in depth.
i: Three pillars: logs for details, metrics for trends and alerts, traces for the path and timing of a request across services.
OpenTelemetry in .NET: ActivitySource and Activity give spans; exporters send traces to X-Ray, Jaeger or Tempo; ASP.NET Core and HttpClient are instrumented automatically.
Log levels per category in configuration; avoid Information-level noise from framework namespaces.
Use LoggerMessage source generators on hot paths; never log secrets or patient data.
Metrics: request rate, errors, latency (p95/p99), queue depth; alert on SLOs, not on single errors.
In IRT: correlation-id middleware and a DelegatingHandler, JSON logs to CloudWatch, Grafana dashboards and alarms.
f: Logging vs tracing?
Logs record events; traces connect timed spans of one request across services.
What should every log entry contain?
Timestamp, level, service, environment, version, correlation id and the relevant business ids.
p1-27.y: I use structured logging with ILogger, so logs are key-value data, not just text, and they go to CloudWatch where we can query them. Every request gets a correlation id that is added to all logs and passed to other services, so I can follow one request end to end. For tracing and metrics we use OpenTelemetry and Grafana dashboards. This is how we find production issues quickly.
p1-27.k: logging, tracing, ilogger, structured logging, correlation id, opentelemetry, observability

p1-28.q: Measure first (Application Insights, CloudWatch, dotnet-counters, a profiler), then fix the biggest bottleneck, which is usually the database: efficient queries, indexes, projections, no N+1. Then use async I/O end to end, caching, response compression, pagination, pooling, and offload long work to background jobs.
i: EF Core: AsNoTracking, Select projections, split queries, compiled queries for hot paths, DbContext pooling.
Avoid sync-over-async and thread-pool starvation; pass CancellationToken.
Caching: output caching or HybridCache for reference data; HTTP caching headers for public data.
Payloads: pagination, smaller DTOs, System.Text.Json source generation, response compression (Brotli/Gzip) where CPU allows.
Platform: upgrading to .NET 8/10 gives free wins (Dynamic PGO); right-size containers and autoscale on latency or CPU.
Prove it: load test with k6 or JMeter before and after; my shipment list fix took [9 seconds to under 300 ms].
f: What is your first step with a slow endpoint?
Find where the time goes: trace spans or logs with durations, then the SQL plan if it is the database.
When does caching hurt?
When data must be consistent (kit allocation) or invalidation is unclear.
p1-28.y: First I measure, because guessing wastes time. Then I fix the biggest problems, which are usually in the database: missing indexes, N+1 queries, or loading too much data. I make calls async, add paging, use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, and cache data that rarely changes. For example, one shipment list query went from about [9 seconds to under 300 milliseconds] just by fixing the query and adding a covering index.
p1-28.k: performance, optimization, caching, async, asnotracking, paging, profiling

p1-29.q: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism that lets a server say which other origins may call it from JavaScript. The browser sends an Origin header (and a preflight OPTIONS request for non-simple calls), and the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-* headers; in ASP.NET Core you define named policies with AddCors and apply UseCors after UseRouting.
i: CORS is not security for your API: it only restricts browsers; curl, Postman and servers ignore it. Authentication and authorization protect the API.
Preflight happens for methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers (Authorization) or JSON content type; cache it with SetPreflightMaxAge.
AllowCredentials cannot be combined with AllowAnyOrigin; list exact origins.
Order: UseCors after UseRouting and before UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization so preflights are answered before auth rejects them.
In IRT the API allows only [the IRT UI origins per environment] from configuration.
f: Does CORS stop CSRF?
No; CSRF uses simple requests that may not need preflight. Use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.
Why does a preflight fail with 401?
The auth middleware ran before CORS or the OPTIONS request was not allowed; fix the order.
p1-29.y: CORS is a browser security rule that blocks a web page from calling an API on a different domain unless the API allows it. In ASP.NET Core I add a named policy with the exact allowed origins, methods and headers, and call UseCors in the right place in the pipeline. I never use allow-any-origin together with credentials. Our React app calls the APIs with a specific allowed origin per environment.
p1-29.k: cors, cross-origin, preflight, browser security, usecors

p1-30.q: I make service-to-service calls resilient with timeouts on every call, retries with exponential backoff and jitter only for transient failures, circuit breakers to fail fast when a dependency is down, idempotent operations so retries are safe, and fallbacks or asynchronous messaging where an immediate answer is not required. In .NET 8 this is Polly v8 through AddStandardResilienceHandler (Part 10 has the deep answer).
i: Timeouts: without them a slow dependency ties up threads and connections; set per-attempt and total timeouts.
Transient = timeouts, 5xx, 408, 429, connection resets; respect Retry-After.
Circuit breaker states: closed, open (fail fast), half-open (trial calls).
Bulkheads and concurrency limits isolate one slow dependency.
Idempotency keys make POST retries safe; consumers dedupe messages by id.
Observe it: metrics on retries and breaker state, alerts when a breaker opens.
f: What is a retry storm?
Many clients retrying aggressively at once, multiplying load on a struggling service; backoff, jitter and breakers prevent it.
Sync call or message?
If the caller does not need the answer now, publish a message and let the consumer retry independently.
p1-30.y: Network calls between services will fail sometimes, so I plan for it. I use IHttpClientFactory with resilience policies: a timeout on every call, retries with backoff for temporary errors, and a circuit breaker so we stop calling a service that is down. In .NET 8, AddStandardResilienceHandler gives this in one line. For work that doesn't need an immediate answer, I use messaging instead of HTTP.
p1-30.k: resilience, polly, retry, circuit breaker, timeout, httpclientfactory

p1-31.q: REST uses HTTP resources and JSON, simple and universal; SOAP (WCF) uses XML envelopes and a strict WSDL contract with WS-* standards; gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for fast, strongly typed service-to-service calls and streaming; GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint.
i: REST: best for public and browser APIs, caching, broad tooling; risk of over- or under-fetching.
SOAP: legacy enterprise integrations, WS-Security, transactions; heavy and verbose; CoreWCF helps migrate.
gRPC: binary, compact, contract-first .proto, bidirectional streaming, deadlines; limited browser support (gRPC-Web), harder to debug by hand.
GraphQL: flexible queries for many front ends, one round trip; needs care with N+1 resolvers (DataLoader), caching and query cost limits.
In IRT: REST for UI and vendors, legacy WCF endpoints in older areas, Kafka and RabbitMQ for async.
f: When would you pick gRPC?
Internal high-throughput service calls or streaming between services you control.
Why not GraphQL everywhere?
Extra complexity in caching, security and performance control that simple REST APIs do not need.
p1-31.y: REST uses HTTP and JSON and is the default for public and web APIs. SOAP, which WCF used, is XML with strict contracts, still found in older enterprise systems. gRPC uses HTTP/2 and binary Protobuf, so it is very fast for service-to-service calls. GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs. In my work we use REST, and I also maintained older WCF services.
p1-31.k: rest, soap, wcf, grpc, graphql, protocols

p1-32.q: Short background work uses hosted services (BackgroundService) with queues such as Channels; durable or scheduled work uses a message broker (RabbitMQ, SQS) or a scheduler (Hangfire, Quartz); long-running or heavy jobs run in separate worker services or Lambda. Never use fire-and-forget Task.Run inside a request. Part 10 covers BackgroundService in depth.
i: Request returns 202 Accepted with a job id, a worker processes it, and the client polls or gets notified.
Hosted services are singletons; create scopes for DbContext.
Graceful shutdown: honour the stopping token and finish or checkpoint work within the shutdown timeout.
Multiple instances run every hosted service; avoid duplicate work with queues or distributed locks.
In IRT: RabbitMQ consumers as BackgroundServices in worker containers, [an SFTP poller], and Ansible-driven deployment jobs outside the app.
f: Why not Task.Run in a controller?
The work is lost on shutdown or crash, exceptions vanish, and it has no retries or visibility.
Hangfire vs hosted service?
Hangfire adds persistence, retries, cron and a dashboard; a hosted service is a simple in-process loop.
p1-32.y: For background work I use a BackgroundService, which is a hosted service that runs a loop alongside the web app, using a scoped service for each unit of work. For queued work I use Channels or a message queue. For example, our SFTP poller runs [every 5 minutes] to pick up vendor files. For heavy or scheduled jobs that must survive restarts, a separate worker or a scheduler is better.
p1-32.k: background work, hosted service, backgroundservice, worker, channels, scheduler

p1-33.q: EF Core's change tracker keeps a snapshot of every entity it loads; on SaveChanges it compares current values with the snapshot (DetectChanges) and generates INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements for what changed. AsNoTracking skips the snapshot and identity resolution, so read-only queries are faster and use less memory.
i: Entity states: Detached, Added, Unchanged, Modified, Deleted; inspect with context.Entry(e).State or ChangeTracker.DebugView.
Identity resolution: a tracked context returns the same instance for the same key; AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution keeps that without tracking.
Updates only include changed columns, which reduces conflicts and log noise.
Long-lived contexts accumulate tracked entities and slow down; keep DbContext short-lived (per request).
Disconnected updates: attach and set state, or load then apply changes; for bulk changes use ExecuteUpdate which bypasses tracking entirely.
In IRT all GET endpoints use AsNoTracking with projections; writes load, modify and save.
f: Is tracking needed to update?
Not strictly; you can Attach and mark properties modified, or use ExecuteUpdate for set-based changes.
Can you make no-tracking the default?
Yes, UseQueryTrackingBehavior(QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking) on the context options.
p1-33.y: EF Core keeps a snapshot of every entity it loads, and when I call SaveChanges it compares and generates updates only for what changed. That is change tracking. It costs memory and time, so for read-only queries, like list screens and reports, I use AsNoTracking, which is faster. I keep tracking for data I am going to update.
p1-33.k: ef core, change tracking, asnotracking, savechanges, dbcontext

p1-34.q: Eager loading fetches related data in the same query with Include/ThenInclude; lazy loading fetches it automatically when you first access the navigation (needs proxies or ILazyLoader); explicit loading fetches it on demand with Entry(e).Collection(...).LoadAsync(). The N+1 problem is one query for the parents plus one more query per parent for its children, which is what lazy loading in a loop produces.
i: Detect N+1 by logging SQL or watching query counts in tests; it often hides behind serialisation of navigations.
Fix with Include, or better, a Select projection that pulls exactly the needed columns in one query.
Large Includes cause cartesian explosion; AsSplitQuery runs one query per collection instead.
Lazy loading is off by default in EF Core and I keep it off in APIs because it hides database calls.
Filtered Include (EF Core 5+): Include(s => s.Shipments.Where(x => x.Status == "Open")).
c:
var sites = await _db.Sites.AsNoTracking()
    .Where(s => s.StudyId == studyId)
    .Select(s => new { s.Name, Open = s.Shipments.Count(x => x.Status == "Open") })
    .ToListAsync(ct);   // one query, no N+1
f: Split query vs single query?
Split avoids duplicated rows for multiple collections but runs several round trips and can see inconsistent data without a transaction.
Why not lazy loading in APIs?
It triggers unpredictable queries, often during JSON serialisation, after the context may be disposed.
p1-34.y: Eager loading uses Include to load related data in the same query. Lazy loading loads related data automatically when you first touch it, and explicit loading is when you ask for it manually. The N+1 problem is when you load a list and then run one extra query per item, which kills performance. I avoid lazy loading in APIs and use Include or, better, a projection with Select to fetch only the columns needed.
p1-34.k: eager loading, lazy loading, explicit loading, include, n+1, ef core

p1-35.q: Migrations are code-reviewed like any change, generated as idempotent SQL scripts (dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent), and applied as a controlled step of the release through FV, UAT and production, never by the app at startup. Scripts are versioned with the release, backward compatible with the previous app version, and kept as evidence.
i: Expand/contract: add new columns or tables first (nullable or with defaults), deploy the app, backfill, then remove old ones in a later release; this allows rollback of the app without database rollback.
Review generated Up code for destructive operations (drops, renames that EF sees as drop and add) and data loss.
Large tables: add indexes ONLINE where the edition allows and batch data migrations to avoid long locks.
Migration bundles (efbundle) are an alternative executable for pipelines.
Keep a __EFMigrationsHistory check in verification so every environment is on the expected migration.
In IRT DB scripts are deployed first in the release order (DB, API, app, UI) by the Ansible/Shell install scripts.
c:
dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentStatusIndex
dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -o release/2024.3/db.sql
f: Why not context.Database.Migrate() at startup?
Several instances could race, it needs elevated DB rights, and regulated releases need a reviewed, controlled script.
How do you roll back a migration?
Prefer forward fixes; with expand/contract the old app still works, so the DB rarely needs rolling back.
p1-35.y: In our GxP environment, the app never applies migrations by itself at startup. We generate idempotent SQL scripts from the migrations, review them like code, and apply them as a controlled step of the release through FV, UAT and production. Scripts are backward compatible with the previous version of the app, and they are kept as validation evidence.
p1-35.k: ef core migrations, sql scripts, regulated, gxp, deployment, idempotent

p1-36.q: EF Core uses optimistic concurrency: mark a concurrency token (a SQL Server rowversion column with [Timestamp] or IsRowVersion), EF adds it to the WHERE clause of updates, and if no row is affected it throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. You then decide: reload and retry, merge, or return 409 Conflict to the user.
i: rowversion changes automatically on every update, so it is the simplest token in SQL Server.
In APIs return the version as an ETag; clients send If-Match, and a mismatch becomes 412 or 409.
Handling: ex.Entries gives current, original and database values for merging or messages.
Pessimistic alternative: UPDLOCK/transactions for high-contention rows (allocating the last kit), used sparingly.
Bulk ExecuteUpdate bypasses the token unless you include it in the Where.
f: Optimistic vs pessimistic?
Optimistic for low contention and web apps (no held locks); pessimistic only for short, high-contention critical sections.
Where else do you use it?
Study configuration edits by several study managers, where silent overwrites would be a GxP data-integrity problem.
p1-36.y: I use optimistic concurrency: a rowversion column on the table, which EF Core checks when it updates. If someone else changed the row first, EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. I catch that and return a 409 Conflict, so the user reloads and tries again. This avoids locking rows while users are editing, which is important for screens where two people may edit the same shipment.

p1-37.q: DbContext is a lightweight unit of work that is not thread-safe, so it should be short-lived: one per request (scoped, the AddDbContext default) or one per unit of work in background services. Never share one instance across concurrent operations; running two queries in parallel on the same context throws InvalidOperationException.
i: Parallel work: create separate contexts with IDbContextFactory<T> (AddDbContextFactory) per task.
Pooling: AddDbContextPool reuses context instances to reduce allocation cost; the context must not hold per-request state in fields.
Singletons and hosted services must not capture a scoped DbContext; create a scope or use the factory.
Long-lived contexts grow their change tracker and give stale data.
Connection pooling is separate and handled by SqlClient; the context opens and closes connections per operation.
f: What error do you get when sharing a context concurrently?
"A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed."
Pool vs factory?
Pooling reduces cost for scoped contexts; the factory gives you control over when to create contexts (and can also be pooled).
p1-37.y: DbContext is designed to be short-lived and it is not thread-safe, so it is registered as scoped, one per request. You must not run two queries on the same DbContext in parallel, and you must not keep it in a singleton. In background services I create a new scope for each job. For high throughput, DbContext pooling can reuse instances safely.
p1-37.k: dbcontext, lifetime, scoped, thread safety, pooling, ef core

p1-38.q: Use FromSql / FromSqlInterpolated or SqlQuery with interpolated strings, which EF converts into parameters, or explicit SqlParameter objects; never concatenate user input into SQL. For commands use ExecuteSql/ExecuteSqlInterpolated, and for stored procedures `FromSql($"EXEC dbo.GetSiteStock {siteId}")`.
i: FromSqlRaw with string concatenation is the classic SQL injection hole; FromSqlRaw is fine only with placeholders and parameters.
FromSql results can be composed with LINQ (EF wraps it as a subquery) if the SQL is composable (not a stored procedure).
SqlQuery<T> (EF Core 8) maps raw SQL to unmapped types such as DTOs.
Use raw SQL for complex reporting, window functions or hints that LINQ cannot express well; keep it in one place and test it.
Least privilege: the app's DB user cannot alter schema in production.
c:
var stock = await _db.Database
    .SqlQuery<KitStock>($"EXEC dbo.GetSiteStock @SiteId = {siteId}")
    .ToListAsync(ct);   // {siteId} becomes a SqlParameter, not string concatenation
f: Is FromSqlInterpolated safe?
Yes, interpolated values become parameters; the danger is building the string first and passing it to FromSqlRaw.
Dapper or EF raw SQL?
Dapper for many hand-written queries and maximum speed; EF raw SQL when you are already in an EF context.
p1-38.y: When I need raw SQL in EF Core, I use FromSql or ExecuteSql with interpolated parameters, which EF Core turns into real SQL parameters, so there is no SQL injection. I never build SQL by joining strings with user input. Stored procedures are called the same way with parameters. I use raw SQL only for things LINQ can't express well, like some reporting queries.
p1-38.k: raw sql, stored procedures, fromsql, sql injection, parameters, ef core

p1-39.q: SaveChanges runs all pending changes in one transaction automatically. For several SaveChanges calls or mixing EF with raw SQL, start an explicit transaction with Database.BeginTransactionAsync and commit at the end; across databases or systems use the outbox pattern rather than distributed transactions.
i: Execution strategies (EnableRetryOnFailure) retry transient failures, but with explicit transactions you must wrap the whole block in strategy.ExecuteAsync.
Savepoints: EF Core creates them automatically when SaveChanges runs inside a user transaction, so a failed SaveChanges can roll back to the savepoint.
TransactionScope works but async needs TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled, and it can escalate to distributed transactions; I prefer explicit DbContext transactions.
Isolation level can be passed to BeginTransaction; defaults to the database default (READ COMMITTED, or snapshot if enabled).
In the CSV import all batches run inside one transaction so a failure rolls back everything.
f: What is the outbox pattern?
Save the business change and the outgoing message in the same DB transaction, then a relay publishes it, so you never lose or invent events.
Why not distributed transactions (MSDTC)?
Slow, fragile and unsupported in many cloud setups; sagas and outbox are the modern approach.
p1-39.y: SaveChanges already runs all its changes in one transaction. When I need several SaveChanges calls or other work to succeed or fail together, I use BeginTransaction and commit at the end. If retries are enabled for SQL Server, I wrap the whole transaction in the execution strategy. Our CSV import saves all rows in one transaction, so a failure halfway saves nothing.
p1-39.k: transactions, savechanges, begintransaction, execution strategy, ef core, rollback

p1-40.q: WCF (Windows Communication Foundation) is the .NET Framework framework for building service-oriented applications over SOAP and other transports. Every endpoint has ABC: Address (where), Binding (how: transport, encoding, security, such as basicHttpBinding or netTcpBinding) and Contract (what: the [ServiceContract] interface).
i: Bindings choose protocol and features: BasicHttpBinding (SOAP 1.1, interop), WSHttpBinding (WS-Security, reliable sessions), NetTcpBinding (fast .NET to .NET), NetNamedPipeBinding (same machine).
Contracts: ServiceContract, OperationContract, DataContract/DataMember, FaultContract for typed errors.
Behaviours configure throttling, instance mode (PerCall, PerSession, Single) and concurrency.
Hosting: IIS/WAS, Windows service or self-host; heavy XML configuration in web.config.
Modern status: no WCF server in .NET 5+, CoreWCF provides a community port; clients still work via System.ServiceModel packages.
In IRT older areas still expose WCF endpoints that we maintain and integrate with.
f: What is a FaultContract?
A typed SOAP fault the service declares so clients can handle specific errors.
PerCall vs PerSession?
PerCall creates a service instance per request (scalable); PerSession keeps one per client session (stateful).
p1-40.y: WCF is Microsoft's older framework for building SOAP services on .NET Framework. Its ABCs are Address, which is where the service lives, Binding, which is how you talk to it, like HTTP or TCP and the security, and Contract, which is what operations it offers. I have maintained WCF services in my earlier work, and today the modern options are REST APIs or gRPC.
p1-40.k: wcf, soap, abc, address, binding, contract, service contract

p1-41.q: I would migrate WCF gradually: inventory endpoints and clients, keep the contracts stable, then either port to CoreWCF on modern .NET when SOAP clients cannot change, or move to REST (ASP.NET Core) or gRPC when clients can. Run old and new side by side behind a facade, compare responses, and cut clients over one by one.
i: Strangler fig pattern: route endpoint by endpoint to the new implementation while the old service keeps running.
Shared business logic moves into .NET Standard or modern libraries first, so both hosts use the same code.
WS-* features (message security, transactions, reliable sessions) need replacements: TLS and OAuth, outbox/sagas, idempotent retries.
Contract tests that replay recorded requests against old and new services prove compatibility.
Plan for configuration (no web.config), hosting (Kestrel, containers) and authentication changes.
f: CoreWCF or gRPC?
CoreWCF when external SOAP clients cannot change; gRPC for internal .NET-to-.NET calls you control.
Biggest risk?
Hidden behaviour in bindings and serializers (DataContract quirks, faults) that clients depend on.
p1-41.y: WCF server is not supported in modern .NET, so I would move the services step by step. First I separate business logic from WCF so it can be reused, then expose the same operations as REST APIs or gRPC on .NET 8 or 10. If old clients still need SOAP, CoreWCF can host the same contracts for a while. We migrate one service at a time and test each one against the old behaviour.
p1-41.k: wcf migration, corewcf, grpc, rest, modernization

p1-42.q: In [early 2026] I upgraded [3] IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10 LTS because .NET 8 support ends in November 2026 and a GxP product must run on a supported runtime. I upgraded shared libraries first, then each service, tests and Docker images, compared performance in validation, and released through FV, UAT and production with [no functional defects] and [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency.
i: Inventory first: a spreadsheet of projects, target frameworks, NuGet packages, Docker base images and pipeline agents; third-party packages were the real critical path.
Order: shared libraries, then services from least to most risky; one pull request per service with a checklist.
Central package management (Directory.Packages.props) after [a version conflict in Microsoft.Extensions packages] kept versions aligned.
Breaking changes reviewed from Microsoft's list, for example BackgroundService now running all of ExecuteAsync on a background thread in .NET 10, which we checked in our workers.
Evidence: before/after p95 latency and memory on the same validation environment, plus full regression and FV documentation.
Container images moved to the .NET 10 runtime images, scanned with [Trivy] before release.
f: How long did it take?
[About six weeks] for the three services inside one release cycle, mostly package updates and validation.
Would you use the .NET Upgrade Assistant?
For .NET Framework to modern .NET yes; for 8 to 10 the changes were small enough to do by hand.
w: I plan risky upgrades with inventory, order and evidence rather than changing everything at once.
I connect technical work to business and compliance reasons (support dates in a GxP product).
p1-42.y: In [early 2026] I upgraded [3] of our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10, because .NET 8 support ends in November 2026 and a GxP product must run on a supported version. I updated shared libraries first, then each service, the tests and the Docker images. We compared performance during validation, released through FV, UAT and production with [no functional defects], and got about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency.

p1-43.q: Usually no: DbContext already is a Unit of Work and DbSet already is a repository, so a generic repository on top mostly hides EF features (Include, projections, AsNoTracking, ExecuteUpdate) and adds code. I use specific, intention-revealing query services or repositories only where they add value: complex reusable queries, aggregate boundaries in DDD, or a seam for a different data source.
i: Testing argument: test data access with a real database (Testcontainers SQL Server); mock at the service boundary instead.
Specification pattern or extension methods (`q.ForStudy(id).Active()`) give reuse without a repository layer.
If a repository exists, return materialised results or DTOs, not IQueryable, to keep query logic in one place.
Unit of Work across repositories is just SaveChanges on the shared scoped context.
In IRT some older services have repositories; new code uses DbContext directly in handlers with query extension methods.
f: When is a repository worth it?
When the domain should not know about EF, for complex aggregates, or when data may come from different stores.
How do you test without repositories?
Integration tests against a real SQL Server container, and unit tests for pure business logic.
p1-43.y: Not always. EF Core's DbContext is already a unit of work and DbSet already behaves like a repository. Adding a generic repository on top often just hides useful features like Include and projections. I add a repository only when it gives real value, like hiding complex queries or making the domain cleaner to test. In some of our services we have repositories, and in newer ones we use DbContext directly with focused query classes.
p1-43.k: repository pattern, unit of work, ef core, dbcontext

p1-44.q: A clustered index defines the physical order of the table's rows: the leaf level is the data itself, so there is only one per table (usually the primary key). A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree of key columns with pointers (the clustered key) back to the rows; a table can have many, and INCLUDE columns can make them covering.
i: Key lookup: when a non-clustered index lacks needed columns, SQL Server looks up each row in the clustered index; many lookups can make the optimizer choose a scan.
Clustered key choice: narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing (INT/BIGINT identity, sequential GUIDs); random GUIDs cause page splits and fragmentation.
Every non-clustered index stores the clustered key, so a wide clustered key bloats all indexes.
Heaps (no clustered index) suit some staging tables, but forwarded records hurt reads.
Columnstore indexes are for analytics over large tables.
My shipment-list fix used a non-clustered index on (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE (display columns), removing scans and key lookups.
f: Can the primary key be non-clustered?
Yes; PK and clustered index are separate concepts, they just default together.
What is a covering index?
An index containing every column a query needs, so no lookups are required.
p1-44.y: A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows, so a table can have only one, and it is usually the primary key. A non-clustered index is a separate structure that points back to the row, and you can have many. A covering non-clustered index includes all the columns a query needs, so SQL Server doesn't have to look up the row. That trick fixed our slow shipment list query.
p1-44.k: clustered index, non-clustered index, covering index, include columns, sql server

p1-45.q: Situation: the IRT site shipment list timed out for a large study ([about 300] sites, [8 to 12 seconds]). I captured the real query from Query Store, read the actual plan (clustered index scan, key lookups, a non-SARGable CONVERT on the date), rewrote the predicate as a range, added a covering index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE display columns and server-side paging. Logical reads fell from [about 400,000 to 2,000] and time from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms].
i: Diagnosis tools: Query Store top resource consumers, actual execution plan, SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON for logical reads and CPU.
Why it was slow: CONVERT(date, ShipmentDate) on the column prevents index seeks; missing index caused a full scan of [millions] of rows; no paging returned everything.
Fix order: SARGable rewrite first (free), then the index, then paging, measuring after each step.
Index design: equality columns first, range last, INCLUDE the selected columns to avoid lookups.
Release: index script reviewed, tested in validation for write impact, released through FV, UAT and production with evidence.
Guard: latency alarm in CloudWatch and Grafana, and the query added to pre-release performance checks.
c:
-- before (non-SARGable)
WHERE CONVERT(date, s.ShipmentDate) = @Day
-- after (index seek possible)
WHERE s.ShipmentDate >= @Day AND s.ShipmentDate < DATEADD(day, 1, @Day)
f: What did the plan show after the fix?
An index seek on the new index, no key lookups, and estimated rows close to actual.
What if the parameters vary a lot?
Watch for parameter sniffing; Query Store can show plan changes, and OPTIMIZE FOR or recompile hints are options.
w: I fix performance with measurements, not guesses, and prove the result with numbers.
I treat a database change with the same release discipline as code in a regulated product.
p1-45.y: Our site shipment list was timing out for a big study, taking about [8 to 12 seconds]. I took the real query from Query Store and read the execution plan. It showed a full scan, key lookups and a CONVERT on a date column that stopped the index being used. I rewrote the date filter as a range, added a covering index and server-side paging. Reads dropped from about [400,000 to 2,000] and the time went to [under 300 milliseconds].
p1-45.k: sql optimization, slow query, execution plan, query store, covering index, story

p1-46.q: SARGable (Search ARGument-able) means a WHERE predicate is written so SQL Server can use an index seek on the column. Wrapping the column in a function or calculation (YEAR(date) = 2024, ISNULL(col, 0) = 1, col + 1 = 5), leading wildcards (LIKE '%abc') or implicit conversions make it non-SARGable and force scans.
i: Rewrite functions on columns into ranges: `Date >= '2024-01-01' AND Date < '2025-01-01'`.
Implicit conversions: comparing an NVARCHAR parameter with a VARCHAR column converts the column; match data types (a common EF/ADO.NET issue with string parameters).
OR across different columns often prevents seeks; consider UNION ALL or separate indexes.
Computed columns with an index can make an expression searchable.
The execution plan warns about implicit conversions with a yellow triangle.
f: Is LIKE 'abc%' SARGable?
Yes, a trailing wildcard can seek; a leading wildcard cannot.
How do EF queries become non-SARGable?
Calling methods on columns in Where (e.g. .Date or ToUpper()) that translate into functions on the column.
p1-46.y: SARGable means the WHERE condition is written so SQL Server can use an index seek. If I wrap the column in a function, like YEAR of OrderDate or CONVERT, or use a leading wildcard in LIKE, SQL Server has to scan every row. The fix is to keep the column clean and move the logic to the value side, for example a date range instead of a function. That was exactly the fix in our shipment query.
p1-46.k: sargable, index seek, where clause, functions on columns, sql server

p1-47.q: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables; LEFT (OUTER) JOIN returns all left rows plus matches or NULLs; RIGHT JOIN the reverse; FULL OUTER JOIN all rows from both with NULLs where there is no match; CROSS JOIN every combination; a self join joins a table to itself, and CROSS/OUTER APPLY run a table expression per left row.
i: Physical join types the optimizer chooses: nested loops (small inputs, indexed inner side), merge join (both sorted), hash join (large unsorted inputs).
LEFT JOIN with a filter on the right table in WHERE turns it into an INNER JOIN; put that filter in the ON clause instead.
Anti-join: find rows with no match using NOT EXISTS (safe with NULLs) or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.Id IS NULL.
APPLY is great for top N per group or calling table-valued functions per row.
c:
-- sites with no shipments in the last 30 days
SELECT s.SiteId, s.Name
FROM dbo.Sites s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Shipments sh
                  WHERE sh.SiteId = s.SiteId AND sh.ShipmentDate >= DATEADD(day, -30, SYSUTCDATETIME()));
f: Which join type is fastest?
It depends on data size, sorting and indexes; the optimizer picks nested loops, merge or hash accordingly.
EF Core equivalent of LEFT JOIN?
GroupJoin with SelectMany/DefaultIfEmpty, or navigation properties; .NET 10 adds LeftJoin operators.
p1-47.y: An inner join returns only rows that match in both tables. A left join returns all rows from the left table, with nulls where there is no match, and a right join is the opposite. A full outer join returns everything from both sides. A cross join gives every combination. I mostly use inner and left joins, for example a left join to show sites even if they have no shipments yet.
p1-47.k: joins, inner join, left join, right join, full outer join, cross join, sql

p1-48.q: Normalisation organises data to remove redundancy and update anomalies (1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial key dependency, 3NF no transitive dependency), which keeps writes consistent. Denormalisation deliberately duplicates data (pre-joined columns, summary tables) to speed up reads at the cost of extra write work and consistency risk.
i: OLTP systems like IRT are normalised to around 3NF because correctness and auditability matter most.
Reporting and read models can be denormalised: indexed views, summary tables or a separate read store fed by events (CQRS).
Keep denormalised data in sync with triggers, application code in the same transaction, or event-driven projections; document which is the source of truth.
Over-normalisation causes many joins; measure before denormalising.
f: What is BCNF?
A stricter 3NF where every determinant is a candidate key.
Example of denormalisation you would accept?
A site's current kit stock count maintained alongside movements, for fast dashboards.
p1-48.y: Normalization means splitting data into related tables so each fact is stored once, which avoids duplicate data and update mistakes. Denormalization means intentionally copying some data to make reads faster, at the cost of keeping copies in sync. For our transactional IRT data we keep it normalized, and for reporting we use denormalized views or read models so reports don't slow down the main system.
p1-48.k: normalization, denormalization, normal forms, database design

p1-49.q: Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads allowed), READ COMMITTED (SQL Server default, no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (rows read cannot change), SERIALIZABLE (no phantoms, range locks), plus SNAPSHOT and READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI), which use row versions in tempdb so readers do not block writers.
i: Locking vs versioning: RCSI gives statement-level consistent reads without shared locks; SNAPSHOT gives transaction-level consistency and can raise update conflicts (error 3960).
NOLOCK equals READ UNCOMMITTED: can read uncommitted, duplicated or missing rows; avoid it in clinical data.
Higher isolation increases blocking and deadlock risk; keep transactions short.
Azure SQL enables RCSI by default; on-prem SQL Server you turn it on per database.
In IRT kit allocation uses a serializable or UPDLOCK pattern for the critical check-and-assign step, while normal reads use READ COMMITTED.
f: What is a phantom read?
Rerunning a range query returns new rows inserted by another transaction.
Why is RCSI popular?
It removes most reader/writer blocking with little code change, at the cost of tempdb version store usage.
p1-49.y: Isolation levels decide how much one transaction can see of another's unfinished work. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, Read Committed is the SQL Server default, Repeatable Read stops rows changing under you, and Serializable also stops new rows appearing, but with more locking. Snapshot isolation uses row versions so readers don't block writers. Higher isolation means more consistency but less concurrency, so I pick the lowest level that is correct.
p1-49.k: isolation levels, read committed, snapshot, serializable, dirty read, transactions

p1-50.q: A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can continue; SQL Server detects the cycle and kills one as the victim (error 1205). Typical causes are accessing tables in different orders, long transactions, missing indexes that make scans lock more rows, and lock escalation.
i: Diagnose with the system_health Extended Events session (xml_deadlock_report) to see the resources, statements and victim.
Prevent: consistent access order, short transactions, proper indexes, RCSI for readers, avoid user interaction inside transactions.
Handle: retry the victim transaction a few times with backoff; EF Core's EnableRetryOnFailure retries 1205 by default for SQL Server.
Async code deadlocks are different: sync-over-async blocking on a captured context.
In Part 3 there is a scenario answer about a sudden rise in deadlocks.
f: What is lock escalation?
SQL Server converting many row or page locks into a table lock (around 5,000 locks), which increases blocking.
Can you choose the victim?
SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW on less important sessions.
p1-50.y: A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so SQL Server kills one of them. Common causes are updating tables in different orders and long transactions with missing indexes. I fix them by keeping transactions short, accessing tables in the same order, and adding indexes. I also make the code retry once on a deadlock error, since the victim can usually succeed on retry.
p1-50.k: deadlock, locking, sql server, retry, transactions

p1-51.q: Stored procedures keep SQL on the server with precompiled, cached plans, a security boundary (EXECUTE rights) and fewer round trips for complex logic; ORM or parameterised inline queries keep logic in code, versioned and testable with the app. Parameter sniffing is when SQL Server compiles and caches a plan using the first parameter values it sees, which can be terrible for later, very different values.
i: Parameterised inline SQL is cached too; performance alone is not a reason for stored procedures.
Sniffing symptoms: the same query is sometimes fast, sometimes slow, depending on which plan is cached (big study vs small study).
Fixes: OPTION (RECOMPILE) for rare heavy queries, OPTIMIZE FOR, separate code paths, better indexes, or Query Store plan forcing; SQL Server 2022 adds Parameter Sensitive Plan optimisation.
Testing: stored procedures need database tests (tSQLt); ORM queries get integration tests with the app.
In IRT complex reports use stored procedures; transactional code uses EF Core.
f: What is Query Store?
A SQL Server feature that records queries, plans and runtime stats over time so you can find regressions and force good plans.
Does EF Core suffer from parameter sniffing?
Yes, it sends parameterised queries, so the same cached plan issue applies.
p1-51.y: Stored procedures keep logic in the database and can be tuned there, while ORM queries keep logic in C# where it is easier to test and version. Both are parameterized and safe. Parameter sniffing is when SQL Server builds a plan for the first parameter value and reuses it for very different values, which can make some calls slow. I fix it with OPTION RECOMPILE, OPTIMIZE FOR, or better indexes, after checking Query Store.
p1-51.k: stored procedures, orm, parameter sniffing, query plan, query store

p1-52.q: I choose SQL Server/RDS for relational, transactional data with joins, constraints and ad-hoc queries (studies, subjects, kits, audit trails); DynamoDB for key-value or simple access patterns needing single-digit millisecond latency at any scale with minimal operations (session state, idempotency keys, event lookups by id). The deciding factor is the access pattern and consistency needs.
i: DynamoDB design starts from queries: partition and sort keys, GSIs; joins and ad-hoc queries are expensive or impossible.
RDS gives ACID across tables, rich SQL, reporting; scaling is vertical plus read replicas.
DynamoDB gives transactions (limited, 100 items) and strong reads per item, global tables, TTL and streams.
Cost: DynamoDB on-demand for spiky traffic; RDS is paid per instance hour.
In IRT the core clinical data is relational; DynamoDB fits [idempotency keys and integration message logs].
f: What is a hot partition?
Too much traffic on one partition key value, causing throttling; spread keys or add write sharding.
Can DynamoDB do reports?
Not well; export to S3 and query with Athena, or stream into an analytics store.
p1-52.y: I choose SQL Server on RDS when the data is relational, needs joins, transactions and complex queries, like our clinical trial data. I choose DynamoDB when access patterns are simple and known, like lookups by key, and I need massive scale with very low latency and no server management. Changing access patterns later is hard in DynamoDB, so for core business data I default to relational.
p1-52.k: sql server, rds, dynamodb, nosql, relational, database choice

p1-53.q: DELETE removes rows one by one, can have a WHERE clause, fires triggers, is fully logged and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE removes all rows by deallocating pages, is minimally logged, resets identity, cannot have WHERE and fails if foreign keys reference the table; DROP removes the table itself, structure and data.
i: TRUNCATE can be rolled back inside an explicit transaction in SQL Server, a common interview trap.
DELETE on huge tables should be batched (DELETE TOP (5000) in a loop) to avoid log growth and lock escalation.
TRUNCATE needs ALTER permission; DELETE needs DELETE permission.
In a GxP system physical deletes of clinical data are rare; we use soft deletes or status changes with audit trail.
f: Does DELETE reset identity?
No; TRUNCATE does (or DBCC CHECKIDENT).
Why batch deletes?
To keep transactions short, limit log growth and avoid blocking other users.
p1-53.y: DELETE removes rows one by one, can have a WHERE clause, fires triggers and is fully logged. TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly by deallocating pages, resets identity, and cannot have a WHERE. DROP removes the whole table, structure included. In production data like ours, we almost always use DELETE or soft deletes, because we need audit history.

p1-54.q: OFFSET/FETCH paging skips N rows and takes the next page; it is simple and supports jumping to any page, but the database still reads and discards all skipped rows, so deep pages get slow, and inserts can shift rows between pages. Keyset (seek) pagination remembers the last key seen and asks for rows after it (WHERE Id > @lastId ORDER BY Id), which stays fast at any depth and is stable.
i: Keyset needs a unique, indexed sort key (or a composite like (ShipmentDate, Id)).
Keyset gives "next/previous" or infinite scroll, not "jump to page 57".
Return a cursor (encoded last key) to clients instead of page numbers.
COUNT(*) for total pages is itself expensive on big tables; consider estimates or omitting totals.
c:
SELECT TOP (50) Id, ShipmentDate, Status
FROM dbo.Shipments
WHERE StudyId = @StudyId AND (ShipmentDate > @LastDate OR (ShipmentDate = @LastDate AND Id > @LastId))
ORDER BY ShipmentDate, Id;
f: Which do you use in IRT screens?
OFFSET/FETCH for normal screens where users jump pages; keyset for exports and APIs that walk large lists.
EF Core support?
Skip/Take for offset; keyset via Where on the last key, or libraries such as MR.EntityFrameworkCore.KeysetPagination.
p1-54.y: OFFSET and FETCH skip a number of rows and take the next page, which is simple, but deep pages get slow because SQL Server still reads the skipped rows. Keyset pagination remembers the last key seen and asks for rows after it, so it stays fast at any depth and is stable when data changes. I use OFFSET for normal admin screens and keyset for large lists or infinite scroll.
p1-54.k: pagination, offset fetch, keyset pagination, seek method, paging

p1-55.q: A CTE (WITH ... AS) names a subquery for readability and recursion within one statement; window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, SUM() OVER) calculate across related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY. Use case: the latest status per shipment, running stock per site, or the time between shipment events.
i: PARTITION BY defines the group, ORDER BY the order inside it, and ROWS/RANGE the frame for running totals.
LAG/LEAD compare with the previous/next row, e.g. time between Dispatched and Delivered.
Recursive CTEs walk hierarchies (site, region, country) with a MAXRECURSION guard.
CTEs are not materialised; referencing one twice may run it twice; use a temp table for reuse.
c:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.ShipmentId, e.Status, e.EventAt,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY e.ShipmentId ORDER BY e.EventAt DESC) AS rn
  FROM dbo.ShipmentEvents e)
SELECT ShipmentId, Status, EventAt FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;   -- latest status per shipment
f: Window function vs GROUP BY?
GROUP BY returns one row per group; window functions keep every row and add the calculation.
Running total?
SUM(Qty) OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY EventAt ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING).
p1-55.y: A CTE is a named temporary result I can use inside one query, which makes complex SQL readable. Window functions like ROW_NUMBER, RANK and SUM OVER calculate across a group of rows without collapsing them. A real use case for me was finding the latest status for each shipment, using ROW_NUMBER partitioned by shipment ordered by date, and taking row number one.
p1-55.k: cte, window functions, row_number, rank, partition by, sql

p1-56.q: Unit tests check one class or function in isolation with dependencies faked; integration tests check components working together with real infrastructure (database, broker, HTTP pipeline); end-to-end tests drive the whole system through the UI or public API like a user. The test pyramid says have many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few slow E2E tests.
i: Speed and stability fall as you go up; confidence in real behaviour rises.
Integration tests with Testcontainers (SQL Server, RabbitMQ) catch mapping, SQL and configuration bugs that mocks hide.
E2E with Playwright covers critical user journeys only (login, randomise, create shipment, CSV import).
Contract tests sit between services to replace many cross-service E2E tests.
Anti-pattern: the ice-cream cone (mostly manual and E2E tests), slow and flaky.
In IRT: xUnit/NUnit with Moq for units, WebApplicationFactory and a test DB for integration, Playwright and Cucumber for E2E, plus FV scripted testing.
f: What do you not unit-test?
Trivial code and framework behaviour; focus on business rules and edge cases.
Testing trophy vs pyramid?
The trophy (Kent C. Dodds) weights integration tests more, popular for front ends; the idea is the same: balance cost and confidence.
p1-56.y: Unit tests check one class or method in isolation and are fast. Integration tests check pieces working together, like an API with a real database. End-to-end tests drive the whole system through the UI. The test pyramid says have many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and only a few end-to-end tests, because the higher ones are slower and more fragile. That is how our test suites are balanced.
p1-56.k: unit test, integration test, end-to-end, test pyramid, testing

p1-57.q: Both are mature .NET test frameworks. xUnit creates a new test class instance per test (constructor for setup, IDisposable for teardown), uses [Fact] and [Theory] with [InlineData], and runs test classes in parallel by default; NUnit uses [Test], [TestCase], [SetUp]/[TearDown] and [OneTimeSetUp], with a rich constraint-based Assert.That model.
i: Shared context in xUnit: IClassFixture<T> per class, ICollectionFixture<T> across classes (for an expensive Testcontainers database).
xUnit v3 (2024+) brings first-class cancellation (TestContext.Current.CancellationToken) and an updated runner.
NUnit has more attributes out of the box (Category, Repeat, Retry, Timeout).
Assertions libraries (FluentAssertions, Shouldly) work with either; check licensing (FluentAssertions v8 is commercial).
I use xUnit in new IRT services and NUnit where older projects already do; consistency in a codebase matters more than the choice.
f: How do you share an expensive database between tests?
An xUnit collection fixture that starts the container once, with data reset per test (Respawn).
Why does xUnit avoid [SetUp]?
A fresh instance per test and constructor setup make test isolation explicit.
p1-57.y: Both are mature .NET test frameworks. xUnit is more modern: it creates a new instance of the test class for every test, uses the constructor for setup, and Fact and Theory attributes. NUnit uses Test and TestCase attributes with SetUp methods and has a lot of built-in assertions. Microsoft's own projects use xUnit, and that is what I use in our services.
p1-57.k: xunit, nunit, test framework, fact, theory

p1-58.q: Moq creates test doubles from interfaces: Setup defines behaviour, Returns/ReturnsAsync/Throws give results, and Verify checks a call happened with expected arguments. I mock things I own that cross a boundary (repositories, gateways, clocks, message publishers), not value objects, DTOs, DbContext or types I do not own.
i: Don't mock what you don't own: wrap third-party SDKs (Rebex, AWS SDK) behind your interface and test the wrapper with integration tests.
Don't mock DbContext/DbSet; use a real database in integration tests.
Prefer state verification (output, saved data) over many Verify calls, which make tests brittle to refactoring.
It.Is<T>(predicate) for argument matching; MockBehavior.Strict only where unexpected calls must fail.
HttpClient: fake the HttpMessageHandler or use WireMock.Net rather than mocking HttpClient.
f: Mock vs stub?
A stub only returns data; a mock also verifies interactions.
Alternatives to Moq?
NSubstitute (simpler syntax) or hand-written fakes.
p1-58.y: I use Moq to replace dependencies with fake objects, set up what they return, and verify important calls, so I can test one class alone. What I don't mock: simple value objects, the code under test itself, and EF Core DbContext, because a mocked DbContext doesn't behave like a real database. For database code I use a real database in a container instead.
p1-58.k: moq, mocking, test doubles, unit testing, verify

p1-59.q: I use WebApplicationFactory<Program> from Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing to host the real API in memory, override configuration and services (real SQL Server in Testcontainers, fake external clients, test authentication), and send real HTTP requests with its HttpClient, asserting status codes, bodies and database state.
i: Expose Program to tests with `public partial class Program { }` when using top-level statements.
ConfigureTestServices to replace external dependencies (SFTP, vendor APIs) with fakes and to add a test auth handler issuing claims.
Database: Testcontainers SQL Server started once per collection, migrations applied, Respawn resets data between tests.
Covers routing, filters, model binding, validation, serialization, auth policies and EF mappings together.
Run in CI on every pull request; Docker must be available on the agents.
f: How do you handle authentication in these tests?
Register a test authentication scheme that creates a ClaimsPrincipal from a header, and make it the default in tests.
In-memory provider or real DB?
Real DB in a container; EF InMemory is not relational and hides bugs.
p1-59.y: I use WebApplicationFactory, which starts the real API in memory with the full pipeline: routing, model binding, filters and authentication. I replace only the external parts, like an SFTP client or a vendor API, with fakes, and use a real SQL Server in a Docker container through Testcontainers. Then I call endpoints with HttpClient and check the status codes and responses.
p1-59.k: integration test, webapplicationfactory, testcontainers, asp.net core testing

p1-60.q: Reliable Playwright tests use user-facing locators (getByRole, getByLabel, getByTestId), rely on auto-waiting and web-first assertions instead of sleeps, keep each test independent with its own data and storage state, and run in CI with traces, screenshots and videos on failure for quick diagnosis.
i: Auto-waiting: actions wait for elements to be visible, enabled and stable; expect(locator).toHaveText() retries until timeout.
Never waitForTimeout; wait for a specific state or network response (page.waitForResponse).
Authentication: log in once in global setup and reuse storageState for all tests.
Test data: create via API in beforeEach and clean up, so tests run in parallel and in any order.
Page Object Model or fixtures keep selectors in one place.
Trace viewer (trace: 'on-first-retry') shows every step, DOM snapshot and network call.
In IRT our E2E covers [login, CSV import preview and confirm, shipment creation] and runs on [Chromium in the pipeline].
f: How do you deal with flaky E2E tests?
Find the cause with traces (timing, data, environment), fix it, and quarantine meanwhile; retries only as a safety net.
Playwright vs Selenium?
Playwright has auto-waiting, multiple browsers in one API, parallelism and tracing built in, so tests are faster and steadier.
p1-60.y: To keep Playwright tests reliable, I use stable selectors like test ids or roles instead of CSS paths, and rely on Playwright's auto-waiting instead of fixed sleeps. Each test sets up its own data so tests don't depend on each other. I keep end-to-end tests to the most important user journeys, and use traces and screenshots on failure to debug quickly.
p1-60.k: playwright, e2e, end-to-end testing, flaky tests, selectors

p1-61.q: BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) describes behaviour as examples in business language before coding; Cucumber runs those examples written in Gherkin (Feature, Scenario, Given/When/Then) by binding each step to code, such as Playwright actions. It creates living documentation that BAs, QA and developers can all read.
i: Write scenarios with the BA and QA in refinement (three amigos), then automate them.
Keep steps declarative (business intent) rather than UI clicks, so scenarios survive UI changes.
Scenario Outline with Examples tables covers many data cases.
In regulated work, Gherkin scenarios map nicely to requirements for traceability.
Downside: the step layer adds maintenance; use BDD for key behaviours, plain tests elsewhere.
c:
Scenario: Block transfer to a live study
  Given the target study "ABC-301" has randomized subjects
  When a study manager requests a configuration transfer to "ABC-301"
  Then the transfer is blocked with reason "Target study is live"
f: Cucumber vs SpecFlow/Reqnroll?
Same idea; Reqnroll is the .NET successor of SpecFlow, Cucumber is the JS/Java family.
Who writes the scenarios?
Together in refinement; QA or BA usually drafts, developers automate.
p1-61.y: BDD means describing behaviour in plain language that business people can read, using Given, When, Then scenarios. Cucumber, or SpecFlow and Reqnroll in .NET, connects each line of the scenario to test code. The main value is shared understanding between the business, QA and developers. In a regulated product, these readable scenarios can also link nicely to requirements.
p1-61.k: bdd, cucumber, gherkin, given when then, specflow, reqnroll

p1-62.q: A quality gate is a set of pass/fail conditions SonarQube applies to new code in each analysis, for example no new bugs or vulnerabilities, all security hotspots reviewed, coverage on new code at least [80 percent] and duplication under [3 percent]. The pipeline fails the build (or blocks the pull request) when the gate fails.
i: "Clean as you code": the gate focuses on new code, so legacy debt does not block delivery while new code stays clean.
Quality profiles define the rules; gates define the thresholds.
PR decoration shows issues inline in Azure DevOps pull requests.
Do not chase the coverage number with assertion-free tests; review what is covered.
Security hotspots need human review; vulnerabilities must be fixed or justified.
Part 3 has a scenario about a failing gate right before a release.
f: What if a rule is wrong for your code?
Mark the issue as won't fix with a reason, or adjust the profile through the team, never silently.
Gate on overall or new code?
New code; overall metrics improve as you touch old code.
p1-62.y: A SonarQube quality gate is a set of conditions that new code must pass, like no new bugs or vulnerabilities, enough test coverage on new code, and limited duplication. It runs in the CI pipeline, and if the gate fails, the pull request can't be merged. It keeps code quality from slowly getting worse without arguing about it in every review.
p1-62.k: sonarqube, quality gate, static analysis, code coverage, ci

p1-63.q: Jest runs JavaScript/TypeScript tests with describe/it, expect matchers, mocking (jest.fn, jest.mock) and snapshot support; for React I use React Testing Library to render components and interact with them the way a user would (getByRole, userEvent), and for Node I test services directly and APIs with supertest.
i: Test behaviour, not implementation: avoid testing internal state or component internals.
Mock network calls with MSW (Mock Service Worker) for realistic API responses.
Fake timers (jest.useFakeTimers) for debounce and retry logic.
Async: await findBy* queries and waitFor; always return or await promises.
Vitest is a faster, Vite-based alternative with the same API.
f: Are snapshot tests useful?
Only small, stable ones; big snapshots get approved blindly.
How do you test a custom hook?
renderHook from React Testing Library.
p1-63.y: For Node.js I use Jest to unit test functions and services, mocking things like the database or HTTP calls, and Supertest to test API routes. For React I use Jest with React Testing Library, which tests components the way a user uses them, by finding buttons and text instead of internal details. I keep tests focused on behaviour, so refactoring doesn't break them.
p1-63.k: jest, react testing library, node testing, supertest, unit test

p1-64.q: I check correctness first (does it meet the requirement and edge cases), then security, tests, readability and design, performance risks, and operability (logging, errors, configuration). I keep comments specific, explain the why, separate must-fix from suggestions, and prefer small pull requests.
i: Correctness: null handling, time zones (my own lesson), concurrency, idempotency, transaction boundaries.
Security: input validation, authorisation on every endpoint, SQL injection, secrets, PHI in logs.
Tests: do they fail if the code is wrong; are integration paths covered.
Data: migrations backward compatible; indexes for new queries.
Automation first: formatting, analyzers and SonarQube handle style, so humans focus on logic.
Tone: questions instead of orders ("what happens if the file is empty?"), and praise good solutions.
f: How long should a review take?
Small PRs within hours; large ones get split or walked through together.
What do you do with a huge PR?
Ask to split it, or review it in a call with the author.
p1-64.y: In a code review I first check that the change does what the story needs and is correct, including edge cases and error handling. Then security, like input validation and secrets, then performance, like N+1 queries, then tests and readability. I keep comments respectful and explain the why. I also review small pull requests faster, so I encourage the team to keep them small.
p1-64.k: code review, pull request, best practices, review checklist

p1-65.q: In GxP, testing is not just a developer activity but documented evidence: requirements trace to test cases, formal validation (FV) runs scripted tests with recorded results and sign-off, defects follow controlled processes, and only validated, change-controlled builds reach production. Automated tests support this but the evidence and traceability are what auditors check.
i: Traceability matrix: requirement, design, code change, unit/integration tests, FV test case, result.
Computer System Validation (CSV) and GAMP 5 risk-based approach: test more where patient risk is higher (randomisation, dosing, blinding).
Test environments are controlled and qualified; no ad-hoc changes during FV.
Regression evidence for every release; deviations documented and assessed.
Automated test results are archived as evidence.
Developers still write unit, integration and Playwright tests, but FV is independent.
f: What is GAMP 5?
Industry guidance for risk-based validation of computerised systems in regulated life sciences.
How do you speed up testing without losing compliance?
More automation with archived evidence and risk-based focus on critical functions.
p1-65.y: In GxP, testing is also documented evidence, not just something developers do. Requirements are traced to test cases, formal validation runs scripted tests with recorded results and sign-off, defects follow a controlled process, and only validated builds reach production. Automated tests help a lot, but what auditors check is the evidence and traceability. That's how we work on our IRT product.
p1-65.k: gxp, regulated testing, validation, traceability, fv, audit

p1-66.q: Hooks give function components state and lifecycle behaviour: useState replaces this.state, useEffect replaces componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount (via its cleanup function), useRef replaces instance fields, and useMemo/useCallback replace manual shouldComponentUpdate optimisations.
i: Think in synchronisation, not lifecycle: an effect keeps something outside React in sync with props/state.
Cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount: cancel fetches with AbortController, clear timers, unsubscribe.
StrictMode in development mounts, unmounts and remounts to reveal missing cleanups.
Rules of hooks: call them at the top level, in the same order, only from components or custom hooks.
Many effects are unnecessary: derive values during render, handle events in handlers, fetch with React Query.
f: What is getDerivedStateFromError's hook equivalent?
None; error boundaries still need class components (or a library like react-error-boundary).
useEffect vs useLayoutEffect?
useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM changes before paint, for measuring layout.
p1-66.y: Hooks let function components do what class lifecycle methods did. useState holds state, and useEffect runs side effects: with an empty dependency list it runs once like componentDidMount, with dependencies it runs when they change, and its cleanup function works like componentWillUnmount. It keeps related logic together instead of splitting it across lifecycle methods, and custom hooks make it reusable.
p1-66.k: react hooks, useeffect, usestate, lifecycle methods, custom hooks

p1-67.q: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official way to use Redux: configureStore sets up the store with good defaults, createSlice defines state, reducers and actions together (with Immer so you can write "mutating" code safely), createAsyncThunk handles async logic, and RTK Query adds data fetching and caching.
