i: Single store, actions describe what happened, reducers are pure functions, selectors read state; components subscribe with useSelector and send actions with useDispatch.
Immer produces immutable updates from mutable-looking code.
RTK Query generates hooks (useGetSitesQuery) with caching, invalidation tags and loading states, replacing hand-written thunks.
Use Redux for complex shared client state; server data often fits RTK Query or React Query better.
Redux DevTools give time-travel debugging.
f: Why are reducers pure?
Predictable state, easy tests and time-travel debugging.
RTK Query vs React Query?
Similar features; RTK Query integrates with the Redux store, React Query is standalone.
p1-67.y: Redux Toolkit is the official, simpler way to write Redux. I create a store with configureStore and define slices with createSlice, which gives the reducers and actions together, and I can write updates that look like mutations because Immer handles immutability. For server data, RTK Query or React Query handles fetching and caching. I use it when shared state is complex, otherwise local state or context is enough.
p1-67.k: redux toolkit, createslice, store, rtk query, state management, react

p1-68.q: Reusable components have a small, typed props API, are composable (children, slots, render props) rather than configured with dozens of flags, own no business logic or data fetching, are accessible by default, and come with documentation and tests. I build them as controlled components with sensible defaults.
i:
Composition over configuration: `...
` scales better than 30 boolean props.
Accessibility: semantic elements, labels, keyboard support, focus management, aria attributes.
Styling via design tokens or CSS variables so themes (dark mode) work.
Storybook documents states (loading, empty, error) and enables visual tests.
Stable APIs: deprecate props before removing them, version a shared component library.
In IRT: [the configurable data table] reused on several screens; Part 9 has the resume-verification answer.
f: Controlled vs uncontrolled for library components?
Support controlled use (value + onChange) with an uncontrolled default for simple cases.
How do you stop a component from growing too many props?
Split it, use composition, and push variations into wrappers.
p1-68.y: A reusable component should do one job, take clear typed props, and not know about where its data comes from. I keep it flexible with props and children, handle loading, empty and error states, and make it accessible. For example, I built a data table component used across our IRT screens, with sorting, paging and row actions, so every screen looks and behaves the same.
p1-68.k: reusable components, react, props, design system, typescript

p1-69.q: Measure first with the React Profiler and browser performance tools, then reduce unnecessary renders (move state down, split context, React.memo, useMemo/useCallback for expensive work or stable props), virtualise long lists, code-split routes with lazy and Suspense, and avoid large bundles and request waterfalls.
i: Virtualisation (react-window, TanStack Virtual) renders only visible rows for tables with thousands of rows.
Keys: stable unique keys for lists; index keys cause wrong state and extra work when items move.
Expensive calculations in useMemo; debounced inputs for search.
Data: cache server data (React Query), prefetch, avoid fetching in deeply nested effects.
React 18 concurrent features: useTransition and useDeferredValue keep typing responsive; React Compiler (React 19 era) auto-memoises.
Bundle: analyse with a bundle analyser, tree-shake, lazy-load heavy libraries.
f: Should you wrap everything in React.memo?
No; it adds comparison cost and complexity. Use it where profiling shows waste.
What is a waterfall?
Sequential requests where one fetch waits for another, often caused by fetching inside nested components.
p1-69.y: First I measure with the React Profiler to see what re-renders. Then I fix the cause: keep state close to where it is used, avoid creating new objects and functions on every render, and use memo, useMemo and useCallback where it actually helps. For long lists I use virtualization and paging, and I split code with lazy loading so the first page loads fast.
p1-69.k: react performance, memo, usememo, usecallback, re-render, virtualization, lazy loading

p1-70.q: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, catching errors at compile time, enabling refactoring and IntelliSense, and documenting contracts between front end and API. interface and type both describe object shapes; interface can be extended and declaration-merged and is preferred for object contracts, while type aliases can express unions, intersections, tuples, mapped and conditional types.
i: Interfaces merge when declared twice (useful for augmenting libraries); types cannot be reopened.
Unions (`type Status = 'Pending' | 'Shipped'`) and discriminated unions model API states precisely.
Utility types: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType help reuse types.
Generate API types from OpenAPI (openapi-typescript, NSwag) so front end and .NET back end stay in sync.
strict mode on; avoid any, prefer unknown with narrowing.
f: Types disappear at runtime: how do you validate API data?
With a runtime schema such as Zod, generating the TS type from the schema.
interface or type for React props?
Either; teams pick one convention. I use type for props with unions, interface for public object contracts.
p1-70.y: TypeScript catches mistakes at compile time, gives great auto-complete, and makes large code bases safer to change. Interface and type are similar: interface is good for object shapes and can be extended or merged, while type can also describe unions, intersections and other combinations. I use interface for props and API models, and type for unions like status values.
p1-70.k: typescript, interface vs type, type safety, union types

p1-71.q: Angular is a complete, opinionated framework (TypeScript, DI, router, forms, HttpClient, RxJS, CLI) suited to large teams that want one standard way; React is a UI library focused on components, where you choose routing, state and data libraries yourself, giving flexibility and a huge ecosystem. IRT has both: Angular modules in older areas and React for newer reusable components.
i: Angular: two-way binding options, modules (now standalone components), signals for fine-grained reactivity (Angular 16+), strong conventions.
React: one-way data flow, JSX, hooks, many meta-frameworks (Next.js).
Learning curve: Angular steeper (RxJS, DI); React simpler core but more choices.
Change detection: Angular zone.js or signals; React re-renders and reconciles a virtual DOM.
Choose by team skills, existing codebase and the need for built-in structure.
f: Can they coexist?
Yes, through micro-frontends or by mounting components in separate parts of the app, as in IRT.
What are Angular signals?
Reactive values that notify dependents precisely, reducing reliance on zone.js change detection.
p1-71.y: Angular is a full framework with everything built in, like routing, forms and dependency injection, and a strong structure, which suits large teams that want conventions. React is a library focused on the UI, more flexible, where you choose your own libraries. Both are good. Our team used React because of its ecosystem and the team's experience.

p1-72.q: JavaScript runs on one thread with a call stack; asynchronous work (timers, I/O, fetch) is handled by the browser or Node, and when it completes its callback is queued. The event loop takes the next task when the stack is empty, but first drains all microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) after each task, then the browser may render.
i: Order: synchronous code, then microtasks (promises), then the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, events).
Long synchronous work blocks everything, including rendering and clicks; split it or use Web Workers.
Node has phases (timers, poll for I/O, check for setImmediate) and process.nextTick, which runs before promise microtasks.
await is syntax over promises, so code after await runs as a microtask.
f: Can a microtask loop starve rendering?
Yes; endlessly queuing microtasks blocks the next task and paint.
setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately?
No; at least after the current task and all microtasks, and browsers clamp nested timers.
p1-72.y: JavaScript runs on one thread with a call stack. When something async happens, like a timer or a network call, the callback waits in a queue. The event loop takes the next item from the queue when the stack is empty. Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before timers, which are macrotasks. That's why a long synchronous loop freezes the page.
p1-72.k: event loop, call stack, microtask, macrotask, javascript, async

p1-73.q: I watch for XSS (never inject unsanitised HTML; React escapes by default), reverse tabnabbing (rel="noopener noreferrer"), token storage (prefer HttpOnly secure cookies or in-memory tokens over localStorage), CSRF with cookie auth (SameSite plus anti-forgery tokens), a strict Content Security Policy, dependency vulnerabilities, and sensitive data exposed in the browser.
i: dangerouslySetInnerHTML only with DOMPurify; avoid href with user-controlled "javascript:" URLs.
CSP with nonces or hashes blocks injected scripts; add frame-ancestors to stop clickjacking.
Never trust the UI for authorisation: hidden buttons are not security.
Keep secrets out of front-end bundles; anything in JS is public.
npm audit, Dependabot/Snyk and lockfiles for supply-chain risk.
I fixed reverse tabnabbing in IRT on [about 40] links and added the ESLint rule so it cannot return.
f: Why is localStorage risky for tokens?
Any XSS can read it; HttpOnly cookies are not readable by scripts.
What does CSP do?
Tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles and frames are allowed, limiting XSS impact.
p1-73.y: The main ones are XSS, so I never insert raw HTML and let React escape output, and I add a Content Security Policy. Then token storage: I prefer secure HttpOnly cookies over local storage. Also CSRF protection, dependency vulnerabilities, and tabnabbing on links that open in a new tab. I actually fixed a tabnabbing issue across about [40] links by adding rel noopener noreferrer.
p1-73.k: frontend security, xss, csrf, csp, tabnabbing, owasp

p1-74.q: Node.js runs JavaScript on one main thread with an event loop and non-blocking I/O handled by libuv (thread pool for file system, DNS and crypto); one process can serve thousands of concurrent connections as long as no request does heavy CPU work. It fits I/O-heavy APIs, gateways, real-time and glue services, not CPU-heavy computation.
i: CPU work blocks every request; move it to worker_threads, a separate service or another language.
Scale across cores with multiple processes (cluster, PM2) or containers.
Streams handle large files and responses with backpressure and low memory.
Event loop lag is the key health metric; monitor it.
My Node service was [the build-log summariser]: fetch logs, parse text, return JSON, a perfect I/O-bound fit.
f: Is Node single-threaded?
JavaScript execution is, but libuv uses a thread pool and the OS handles network I/O asynchronously.
What blocks the event loop?
Synchronous fs calls, big JSON.parse, heavy regex or loops, and crypto without async APIs.
p1-74.y: Node.js runs JavaScript on one main thread with an event loop, and all input and output, like network and files, is non-blocking. So one process can handle many concurrent connections well. It is a good fit for I/O-heavy services, like APIs that call other services or process text. It is a poor fit for heavy CPU work, unless you move it to worker threads.
p1-74.k: node.js, concurrency, event loop, non-blocking, libuv

p1-75.q: I structure a Node/TypeScript microservice by feature with clear layers: routes/controllers for HTTP, services for business logic, repositories or clients for data and external APIs, schemas (Zod) for validation, central config and logging, and one error-handling middleware; plus health endpoints, tests and a Dockerfile, using the same pipeline template as our .NET services.
i: Config validated at startup (Zod over process.env), failing fast on missing values.
Logging with pino (JSON) including correlation ids, shipped to CloudWatch.
Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close connections.
Dependency injection by constructor parameters or a small container, so tests can pass fakes.
strict TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier, Jest/Vitest, supertest for API tests.
c:
const Config = z.object({ PORT: z.coerce.number().default(8080), ADO_URL: z.string().url() });
export const config = Config.parse(process.env);
f: Express or Fastify?
Fastify for performance and built-in schema validation; Express for familiarity and ecosystem.
How do you share types with the front end?
A shared package or types generated from OpenAPI.
p1-75.y: I structure a Node TypeScript service in layers: routes or controllers for HTTP, services for business logic, and a data layer for the database or external calls. Configuration comes from environment variables and is validated at startup, inputs are validated with a schema library like Zod, and errors go through one error middleware. It has the same logging, health checks and Docker setup as our .NET services.
p1-75.k: node.js, typescript, microservice structure, express, layers

p1-76.q: FastAPI is a modern async Python framework built on Starlette and Pydantic: type hints drive request validation, serialisation and automatic OpenAPI docs, and it is very fast for Python. Flask is a minimal, synchronous-first micro-framework where you add validation, docs and structure yourself; simple and flexible with a huge ecosystem.
i: FastAPI: dependency injection with Depends, async endpoints, automatic /docs, Pydantic v2 performance.
Flask: great for small internal tools and templates; async support exists but the ecosystem is mostly sync.
Both run in containers behind a reverse proxy (uvicorn/gunicorn).
I used FastAPI for [the vendor file pre-validation service] and Flask for [a small release-status endpoint].
f: Why is FastAPI fast?
Async I/O on Starlette/uvicorn and Pydantic's Rust-based validation core in v2.
When would you still pick Flask?
Very small apps, server-rendered pages, or teams already on Flask.
p1-76.y: Flask is a small, simple framework where you add what you need, and it is synchronous by default. FastAPI is newer and async-first, uses Python type hints with Pydantic for automatic validation, and generates OpenAPI documentation for free. For a new API I would choose FastAPI. We used it for a [vendor file validation service].

p1-77.q: FastAPI endpoints declared with async def run on the event loop, so they must await I/O and avoid blocking calls; plain def endpoints run in a thread pool automatically. Validation comes from Pydantic models and type hints: FastAPI parses the request into models, returns 422 with detailed errors when validation fails, and uses the same models to generate OpenAPI.
i: Blocking libraries inside async def (requests, sync DB drivers) block the whole loop; use httpx or async drivers, or a plain def endpoint.
Pydantic validators (field_validator, model_validator) express business rules such as "site code must match pattern".
response_model filters output and documents it.
Background tasks for small post-response work; Celery or queues for heavy work.
f: What status does FastAPI return for invalid input?
422 Unprocessable Entity with a list of field errors.
def vs async def?
async def for non-blocking async I/O; def for blocking code, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool.
p1-77.y: In FastAPI, I declare endpoints with async def, so slow input and output, like database or HTTP calls, don't block the server. For validation, I describe the request as a Pydantic model with type hints, and FastAPI checks every request automatically and returns a 422 with the exact field errors if something is wrong. The same models also produce the API documentation.

p1-78.q: Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core solve the same problems with similar concepts: DI containers, middleware/filter chains, controllers with attribute routing, configuration with profiles/environments, ORMs (JPA/Hibernate vs EF Core), and production features (Actuator vs health checks and metrics). Differences are mostly ecosystem and language: Java/JVM with Spring's annotations and auto-configuration vs C#/.NET with explicit Program.cs setup.
i: Startup: Spring auto-configures from the classpath; ASP.NET Core registers explicitly in Program.cs.
Performance: both are fast; .NET often leads TechEmpower benchmarks, Java has GraalVM native images, .NET has native AOT.
Concurrency: Java 21 virtual threads vs .NET async/await.
I can work in Spring Boot by mapping concepts, as in Part 9's comparison table.
f: What is Spring's equivalent of middleware?
Servlet filters and Spring Security's filter chain; interceptors for MVC-level concerns.
Biggest mindset change?
Annotation-driven magic in Spring vs explicit configuration in modern .NET.
p1-78.y: Spring Boot and ASP.NET Core are very similar. Both have dependency injection built in, controllers, middleware or filters, configuration by environment, and good ORMs: JPA with Hibernate on Java, and EF Core on .NET. The main differences are the language and ecosystem. Since the ideas map almost one to one, I can pick up Spring Boot quickly with my ASP.NET Core background.
p1-78.k: spring boot, asp.net core, java, comparison

p1-79.q: I keep services consistent across .NET, Node.js and Python with shared standards rather than shared code: REST and event contracts defined in OpenAPI and schemas, the same structured logging fields and correlation ids, the same health endpoints, Docker conventions, one Azure DevOps pipeline template, and the same security and testing rules.
i: Contracts first: OpenAPI and JSON Schema reviewed before implementation; generated clients.
Observability: same log fields (service, env, version, correlationId) and OpenTelemetry in every language.
Pipeline template: build, test, scan (SonarQube, dependency scan), image build, deploy, identical stages.
Templates/scaffolds per language so new services start compliant.
Security: same auth library patterns, secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, no secrets in env files.
f: Do you share code libraries across languages?
No; share contracts and conventions, and keep per-language libraries small.
How do you enforce it?
Templates, pipeline gates and review checklists, not documents alone.
p1-79.y: I keep services consistent with shared standards rather than shared code. Every service, whether .NET, Node or Python, follows the same API and event contracts, the same structured logging fields and correlation ids, the same health endpoints, the same Docker conventions, and one pipeline template in Azure DevOps. So any engineer can operate any service, whatever the language.

p1-80.q: Node uses npm/pnpm with package.json and a committed lockfile (package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml) and `npm ci` in pipelines for reproducible installs; Python uses virtual environments with pinned dependencies (requirements.txt with hashes, or Poetry/uv with a lock file). In both I scan for vulnerabilities, update regularly with Dependabot or Renovate, and use internal feeds (Azure Artifacts) as a proxy.
i: Semantic versioning ranges (^, ~) are resolved once into the lockfile; builds use the lockfile only.
Separate dev and prod dependencies to keep images small.
npm audit, pip-audit, Snyk or Mend in CI; fail on criticals.
Supply chain: verify package names (typosquatting), restrict install scripts, use upstream proxy feeds.
.NET equivalent: central package management with Directory.Packages.props and packages.lock.json.
f: npm install vs npm ci?
npm ci installs exactly from the lockfile, fails if it is out of sync, and is faster for CI.
Why pin Python dependencies?
Unpinned installs can pull new versions and break builds unexpectedly.
p1-80.y: In Node I use npm with a committed package-lock file and npm ci in pipelines, so builds are repeatable. In Python I use a virtual environment with pinned versions in requirements or a Poetry lock file. In both, I scan for vulnerabilities in the pipeline and update dependencies regularly, a few at a time, with tests running.
p1-80.k: dependency management, npm, package-lock, pip, poetry, vulnerabilities

p1-81.q: I choose by fit for the job, team skills and operability: .NET for core domain services with complex logic, transactions and performance; Node.js for I/O-bound glue, real-time and front-end-adjacent services; Python for data processing, validation and scripting or ML libraries. A new language must justify the extra cost of tooling, support and on-call knowledge.
i: Default to the team's main stack (.NET in IRT) unless there is a clear benefit.
Consider libraries available (Pydantic for validation, Azure DevOps SDKs in C#), performance needs and hosting (Lambda cold starts).
Operational cost: pipelines, monitoring, security patching and who can support it at 2 a.m.
Document the decision in an ADR (architecture decision record).
f: Have you said no to a language choice?
[Yes, a proposal to write a small service in Go]; nobody else could support it, so we used .NET.
What is an ADR?
A short document recording a decision, its context, options and consequences.
p1-81.y: I choose based on the team and the job, not personal taste. For core business services I default to .NET, because the team knows it, it is fast and our tooling is built around it. I'd choose Node for small input-output heavy tools, and Python for data handling or scripts. The service must fit our standards for logging, testing and deployment, whatever the language.
p1-81.k: language choice, technology choice, .net, node, python

p2-1.q: I use ECS (on Fargate or EC2) for long-running containerised services and workers with steady traffic, Lambda for short, event-driven or spiky work (S3 events, queue triggers, schedules) where pay-per-use and zero servers win, and plain EC2 when I need full control of the OS, special software, or licensing that containers or Lambda cannot handle.
i: Lambda limits: 15-minute max duration, up to 10 GB memory, cold starts, concurrency limits; costly at high steady load.
ECS Fargate: no servers to patch, per-task CPU/memory billing; ECS on EC2 is cheaper at scale and allows GPUs or daemon tasks.
EC2: legacy apps, Windows services with installers, custom agents; you own patching, scaling and AMIs.
Cost rule of thumb: spiky or low traffic favours Lambda; constant high traffic favours containers.
In IRT: .NET APIs and RabbitMQ workers on ECS, Lambda for [event-driven pieces such as S3 file arrival notifications], EC2 for [the on-prem-like deployment nodes and tooling servers].
f: Can Lambda run a full ASP.NET Core API?
Yes, with the Lambda ASP.NET Core hosting adapter, but cold starts and per-request cost need checking.
Fargate vs ECS on EC2?
Fargate for simplicity; EC2 capacity providers for cost control at scale or special hardware.
p2-1.y: I use ECS with Fargate for long-running services like our APIs, because containers run all the time with no servers to manage. I use Lambda for short, event-driven tasks, like reacting to a file landing in S3, where I pay only when it runs. I use EC2 when I need full control of the machine, special software, or very steady heavy load. Our IRT services run on ECS.
p2-1.k: ecs, lambda, ec2, fargate, compute choice, aws

p2-2.q: An ECS cluster is a logical group of capacity (Fargate or EC2 instances); a task definition is the versioned blueprint (images, CPU, memory, ports, environment, secrets, IAM roles, logging); a task is a running copy of it; a service keeps the desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones, registers them with a load balancer and performs rolling or blue/green deployments.
i: Two IAM roles: the task execution role (pull images from ECR, write logs, read secrets at start) and the task role (what your code may call, e.g. S3, SQS).
Networking: awsvpc mode gives each task its own ENI and security group.
Deployments: rolling with minimumHealthyPercent/maximumPercent and the deployment circuit breaker with automatic rollback, or CodeDeploy blue/green.
Service auto scaling with target tracking on CPU, memory or ALB request count per target.
Service Connect or Cloud Map for service discovery between services.
Logs via the awslogs driver to CloudWatch Logs, or FireLens.
f: Task role vs execution role?
Execution role is used by ECS to start the task; the task role is assumed by your application code at runtime.
What happens when a task fails its health check?
The service stops it and starts a replacement, and the ALB stops routing to it.
p2-2.y: In ECS, a cluster is the logical group where things run. A task definition is like a blueprint: the image, CPU, memory, environment variables, secrets and IAM role. A task is one running copy of it, and a service keeps the desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones and connects them to the load balancer. With Fargate, AWS runs the servers for us.
p2-2.k: ecs, cluster, task definition, task, service, fargate

p2-3.q: API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs: it receives requests, authenticates and authorises them (JWT, Cognito, Lambda authorizers, IAM), throttles and applies usage plans, validates and transforms requests, and routes them to Lambda, HTTP backends or AWS services, with logging and metrics built in.
i: REST APIs (v1) have more features (usage plans, API keys, request validation, caching, WAF); HTTP APIs (v2) are cheaper and faster with JWT authorizers.
Private integrations reach services in a VPC through VPC Link to an NLB or ALB.
Limits: 29-second default integration timeout (raisable for some APIs), 10 MB payload.
Throttling is token-bucket based per account, stage and method; returns 429.
Custom domains, stages (dev, uat, prod), canary releases per stage.
f: API Gateway or ALB?
API Gateway for API management and serverless; ALB for container services with high steady traffic (Part 5 has the table).
How do you secure it?
JWT/OAuth authorizers, WAF, resource policies, throttling and mutual TLS where needed.
p2-3.y: API Gateway is the front door for APIs. It handles routing to backends like Lambda or HTTP services, authentication with JWT or IAM, throttling, request validation, usage plans and API keys. So the services behind it can focus on business logic. For containers with heavy traffic, an Application Load Balancer is often cheaper, so the choice depends on what features we need.
p2-3.k: api gateway, throttling, routing, authentication, aws

p2-4.q: A cold start is the extra latency when Lambda creates a new execution environment: download code, start the runtime, run initialisation, then the handler. It happens on the first request, after idle periods and when scaling out. Reduce it with smaller packages, less work at init, more memory (more CPU), Provisioned Concurrency, SnapStart and, for .NET, native AOT.
i: .NET options: ReadyToRun or native AOT (`PublishAot`) cut startup a lot; avoid heavy reflection and DI scanning at init.
SnapStart (Java, Python and .NET 8 managed runtime) snapshots the initialised environment and restores it.
Provisioned Concurrency keeps environments warm (costs money); schedule it for business hours.
VPC cold-start penalty was largely fixed by Hyperplane ENIs, but still keep dependencies light.
Initialise SDK clients outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.
f: Does memory affect cold start?
Yes; CPU scales with memory, so more memory often means faster init and can even reduce cost.
How do you measure it?
The Init Duration field in REPORT log lines, or X-Ray traces.
p2-4.y: A cold start is the extra delay when Lambda has to create a new environment and load my code before the first request. For .NET it can be noticeable. I reduce it with more memory, which also gives more CPU, smaller packages, Native AOT or SnapStart, and provisioned concurrency to keep instances warm for critical functions. For steady traffic, a container on ECS avoids cold starts completely.
p2-4.k: lambda, cold start, provisioned concurrency, snapstart, native aot

p2-5.q: DynamoDB modelling starts from access patterns, not entities: list every query, choose a partition key with high cardinality and even traffic, a sort key for ranges and ordering, and add GSIs for other patterns. Often several entity types share one table (single-table design) with generic keys like PK = STUDY#42, SK = SITE#7.
i: Item collections: items sharing a partition key can be fetched together with one Query.
Avoid scans; every request should be GetItem or Query by key.
Hot partitions: spread writes with sharded keys if one key gets most traffic.
Item limit 400 KB; large payloads go to S3 with a pointer.
Use conditional writes for idempotency and optimistic locking (version attribute), TTL for expiry, Streams for change events.
c:
PK            SK                  Attributes
IDEMP#a1b2    REQ                 status=Done, response=..., ttl=1718000000
STUDY#42      SITE#007            name, country
STUDY#42      SHIPMENT#2024-06-01#881   status, kitCount
f: Single-table design always?
No; it optimises known patterns but is hard to evolve; separate tables are fine for simple cases.
Query vs Scan?
Query reads one partition by key; Scan reads the whole table and is slow and expensive.
p2-5.y: In DynamoDB I start from the access patterns, not from tables and joins. I choose a partition key that spreads load evenly and a sort key for ranges, like customer id and order date. Often several entity types live in one table. For other query patterns I add global secondary indexes. Getting the keys wrong is expensive to change later, so I design them carefully up front.
p2-5.k: dynamodb, partition key, sort key, gsi, single table design, nosql

p2-6.q: The main patterns are cache-aside (app reads cache, on miss loads from DB and stores it), read-through, write-through (write cache and DB together), write-behind (write cache, persist later) and refresh-ahead. ElastiCache (Redis or Valkey) is AWS's managed in-memory cache, used for shared caches, sessions, rate limits, distributed locks and token denylists.
i: Cache-aside is the most common and simplest; set TTLs and invalidate on writes.
Stampede protection: locks or HybridCache, jittered TTLs, early refresh.
Eviction policies (allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl) and memory limits must be set deliberately.
Redis replication with Multi-AZ failover; cluster mode for sharding.
Never cache without a plan for invalidation and consistency.
In IRT: [study configuration and reference data] cached; the logout fix used ElastiCache for the jti denylist with TTLs.
f: Redis vs Memcached?
Redis has data structures, persistence options, replication and pub/sub; Memcached is simpler, multithreaded, cache-only.
What is a hit ratio?
The share of reads served from cache; monitor it to judge if caching works.
p2-6.y: The most common is cache-aside: the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and stores the result with an expiry time. Write-through updates the cache when writing the database. I always set TTLs and invalidate on changes. We used ElastiCache Redis for reference data, and also for our token logout denylist, where lookups take about [1 millisecond].
p2-6.k: caching, elasticache, redis, cache-aside, write-through, ttl

p2-7.q: ALB (Application Load Balancer) works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC): routing by path, host, headers and query, TLS termination, redirects, OIDC authentication and WebSockets. NLB (Network Load Balancer) works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS): extreme throughput, very low latency, static IPs/Elastic IPs and source IP preservation.
i: ALB targets: instances, IPs, Lambda; NLB targets: instances, IPs and even an ALB.
Use NLB for non-HTTP protocols, PrivateLink services, or when clients need fixed IPs.
API Gateway private integrations (REST APIs) need an NLB via VPC Link.
Health checks: ALB uses HTTP paths; NLB can use TCP or HTTP.
Gateway Load Balancer is the third type, for inline appliances (firewalls).
f: Which one for your .NET APIs?
ALB, for path routing to several ECS services and HTTP health checks.
Can ALB give static IPs?
Not directly; put an NLB or Global Accelerator in front.
p2-7.y: An Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, so it understands HTTP: it can route by path or host name, terminate TLS, and do health checks on HTTP endpoints. A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 with TCP and UDP, so it is extremely fast, keeps static IPs, and suits non-HTTP traffic. For our web APIs on ECS we use an ALB.
p2-7.k: alb, nlb, load balancer, layer 7, layer 4, aws

p2-8.q: S3 is durable object storage (eleven nines durability) used for files, backups, data lakes, static websites, logs and artifacts. A presigned URL grants temporary access to one object operation (GET or PUT) using the signer's permissions, so clients can download or upload directly to S3 without AWS credentials and without passing through your API.
i: Presigned URLs expire (up to 7 days with IAM user credentials, shorter with temporary credentials); keep them short (minutes).
Uploads: presigned PUT or POST (POST policies can restrict size and content type); multipart for large files.
Storage classes and lifecycle rules (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier) cut cost.
Security: Block Public Access, bucket policies, SSE-KMS, versioning, Object Lock for WORM retention (useful for GxP evidence).
Events: S3 notifications to Lambda, SQS or EventBridge trigger processing.
f: Who can use a presigned URL?
Anyone who has it until it expires, so treat it like a short-lived secret.
Why upload directly to S3?
It offloads large transfers from your API, avoiding timeouts and memory pressure.
p2-8.y: S3 is object storage for files: uploads, exports, backups, logs and static websites. It is very durable and cheap. A presigned URL is a temporary link, signed with our credentials, that lets a client upload or download one specific object directly, without going through our API and without AWS credentials. It is great for large file uploads, like CSV imports.
p2-8.k: s3, presigned url, object storage, file upload, aws

p2-9.q: Least privilege means every identity gets only the actions on the specific resources it needs, nothing more. I do it with roles (not users) for workloads, narrow policies scoped by resource ARN and conditions, separate roles per service, permission boundaries and SCPs as guardrails, and I refine policies with IAM Access Analyzer and CloudTrail data.
i: Start from AWS managed policies only for prototypes; move to customer-managed, resource-scoped policies.
Conditions: aws:SourceVpce, aws:PrincipalTag, kms:EncryptionContext, time or MFA requirements.
Access Analyzer generates policies from actual CloudTrail activity and finds public or cross-account access.
SSO (IAM Identity Center) for people with short-lived credentials; no long-term access keys.
Separate AWS accounts per environment limit blast radius.
f: Identity-based vs resource-based policies?
Identity policies attach to users and roles; resource policies attach to resources (S3 buckets, KMS keys) and can grant cross-account access.
How do explicit denies work?
An explicit Deny anywhere (policy, SCP, boundary) always wins over Allows.
p2-9.y: Least privilege means every identity gets only the permissions it needs, nothing more. I give each ECS service its own task role, scope actions to specific resources like one bucket or one secret, and avoid wildcards. I use roles with temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys. I review permissions regularly with IAM Access Analyzer and remove what isn't used.
p2-9.k: iam, least privilege, roles, policies, task role, security

p2-10.q: A typical layout is a VPC across at least two availability zones with public subnets for load balancers and NAT gateways, private subnets for ECS tasks and Lambda, and isolated database subnets for RDS and ElastiCache; security groups allow only the needed flows (ALB to app, app to database), and VPC endpoints keep AWS traffic private.
i: Ingress: Route 53, CloudFront/WAF, ALB or API Gateway in public subnets.
Egress: NAT gateway per AZ for internet calls; gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (free), interface endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch.
Security groups reference each other (app SG allows from ALB SG) instead of IP ranges.
Connectivity to on-prem or other VPCs: Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, Transit Gateway.
VPC Flow Logs for network troubleshooting and audit.
f: Why NAT per AZ?
So one AZ failure does not cut outbound access for the others, and to avoid cross-AZ data charges.
How do private tasks pull ECR images without NAT?
Interface endpoints for ECR API and Docker plus the S3 gateway endpoint.
p2-10.y: A typical layout is one VPC across at least two availability zones. Public subnets hold only the load balancer and NAT gateway. Private subnets hold the ECS services, and separate private subnets hold databases like RDS. Security groups allow only the needed traffic, for example the database accepts only the service's security group. Outbound internet goes through NAT, and AWS services through VPC endpoints.
p2-10.k: vpc, subnets, network layout, security groups, nat gateway, availability zones

p2-11.q: Infrastructure as code defines servers, networks, databases and permissions in versioned files (Terraform, CloudFormation, Bicep) that tools apply automatically. It makes environments reproducible and consistent, reviewable through pull requests, auditable, and quick to recreate, removing manual console changes and drift.
i: Declarative (desired state) vs imperative (steps); most IaC tools are declarative.
Benefits in GxP: change history, peer review and repeatable environments support validation.
Plan or change sets show the impact before applying.
Testing IaC: validate, lint (tflint, cfn-lint), policy as code (Checkov, OPA), and plan reviews.
Modules and templates standardise patterns such as "ECS service with ALB and alarms".
f: What is configuration drift?
The real infrastructure differing from the code because of manual changes.
IaC vs configuration management?
IaC provisions resources; tools like Ansible configure software on them (with overlap).
p2-11.y: Infrastructure as code means defining servers, networks, databases and permissions in code files, like Terraform or CloudFormation, instead of clicking in the console. The benefits are that environments are repeatable and consistent, every change is reviewed in a pull request and tracked in Git, and we can rebuild an environment quickly. In a regulated product, that history is also great evidence.
p2-11.k: infrastructure as code, iac, terraform, cloudformation

p2-12.q: CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC service: JSON/YAML templates, state managed by AWS in stacks, change sets, drift detection and day-one support for many AWS features. Terraform is HashiCorp's multi-cloud tool using HCL with providers for AWS, Azure and many SaaS tools, an explicit state file, a large module ecosystem and plan/apply workflow.
i: State: CloudFormation stores it for you; Terraform needs a remote backend (S3 with locking).
Rollback: CloudFormation rolls back failed stacks automatically; Terraform stops and leaves partial changes to fix forward.
Abstractions: CDK generates CloudFormation from TypeScript or C#; Terraform has modules and CDKTF.
Licensing: Terraform moved to the Business Source License in 2023; OpenTofu is the open-source fork.
In IRT [core stacks were in CloudFormation and newer tooling in Terraform]; Part 9 explains why both.
f: Which would you choose for a new AWS-only project?
Either works; CloudFormation/CDK for AWS-native teams, Terraform if multi-cloud or SaaS resources matter.
What is a change set?
A preview of what a CloudFormation update will add, modify or replace.
p2-12.y: CloudFormation is AWS's own service, so the state is managed by AWS, and it supports AWS features well. Terraform works with many providers, not only AWS, has a nice plan step showing exactly what will change, and a big module ecosystem, but I must manage its state file. In my work, core platform stacks were in CloudFormation and newer pieces used Terraform.

p2-13.q: Terraform state is a JSON file mapping your configuration to real resource IDs and attributes; Terraform uses it to plan changes. I keep it in a remote backend (S3 with versioning and encryption, with DynamoDB or S3 native locking), one state per environment and component, with access restricted because state can contain secrets.
i: Locking prevents two applies corrupting state.
terraform state mv/rm and import blocks refactor or adopt resources without destroying them.
Smaller states (per component) reduce blast radius and speed up plans.
Never edit state by hand; never commit it to Git.
Outputs and terraform_remote_state or data sources share values between states.
f: What if state is lost?
Terraform forgets resources; restore from S3 versioning or re-import (Part 6 has the detail).
Why separate states per environment?
An apply in dev can never touch production resources.
p2-13.y: Terraform state is a file that maps my code to the real resources it created, so Terraform knows what to change. I store it remotely, in an S3 bucket with encryption and versioning, with locking so two people can't apply at the same time. It can contain secrets, so access is restricted. I keep separate state for each environment.
p2-13.k: terraform state, remote state, s3 backend, state locking

p2-14.q: The workflow is write, init, plan, apply: write HCL, `terraform init` downloads providers and configures the backend, `terraform plan` shows the diff between code, state and reality, and `terraform apply` executes the reviewed plan. In pipelines the plan is saved, reviewed in the pull request, approved and then applied exactly.
i: fmt and validate in CI; tflint and Checkov for best practices and security.
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan` guarantees what was reviewed is what runs.
Destroy or replace actions (-/+) need extra scrutiny.
Lock provider versions (.terraform.lock.hcl) and module versions.
Run per environment with separate backends and tfvars.
f: What does refresh do?
Updates state from real infrastructure; plan does it by default.
Who can apply to production?
Only the pipeline identity after approval, not individuals from laptops.
p2-14.y: The workflow is: write or change the code, run terraform init to set up providers and the backend, terraform plan to see exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed, then review that plan, and terraform apply to make the changes. In a team, the plan runs in the pipeline on the pull request, and apply runs after approval.

p2-15.q: Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches the IaC code, usually from manual console changes, hotfixes or other tools. I avoid it by making the pipeline the only way to change infrastructure (read-only console access), detecting it regularly (scheduled terraform plan, CloudFormation drift detection, AWS Config rules) and fixing it by updating code or re-applying.
i: Use lifecycle ignore_changes only for fields legitimately managed elsewhere (desired count changed by autoscaling).
Emergency changes are allowed but must be back-ported to code within a set time.
Tag resources with "managed-by" so manual resources stand out.
Alerts when scheduled plans show changes.
f: Drift detected in production: overwrite or adopt?
Understand why first; if the manual change was correct, put it in code; otherwise apply code to restore.
How does ECS autoscaling cause false drift?
The desired count changes; ignore it in Terraform so plans stay clean.
p2-15.y: Drift is when the real infrastructure no longer matches the code, usually because someone changed something manually in the console. I avoid it by making all changes through code and pipelines, limiting console write access, and running regular plans or drift detection to spot differences. When drift is found, we either update the code or revert the manual change.
p2-15.k: drift, drift detection, infrastructure as code, terraform, cloudformation

p2-16.q: An image is an immutable, layered template containing the app and its filesystem; a container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process and network. A Dockerfile is the recipe of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, USER, ENTRYPOINT) that builds the image layer by layer.
i: Layers are cached and shared; order instructions from least to most frequently changing.
Images are identified by digest (sha256), tags are movable labels; deploy by digest or immutable tags.
Containers share the host kernel, unlike VMs, so they start in milliseconds.
OCI standard means images run on Docker, containerd, ECS, Kubernetes alike.
f: Container vs VM?
Containers isolate processes and share the kernel; VMs virtualise hardware with their own OS.
Why are images immutable?
Reproducibility: the same image runs identically in every environment.
p2-16.y: An image is a read-only package with the app and everything it needs to run. A container is a running instance of that image, like an object created from a class. A Dockerfile is the recipe that builds the image, step by step: the base image, copying files, building, and the command to start. We build one image per service and run it everywhere.

p2-17.q: A production .NET Dockerfile is multi-stage: build and publish with the SDK image, then copy only the published output into a small runtime image (aspnet, Alpine or chiseled), run as a non-root user, expose port 8080, set health checks in the orchestrator, and keep secrets out of the image.
i: Copy the .csproj files and restore first to cache NuGet restore layers.
.NET 8+ images run on port 8080 and include a non-root `app` user (`USER $APP_UID`).
Chiseled Ubuntu images have no shell or package manager: smaller and fewer CVEs.
.dockerignore excludes bin, obj, .git and secrets.
Pin base image versions or digests; scan with Trivy in CI.
c:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["Shipments.Api/Shipments.Api.csproj", "Shipments.Api/"]
RUN dotnet restore "Shipments.Api/Shipments.Api.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "Shipments.Api/Shipments.Api.csproj" -c Release -o /app --no-restore

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0-noble-chiseled
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app .
USER $APP_UID
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Shipments.Api.dll"]
f: How do you debug a chiseled container without a shell?
Use logs, a sidecar or ephemeral debug container, or a debug image variant in non-production.
Why multi-stage?
The SDK and source never reach the final image, making it smaller and safer.
p2-17.y: I use a multi-stage Dockerfile. The first stage uses the SDK image to restore and publish, copying the project files first so the restore layer is cached. The final stage uses the small ASP.NET runtime image, or a chiseled image, copies only the published output, runs as a non-root user and sets the entry point. The result is small, secure and fast to build.
p2-17.k: dockerfile, multi-stage build, .net docker, non-root, chiseled image

p2-18.q: The core Kubernetes objects are Pod (one or more containers sharing network and storage), Deployment (declares replicas and rolling updates through ReplicaSets), Service (stable virtual IP and DNS for a set of pods), Ingress (HTTP routing from outside), ConfigMap and Secret (configuration), Namespace (isolation), plus StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job/CronJob, PersistentVolumeClaim and HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
i: Labels and selectors connect objects: a Service finds pods by labels.
Controllers continuously reconcile actual state to desired state.
StatefulSet gives stable identities and storage (databases, brokers); DaemonSet runs one pod per node (log agents).
Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor to Ingress.
RBAC (Role, RoleBinding, ServiceAccount) controls who can do what.
f: Pod vs container?
A pod is the scheduling unit and can hold several tightly coupled containers (sidecars).
Why not create pods directly?
Bare pods are not recreated if they die; Deployments manage them.
p2-18.y: A Pod is the smallest unit, one or more containers running together. A Deployment manages pods, keeps the right number running and does rolling updates. A Service gives pods a stable name and load-balances to them. An Ingress routes outside HTTP traffic to services. ConfigMaps and Secrets hold configuration, and a Namespace groups resources.
p2-18.k: kubernetes, pod, deployment, service, ingress, configmap, secret, namespace

p2-19.q: A Deployment YAML declares the replica count, the label selector, and the pod template: container image and tag, ports, environment from ConfigMaps and Secrets, resource requests and limits, liveness, readiness and startup probes, security context, and the update strategy (maxSurge, maxUnavailable).
i: Requests drive scheduling and autoscaling; limits cap usage (memory limit breach = OOMKilled).
Probes gate traffic and restarts; readiness must reflect real ability to serve.
securityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop capabilities.
Graceful shutdown: terminationGracePeriodSeconds and a preStop hook so load balancers drain.
Templating with Helm or Kustomize per environment.
f: Should you set CPU limits?
Many teams set only CPU requests, because CPU limits cause throttling; memory limits are essential.
What does maxUnavailable 0 mean?
Never go below the desired replicas during a rollout.
p2-19.y: A Deployment YAML has the number of replicas, a selector that matches the pod labels, and a pod template. The template lists the container image and tag, ports, environment variables from ConfigMaps and Secrets, CPU and memory requests and limits, and liveness and readiness probes. It also has the rolling update strategy, like how many pods can be down at once.
p2-19.k: kubernetes, deployment yaml, replicas, probes, resources, rolling update

p2-20.q: A liveness probe asks "is the process healthy, or should it be restarted?"; a readiness probe asks "can it receive traffic right now?", and failing removes the pod from load balancing without restarting it; a startup probe protects slow-starting apps by disabling the other probes until startup succeeds.
i: Liveness must be cheap and only check the process itself; checking the database in liveness causes restart storms when the DB blips.
Readiness can check critical dependencies and warm-up state.
ASP.NET Core health checks: tag checks and map /health/live and /health/ready with predicates.
ECS has container health checks and ALB target health checks with similar roles.
f: What happens if readiness fails on all pods?
The Service has no endpoints, so requests fail; that is why readiness checks must be well designed.
Why a startup probe?
So a slow start (migrations, cache warm-up) is not killed by the liveness probe.
p2-20.y: A liveness probe checks if the app is still alive, and if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. A readiness probe checks if it can take traffic, and if it fails, the pod is removed from the service but not restarted. A startup probe gives slow-starting apps time before the other probes begin. In .NET I map these to health check endpoints.
p2-20.k: liveness probe, readiness probe, startup probe, health checks, kubernetes

p2-21.q: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration; Secrets hold sensitive values (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default, so enable encryption at rest and RBAC). Containers receive both as environment variables or mounted files; in AWS I prefer pulling secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store (ECS secrets, External Secrets Operator or the CSI driver) so they are rotated and audited centrally.
i: 12-factor: configuration via environment, same image for every environment.
Mounted files update when the ConfigMap changes (env vars do not); apps can watch files.
Immutable ConfigMaps improve performance and avoid accidental changes.
Never bake secrets into images or Git; scan for leaks.
In ECS: task definition environment for config, `secrets` referencing Secrets Manager ARNs for credentials.
f: Is a Kubernetes Secret secure?
Only with encryption at rest, RBAC and no broad read access; base64 is encoding, not encryption.
How does .NET read nested config from env vars?
Double underscore: Sftp__Vendors__DepotA__Host.
p2-21.y: A ConfigMap holds normal configuration, like URLs or feature flags, and a Secret holds sensitive values like passwords, which are only base64 encoded, so they need encryption and access control. Containers get them as environment variables or files. In ECS, we pull secrets from Secrets Manager and Parameter Store into the task at startup, and the code reads them through normal .NET configuration.
p2-21.k: configmap, secret, configuration, environment variables, secrets manager

p2-22.q: Kubernetes scales pods with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler based on metrics (CPU, memory, custom metrics like queue length via KEDA) and scales nodes with the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter; ECS scales tasks with Service Auto Scaling (target tracking on CPU, memory or ALB requests per target, step scaling on CloudWatch alarms) and scales EC2 capacity with capacity providers.
i: Target tracking: "keep average CPU near 60 percent"; the system adds or removes capacity automatically.
Scale on the real bottleneck: queue depth for workers, request count or latency for APIs.
Cooldowns and stabilisation windows prevent flapping; scale out fast, in slowly.
Requests must be set correctly for HPA CPU percentages to make sense.
Scheduled scaling for known peaks; minimum capacity for availability.
f: KEDA?
Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling: scales on external metrics such as RabbitMQ queue length, even to zero.
How do you scale RabbitMQ consumers on ECS?
Step scaling on a CloudWatch metric of queue depth or messages per consumer.
p2-22.y: In Kubernetes, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes pods based on CPU, memory or custom metrics, and a cluster autoscaler adds nodes when needed. In ECS, service auto scaling uses target tracking, for example keep CPU at 60 percent or a certain number of requests per target. In both cases, the app must be stateless and shut down gracefully.
p2-22.k: autoscaling, hpa, ecs service auto scaling, target tracking, scaling

p2-23.q: Docker builds and runs containers on a single host; Kubernetes is a portable orchestrator that schedules containers across a cluster with self-healing, scaling, service discovery and a huge ecosystem; ECS is AWS's own simpler orchestrator, deeply integrated with IAM, ALB and CloudWatch, without a control plane to manage.
i: Docker Compose is fine for local development and tests, not production orchestration.
Kubernetes: more power and portability, more complexity (networking, upgrades, add-ons).
ECS: fewer concepts, lower operational load, AWS lock-in.
EKS is managed Kubernetes on AWS; Fargate can run both ECS tasks and EKS pods.
IRT production runs on ECS; Kubernetes is used for [some internal workloads] (see Part 9 for the honest answer).
f: When choose Kubernetes over ECS?
Multi-cloud or on-prem portability, a platform team, or ecosystem needs (operators, service mesh).
Is Docker needed on Kubernetes nodes?
No; Kubernetes uses containerd or CRI-O; Docker-built images still run because they are OCI images.
p2-23.y: Docker builds and runs containers on one machine. Kubernetes and ECS are orchestrators that run many containers across many machines, handle scaling, restarts, rolling deployments and service discovery. Kubernetes is open source, portable and very powerful but complex. ECS is AWS's simpler, managed option. Our production runs on ECS.

p2-24.q: Continuous integration means every change is merged often and automatically built and tested; continuous delivery means every passing build is releasable and deployment to production is a push-button decision; continuous deployment goes further and deploys every passing change to production automatically, with no manual gate.
i: CI needs fast, reliable tests and trunk-based or short-lived branches.
Continuous delivery fits regulated products: automated up to production, with human approval and change control before release.
Continuous deployment needs strong automated tests, feature flags, monitoring and automatic rollback.
DORA metrics measure delivery: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore.
f: Which does IRT use?
Continuous integration and continuous delivery with formal FV, UAT and production approvals.
How do feature flags help?
They separate deploying code from releasing features, so incomplete work can ship turned off.
p2-24.y: Continuous integration means every change is merged often and automatically built and tested. Continuous delivery means every passing build is ready to release, but a person decides when to deploy to production. Continuous deployment goes further and deploys every passing change to production automatically. In our regulated product we do continuous delivery, because production needs approvals.
p2-24.k: ci, continuous delivery, continuous deployment, ci/cd, pipeline

p2-25.q: A YAML build pipeline triggers on pull requests and merges: restore, build, unit tests with coverage, SonarQube analysis and quality gate, dependency scanning, publish versioned artifacts and Docker images. The release then promotes the same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production with approvals and checks at each stage, using Ansible, Python and Shell scripts for multi-node installs, and every environment traces back to one tagged version.
i: Branch policies require a green build and reviewers before merge.
Versioning: semantic version plus build number and commit hash stamped into the artifact.
Environment approvals and checks (business hours, change request id) in Azure DevOps environments.
Post-deploy verification: version check on every node, health endpoints and smoke tests.
Since [2025] most deployments are driven through the CIRT MCP server, which triggers the same releases.
c:
trigger: { branches: { include: [ main, release/* ] } }
stages:
- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: build
    steps:
    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      inputs: { command: test, projects: '**/*Tests.csproj', arguments: '--collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"' }
    - task: SonarQubeAnalyze@6
    - task: PublishPipelineArtifact@1
      inputs: { targetPath: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)', artifact: 'drop' }
f: How do you make sure production gets exactly what was tested?
Build once, promote the same immutable artifact; never rebuild per environment.
What checks run before production?
Approvals by release manager and QA, change request reference, FV and UAT sign-off evidence.
p2-25.y: Our YAML build pipeline runs on pull requests and merges: restore, build, unit tests with coverage, SonarQube quality gate, dependency scan, then it publishes versioned artifacts and Docker images. The release pipeline promotes that same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production, with approvals at each stage, using Ansible, Python and Shell scripts for multi-node installs. Every environment traces back to one tagged version.
p2-25.k: azure devops, pipeline, release, ci/cd, artifacts, approvals

p2-26.q: YAML pipelines define build and deployment as code in the repository (versioned, reviewed, branchable, reusable templates, multi-stage with environments and checks); classic release pipelines are configured in the web UI with a visual designer, which is easier to start with but harder to review, version and reuse. Microsoft's direction is YAML.
i: YAML templates (extends, stage templates) standardise pipelines across many services.
Environments with approvals, checks and deployment history replace classic stage approvals.
Classic still has features some teams rely on (gates UI, release variables per stage, easier artifact triggers), especially on older on-prem Azure DevOps Server.
Migration: export classic definitions and recreate as YAML stages step by step.
On our on-prem Azure DevOps Server we have [YAML builds and some classic release definitions], which the MCP server drives through the REST API.
f: Why does pipeline-as-code matter in GxP?
Pipeline changes are reviewed and versioned like application code, which supports change control.
What is an extends template?
A required base template that pipelines must extend, enforcing mandatory steps such as scans.
p2-26.y: YAML pipelines are defined in code in the repository, so they are reviewed, versioned and reusable with templates. Classic release pipelines are designed in the web UI, which is easy to start with and visual, with good approval gates, but changes are not in Git. New work should use YAML with environments and approvals. Some of our older release definitions are still classic.
p2-26.k: azure devops, yaml pipelines, classic release, pipeline as code

p2-27.q: We use short-lived feature branches from main merged through pull requests with build validation and reviews, release branches cut for each release (release/2024.3) where only fixes go, hotfix branches from the release tag, and annotated tags marking exactly what was released to each environment so builds are traceable.
i: Fixes on a release branch are merged back to main (or cherry-picked) so they are not lost.
Semantic versions in tags (v2024.3.1) and in artifacts.
Trunk-based development with feature flags is the alternative for faster delivery.
GitFlow's develop branch adds overhead; most teams simplified to main plus release branches.
As release integrator I merge team features, resolve conflicts and create the tags.
f: Why tag releases?
To reproduce exactly what is in production and to compare releases for audit and debugging.
Merge or rebase?
Squash or merge commits for PRs per team convention; never rewrite shared history.
p2-27.y: We use a main branch that is always releasable, short-lived feature branches merged by pull request with reviews and checks, and release branches for each release so fixes can go in while new work continues. Every release build is tagged with its version, so we can always tell exactly what code is in each environment. Hotfixes are merged back to main.
p2-27.k: branching strategy, git, tagging, release branch, feature branch

p2-28.q: Ansible is an agentless automation tool that runs YAML playbooks over SSH or WinRM to configure servers and install software. In IRT our release installs ran through Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts across the multi-node environments; idempotency means running a task again leaves the same end state, so reruns after a failure are safe.
i: Modules are idempotent by design (copy, template, service: state=started); raw shell commands are not unless guarded with creates/removes or changed_when.
Inventories define nodes per environment; group_vars hold environment settings; Ansible Vault encrypts secrets.
Roles organise reusable steps; handlers restart services only when something changed.
--check and --diff do a dry run; serial controls rolling updates across nodes.
The MCP deployment tools trigger the same release stages that run these playbooks.
c:
- name: Deploy shipments service
  hosts: app_nodes
  serial: 1                      # one node at a time
  tasks:
    - name: Copy release package
      ansible.builtin.unarchive: { src: "shipments-{{ version }}.zip", dest: /opt/irt/shipments }
      notify: restart shipments
  handlers:
    - name: restart shipments
      ansible.builtin.service: { name: shipments, state: restarted }
f: Ansible vs Terraform?
Terraform provisions infrastructure; Ansible configures and deploys onto it.
How do you make a shell task idempotent?
Add creates: or a condition, or check state first and set changed_when properly.
p2-28.y: Ansible is an agentless automation tool that runs YAML playbooks over SSH to configure servers and install software. Our release installs ran through Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts across the multi-node environments. Idempotency means running the same task again leaves the same result, so if a deployment fails halfway, we can safely run it again.
p2-28.k: ansible, playbook, idempotency, configuration management, automation

p2-29.q: Rolling deployment replaces instances gradually with the new version; blue-green runs a full new environment (green) next to the old (blue) and switches traffic at once, allowing instant rollback; canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watches metrics, then increases gradually.
i: Rolling: cheap and default in ECS/Kubernetes; old and new versions run together briefly, so changes must be backward compatible.
Blue-green: double capacity during the switch; database must work for both versions.
Canary: needs good metrics and automated analysis (Argo Rollouts, CodeDeploy, App Mesh weights).
Feature flags complement all three by decoupling release from deployment.
IRT releases are rolling node by node in controlled windows, with verification after each node.
f: Which is safest for database changes?
Any, if you use expand/contract migrations so both versions work with the schema.
How do you roll back a canary?
Shift traffic back to the stable version automatically when error or latency thresholds break.
p2-29.y: Rolling deployment replaces instances a few at a time, which is simple and needs no extra servers. Blue-green runs the new version beside the old one and switches all traffic at once, so rollback is instant. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version first and increases it if metrics look good. ECS gives us rolling updates with automatic rollback.
p2-29.k: blue green, canary, rolling deployment, deployment strategies, rollback

p2-30.q: I plan rollback so the application can roll back without rolling back the database: schema changes are backward compatible (expand/contract), applied before the app, and destructive steps happen only in a later release. If a database rollback is really needed, there is a tested down script or a restore point, decided in advance in the release plan.
i: Expand: add columns/tables (nullable or defaulted), deploy app writing both; contract: drop old structures in a later release.
Data migrations are reversible or backed up (copy tables) before running.
Practise rollback in UAT; document the decision criteria and owner.
Feature flags turn off new behaviour without a deployment.
In GxP the rollback plan is part of the change request and approved with it.
f: Why not just restore a backup?
You lose data written since the backup; it is the last resort.
How long do you keep the old columns?
At least one release after the app stops using them, so rollback remains possible.
p2-30.y: The key is to make database changes backward compatible, so the previous app version still works with the new schema. I use expand and contract: first add new columns or tables, deploy the app, and only remove old ones in a later release. Then rolling back the app does not need a database rollback. For risky changes we take a backup and have tested rollback scripts.
p2-30.k: rollback, database changes, expand contract, backward compatible, release

p2-31.q: In GxP, every release follows change control: documented change requests with impact and risk assessment, traceability from requirements to tests, formal validation (FV) with evidence, independent QA and TechOps installs in qualified environments, UAT sign-off, approved deployment windows, and post-deployment verification, with everything recorded for audit.
i: Separation of duties: developers do not deploy to production themselves.
Only validated artifacts move forward; no rebuilds between environments.
Deviations and incidents are documented with CAPA (corrective and preventive actions).
Automation helps if it is itself controlled and validated (our MCP server keeps approvals in Azure DevOps).
Release cadence is slower and planned; hotfixes still need expedited change control.
f: What is CAPA?
Corrective and Preventive Action: fixing a problem and preventing recurrence, with documentation.
How do you speed things up in GxP?
Automate evidence collection, test early, and keep changes small and well-documented.
p2-31.y: In GxP, every release is controlled and documented. There is an approved change request, the build is validated in FV with scripted tests and evidence, users accept it in UAT, and production deployment needs approvals and a record of what was installed. The same validated artifact must be promoted, never rebuilt. That's why automation must keep audit trails and human approvals.
p2-31.k: gxp, release management, change control, validation, regulated

p2-32.q: Logs are timestamped records of discrete events with detail (errors, requests, business events); metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU) that are cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts; traces follow a single request across services as a tree of timed spans, showing where time and errors occur.
i: Use metrics to detect, traces to locate, logs to explain.
Correlate them: trace id in logs, exemplars in metrics linking to traces.
Cardinality: avoid high-cardinality labels (user id) in metrics; put those in logs and traces.
OpenTelemetry standardises all three signals.
f: Why not just logs?
Logs are expensive to query at scale and poor for trends; metrics alert faster and cheaper.
What are percentiles?
p95 latency means 95 percent of requests were faster; averages hide slow tails.
p2-32.y: Logs are detailed records of events, like an error with its message and context. Metrics are numbers over time, like request rate, error rate and latency, which are cheap to store and great for alerts and dashboards. Traces follow one request as it moves through several services, showing where the time goes. Together they tell me what is wrong, where, and why.
p2-32.k: logs, metrics, traces, observability, three pillars

p2-33.q: CloudWatch is AWS's native monitoring: Logs (with Logs Insights queries), Metrics (AWS and custom), Alarms (with SNS actions), dashboards and X-Ray traces. Grafana is a visualisation layer that queries CloudWatch and other sources (Prometheus, Loki) in one place with richer dashboards and alerting. We use CloudWatch as the data store and Grafana for team dashboards.
i: Logs Insights: `fields @timestamp, @message | filter CorrelationId = "abc" | sort @timestamp`.
Metric filters turn log patterns into metrics (count of "SFTP transfer failed").
Embedded Metric Format lets apps emit metrics through structured logs.
Alarms: composite alarms reduce noise; anomaly detection for seasonal metrics.
Grafana: one dashboard per service with golden signals, plus business panels (shipments processed).
c:
fields @timestamp, level, message, CorrelationId
| filter service = "shipments-api" and level = "Error"
| stats count() by bin(5m)
f: How do you control CloudWatch Logs cost?
Retention policies, sensible log levels, and avoiding verbose debug logs in production.
Where do you look first in an incident?
The service's Grafana dashboard for golden signals, then Logs Insights for errors.
p2-33.y: We send logs to CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights to query them, for example by correlation id or error type. CloudWatch metrics and alarms watch things like error rate, latency and CPU. Grafana dashboards show service health in one place, and we check them after every release to confirm everything is normal.
p2-33.k: cloudwatch, grafana, logs insights, dashboards, alarms, monitoring

p2-34.q: The four golden signals from Google's SRE book are latency (how long requests take, separating successes and failures), traffic (demand, such as requests per second), errors (rate of failed requests) and saturation (how full the system is: CPU, memory, queue depth, connection pools). Monitoring them gives a quick health picture of any service.
i: RED method for services: Rate, Errors, Duration; USE method for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors.
Use percentiles (p95, p99) for latency, not averages.
Saturation predicts problems before errors appear (queue growth, pool exhaustion).
Business signals complete the picture (shipments processed per hour).
f: Which signal warns earliest?
Saturation, because queues and pools fill before latency and errors spike.
Why separate failed request latency?
Fast failures (instant 500s) can make average latency look better while things are broken.
p2-34.y: The four golden signals from Google's SRE book are latency, which is how long requests take, traffic, which is how many requests, errors, which is the rate of failures, and saturation, which is how full the system is, like CPU, memory or queue depth. If I monitor only four things for a service, it is these.
p2-34.k: golden signals, latency, traffic, errors, saturation, sre, monitoring

p2-35.q: I start by stabilising (mitigate impact), then build a timeline, gather evidence (metrics, logs, traces, recent changes), form hypotheses and test them one at a time until I find a cause that explains every symptom; then I fix it, verify, and write a blameless post-mortem with actions so it does not recur.
i: Ask what changed: deployments, config, data volume, vendor behaviour, certificates.
5 whys or a fishbone diagram to go from symptom to root cause.
Reproduce in a lower environment when possible.
Distinguish trigger (the event) from root cause (the weakness) and contributing factors.
Example: the RabbitMQ outage: trigger = large vendor file and memory alarm; root cause = publishing without confirms; fix = publisher confirms plus alerts.
f: What is a blameless post-mortem?
A review focused on systems and processes, not individuals, so people share facts openly.
When is RCA complete?
When the cause explains all symptoms, the fix is verified and prevention actions are tracked.
p2-35.y: First I limit the impact, for example by rolling back. Then I collect facts: when it started, what changed, which users, and the logs, metrics and traces. I form a hypothesis and test it, and I keep asking why until I find the real cause, not just the symptom. Finally we write a blameless review with actions, like a test or alert, so it does not happen again.
p2-35.k: root cause analysis, rca, incident, troubleshooting, post-mortem, 5 whys

p2-36.q: A good alert is actionable (someone must do something now), urgent, tied to user impact or an SLO, has a clear owner and a runbook link, fires rarely when nothing is wrong, and carries enough context (service, environment, dashboard link) to start immediately.
i: Alert on symptoms (error rate, latency SLO burn) rather than every cause (CPU 80 percent).
Use multi-window burn-rate alerts for SLOs to catch fast and slow burns.
Tune thresholds and durations to avoid flapping; review noisy alerts regularly.
Non-urgent issues go to tickets or dashboards, not pages.
Every alert should have a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate.
f: What is alert fatigue?
Too many low-value alerts make people ignore all alerts, including important ones.
Example of a good alert in IRT?
Shipment status messages in DLQ greater than zero for 10 minutes, linked to the replay runbook.
p2-36.y: A good alert is actionable: when it fires, someone needs to do something, and it says what is wrong and links to a runbook. It is based on user impact, like error rate or latency, rather than every CPU spike. It has sensible thresholds and durations so it doesn't flap. Too many noisy alerts make people ignore the important ones.
p2-36.k: alerting, alerts, on-call, runbook, alert fatigue

p2-37.q: Kafka is a distributed, append-only log: messages are retained for a period, consumers track their own offsets, many consumer groups can read the same stream and replay it, and ordering is per partition with very high throughput. RabbitMQ is a message broker with queues and flexible routing (exchanges), per-message acknowledgements, priorities and TTLs; messages are removed once consumed.
i: Kafka fits event streaming, multiple independent consumers, replay, audit-like history, analytics.
RabbitMQ fits task queues, commands, request/reply, complex routing, per-message retry and DLQ.
Scaling: Kafka by partitions; RabbitMQ by queues and competing consumers (quorum queues for HA).
RabbitMQ Streams add log-like replay; Kafka adds queue-like features in newer versions (share groups).
In IRT: Kafka for shipment status events consumed by several services; RabbitMQ for notifications and work queues.
f: Which gives ordering?
Kafka per partition (by key); RabbitMQ per queue with a single consumer.
Which is easier to operate?
RabbitMQ for small setups; Kafka is simpler as a managed service (MSK, Confluent).
p2-37.y: Kafka is a distributed log: messages are kept for a retention period, many consumer groups can read the same events, and it can replay them and handle very high volume. RabbitMQ is a message broker with queues: a message is delivered to a consumer and removed once acknowledged, with flexible routing and per-message retries. We use Kafka for shipment status events and RabbitMQ for task-style work.
p2-37.k: kafka, rabbitmq, messaging, comparison, message broker

p2-38.q: A topic is a named stream of events split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers and replicated. Producers choose the partition by key (same key, same partition, same order); a consumer group shares the partitions among its consumers so each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, while different groups read independently.
i: Parallelism is capped by partition count within a group.
Offsets are committed per group and partition; consumers resume from them after restarts.
Rebalancing reassigns partitions when consumers join or leave; cooperative rebalancing reduces pauses.
Choose keys for ordering needs (ShipmentId) and even distribution.
Retention by time or size, independent of consumption.
f: Can you reduce partitions?
No; you can only add them, and adding changes key-to-partition mapping for new messages.
What happens with two groups on one topic?
Each group gets every message, so different services can process the same events.
p2-38.y: A topic is a named stream of events, like shipment-status. Each topic is split into partitions, which allow parallel processing, and order is kept only inside a partition. A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group. So more partitions mean more parallelism, and we use the shipment id as the key to keep its events in order.
p2-38.k: kafka, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, ordering

p2-39.q: RabbitMQ has four main exchange types: direct (routes to queues whose binding key equals the routing key), topic (pattern matching with * for one word and # for zero or more, like shipment.*.delivered), fanout (broadcasts to all bound queues, ignoring keys) and headers (routes on message header values). The default exchange routes directly to the queue named by the routing key.
i: Direct for commands to specific workers; topic for event categories; fanout for broadcast notifications.
Alternate exchanges catch unroutable messages; mandatory flag returns them to the publisher.
Dead-letter exchanges route rejected or expired messages.
Consistent-hash exchange (plugin) spreads by key for sharding.
c:
await channel.ExchangeDeclareAsync("shipments", ExchangeType.Topic, durable: true);
await channel.QueueBindAsync("notify-sites", "shipments", "shipment.*.delivered");
