For example, I call Upload on an ISftpClient, and depending on configuration it runs the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro version, without the calling code knowing which.

p4-21.q: Abstraction exposes what something does and hides how; interfaces and abstract classes model the essential contract. Callers depend on ISftpClient without knowing any library details.
i: Good abstractions are small and stable; leaky abstractions expose implementation details (library exceptions).
We mapped provider exceptions to our own to avoid leaking.
Don't abstract too early; wait for a second implementation or a testing need.
Abstraction levels: repository hides SQL, ISftpClient hides libraries, the service layer hides workflow; each layer talks only to the one below.
f: What is a leaky abstraction?
One where callers must understand the hidden implementation to use it correctly.
Abstraction vs interface keyword?
Abstraction is the concept; interfaces are one way to express it.
p4-21.y: Abstraction means showing only what a user of a class needs and hiding the details. An interface like ISftpClient only exposes connect, upload and download, while each library deals with its own complex details inside. Callers work with the simple idea of a file transfer, which makes the code easier to use, test and change.

p4-22.q: A class is the blueprint (type definition with fields, properties and methods); an object is an instance created from it at runtime with its own state on the heap. Many objects can come from one class.
i: Static members belong to the type, not instances.
Records and structs are also types; structs create values, not heap objects (unless boxed).
Object header holds sync block and method table pointer.
Records add value-based equality and with-expressions; structs are copied by value; classes are referenced.
f: Where are objects stored?
On the managed heap; references point to them.
What's a static class?
A class that can't be instantiated and holds only static members.
p4-22.y: A class is the blueprint, it defines the properties and methods. An object is an actual instance created from that class at runtime, with its own data in memory. For example, Shipment is the class, and each shipment loaded from the database is a separate object.

p4-23.q: Overloading is the same method name with different parameters in one class, resolved at compile time; overriding is a derived class replacing a virtual base method with the same signature, resolved at runtime by the actual object type.
i: Return type alone can't distinguish overloads.
Overload resolution picks the best match; optional parameters and params can create ambiguity.
Covariant return types (C# 9) let overrides return a more derived type.
Overload resolution happens at compile time on static types: passing an object-typed variable picks the object overload even if it holds a string.
f: Can you override a non-virtual method?
No; you can only hide it with new.
Can static methods be overridden?
No; static abstract interface members are a different feature for generic math.
p4-23.y: Overloading means the same method name with different parameters in the same class, and the compiler picks the right one at compile time. Overriding means a derived class provides its own version of a virtual method from the base class, and the right one is chosen at runtime based on the actual object. So overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime polymorphism.
p4-23.k: overloading, overriding, polymorphism, compile time, runtime

p4-24.q: virtual in the base class marks a method as replaceable; override in the derived class supplies the new implementation, and a call through a base reference runs the override because dispatch uses the runtime type.
i: abstract methods are implicitly virtual and must be overridden.
base.Method() calls the base implementation from an override.
Calling virtual methods in constructors is risky: the derived override runs before the derived constructor finishes.
Virtual calls go through the method table (vtable); the JIT can devirtualize when the exact type is known, e.g. sealed classes.
f: Are methods virtual by default in C#?
No, unlike Java; you must mark them.
Why avoid virtual calls in constructors?
Derived fields may not be initialised yet.
p4-24.y: The virtual keyword on a base class method says derived classes are allowed to replace it. The override keyword in the derived class actually replaces it. Then even if I call the method through a base class reference, the derived version runs. Without virtual, the method can't be overridden.

p4-25.q: override replaces a virtual method so base-typed references call the derived version; new hides the base method (method hiding), so which runs depends on the declared reference type, a common source of bugs.
i: The compiler warns (CS0108) when hiding without new.
Hiding breaks polymorphism; use rarely, e.g. when a base library adds a conflicting member.
Real-world use: hiding happens accidentally when a base library adds a member with the same name; treat CS0108 as an error.
f: When is new useful?
To intentionally shadow a member you can't change, with a clear reason.
What does the CS0108 warning mean?
You're hiding an inherited member without saying new.
p4-25.y: Override replaces a virtual method, so the derived version runs even through a base reference. The new keyword hides the base method instead: if I call through a base reference, the base version runs, and through the derived reference, the new one runs. That's method hiding, and it is usually confusing, so I avoid it and treat that compiler warning as an error.
p4-25.k: new keyword, method hiding, override, inheritance

p4-26.q: A sealed class can't be inherited (string is sealed); a sealed override stops further overriding down the chain. I use it to express design intent and safety, and it lets the JIT devirtualize calls for a small performance gain.
i: Many analyzers (CA1852) suggest sealing internal types that aren't inherited.
Sealed records are common for DTOs and messages.
Sealing public library types is a compatibility decision.
Records can be sealed and their ToString can be sealed (C# 10) so derived records keep it.
f: Why is string sealed?
For immutability and security guarantees and performance.
Can you seal a method that isn't an override?
No, sealed applies to overrides only.
p4-26.y: A sealed class can't be inherited, which protects its design and can even let the runtime optimise calls. A sealed method is an override that stops further overriding in deeper classes. I seal classes by default when they aren't designed for inheritance, like most of our service classes.

p4-27.q: The stack is per-thread LIFO memory for method frames, locals and value types, very fast and freed when the method returns; the heap is shared managed memory for objects (reference types), cleaned by the GC. Value types live where they're declared: inside a heap object's fields, they're on the heap.
i: Default stack size about 1 MB per thread (Windows main thread); deep recursion causes StackOverflowException, which can't be caught.
stackalloc and Span<T> allow stack buffers.
Large objects (85,000 bytes or more) go to the Large Object Heap.
Captured locals in lambdas or async methods move to heap objects.
f: Are structs always on the stack?
No; fields of a class, array elements, boxed values and captured variables live on the heap.
What is the LOH?
The Large Object Heap for objects of 85 KB or more, collected with Gen 2.
p4-27.y: The stack stores method calls and their local variables, it's very fast and is cleared automatically when the method returns. The heap stores objects created with new, which live until the garbage collector removes them. Reference types live on the heap, while value types live wherever they are declared, so a local int is on the stack but an int field of a class is on the heap.
p4-27.k: stack, heap, memory, value types, reference types

p4-28.q: Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (int to object); unboxing casts it back to the exact type. Each box costs an allocation and GC work, so I avoid it with generics (List<int> instead of ArrayList) and by avoiding object parameters for value types.
i: Hidden boxing: string.Format with value types (older), interfaces on structs, non-generic collections, enums in some APIs.
Unboxing to the wrong type throws InvalidCastException.
Interpolated string handlers (C# 10) avoid boxing in many cases.
Generic constraints (where T : struct) and generic interfaces (IEquatable<T>) avoid boxing in comparisons.
f: How do you find boxing?
Allocation profilers or IL inspection (box instructions).
Does calling an interface method on a struct box?
Yes through an interface reference, but not with a constrained generic.
p4-28.y: Boxing is when a value type, like an int, is wrapped into an object on the heap, for example when you put it into an object variable or an old non-generic collection. Unboxing is getting the value back with a cast. It costs memory and time, so in hot code I avoid it by using generics, like List of int instead of ArrayList.
p4-28.k: boxing, unboxing, value types, performance, generics

p4-29.q: IDisposable.Dispose releases unmanaged or expensive resources (connections, streams, SFTP sessions) deterministically. A using statement calls Dispose at the end of the block even on exceptions; a C# 8 using declaration disposes at the end of the enclosing scope; IAsyncDisposable with await using handles async cleanup.
i: Dispose pattern with a finalizer only when you directly own unmanaged handles; prefer SafeHandle.
Don't dispose objects you don't own (DI-injected services).
HttpClient: don't dispose per request; use IHttpClientFactory.
f: What happens if you forget Dispose?
Resources stay open until the GC finalizes them, if ever, causing leaks like connection pool exhaustion.
Dispose vs finalizer?
Dispose is deterministic and called by you; finalizers run non-deterministically on the GC thread.
p4-29.y: IDisposable is for objects that hold resources the garbage collector doesn't manage, like files, database connections or streams, and its Dispose method releases them. The using statement calls Dispose automatically at the end of the block, even if there's an exception. The newer using declaration does the same at the end of the current scope, with less nesting.
p4-29.k: idisposable, using statement, using declaration, dispose, resources

p4-30.q: const is a compile-time constant, implicitly static and baked into calling assemblies; readonly is set at declaration or in the constructor, per instance; static readonly is set once per type at runtime, for values like objects or computed values that can't be const.
i: Changing a public const requires recompiling consumers; prefer static readonly for public values that might change.
readonly on a reference prevents reassignment, not mutation of the object.
readonly struct and readonly members prevent defensive copies.
Example: public const int MaxRows = 10000 in a library; changing it to 20000 doesn't affect already-compiled consumers until rebuilt.
f: Can const be a DateTime?
No, only primitive types, strings and enums (or null).
Is a readonly List immutable?
No, you can still add items; use ImmutableList or IReadOnlyList.
p4-30.y: A const is fixed at compile time and copied into any code that uses it, so it's only for values that never change, like pi. A readonly field is set once, in the declaration or constructor, and can differ per object. A static readonly is set once for the whole class at runtime. I use static readonly for things like configuration defaults, because changing a const needs every caller recompiled.

p4-31.q: ref passes a variable by reference (must be initialised; callee may change it); out requires the callee to assign it (TryParse pattern); in passes by read-only reference, avoiding copies of large structs. C# 12 added ref readonly parameters.
i: Not allowed in async methods or iterators (ref locals limited; C# 13 relaxed some rules).
ref returns and ref locals for high-performance code.
Prefer returning tuples or records for multiple results in normal code.
ref struct types (like Span<T>) can only live on the stack, which is why they can't be used in async methods.
f: Why use in?
To avoid copying large structs without allowing changes.
out vs returning a tuple?
out fits the Try pattern; tuples are often clearer otherwise.
p4-31.y: These are ways to pass parameters by reference. ref means the variable must be set before the call and the method can change it. out means the method must set it, like in int.TryParse. in passes a read-only reference, which avoids copying large structs without letting the method change them.
p4-31.k: ref, out, in, parameters, by reference

p4-32.q: Nullable reference types (C# 8) make reference types non-nullable by default; string? marks a nullable one, and the compiler warns on possible null dereferences or assigning null. It catches NullReferenceExceptions at compile time; it's enabled by default in new projects.
i: It's compile-time analysis only; runtime can still have nulls (deserialization, reflection).
Attributes like [NotNullWhen(true)], [MaybeNull] help the analysis.
The null-forgiving operator ! silences warnings; use sparingly.
Turn warnings into errors (Nullable enable plus TreatWarningsAsErrors) for new code.
f: Does it change runtime behaviour?
No, only warnings and metadata.
How do you migrate a big codebase?
File by file with #nullable enable, starting with core models.
p4-32.y: Nullable reference types, turned on with a project setting, make the compiler warn me when a reference might be null and I use it without checking. I mark things that can be null with a question mark, like string question mark. It catches many NullReferenceException bugs at compile time. All our newer projects have it enabled.
p4-32.k: nullable reference types, null safety, null reference exception

p4-33.q: Pattern matching tests and deconstructs values concisely: type patterns with is, switch expressions, property patterns, relational and logical patterns (and, or, not) and list patterns (C# 11). It replaces long if/else chains with readable, compiler-checked logic.
i: Switch expressions warn on non-exhaustive matches.
is not null is the clearest null check.
Real use: switch expressions on ShipmentStatus to compute next allowed transitions, with the compiler warning on missing cases.
f: What is a discard?
_ matches anything without binding it.
Is pattern matching slower?
No, it compiles to efficient type checks and comparisons.
p4-33.y: Pattern matching lets me check the shape or type of a value and pull data out of it in one step, using is, switch expressions, property patterns and relational patterns. It makes branching code shorter and clearer. For example, I use a switch expression on shipment status to decide the next allowed status, and the compiler warns me if I miss a case.
p4-33.k: pattern matching, switch expression, is, c#

p4-34.q: Extension methods are static methods in a static class whose first parameter has this T, so they can be called as if they were instance methods; LINQ is built on them. We use them for things like service registration (services.AddSftpProviders()) and small helpers.
i: They can't access private members and lose to real instance methods with the same signature.
C# 14 adds extension members (extension blocks) including extension properties and static extensions.
Keep them discoverable and in clear namespaces.
f: Can you extend a sealed class?
Yes, extension methods work on any type.
What's new in C# 14?
Extension blocks that allow extension properties and static members.
p4-34.y: An extension method is a static method that looks like a method on an existing type, by using the this keyword on its first parameter. All of LINQ is built this way. I use them for small helpers, like a ToPagedResult method on IQueryable, and for clean service registration, like AddSftpClients on IServiceCollection.

p4-35.q: An enum is a named set of integer constants such as enum ShipmentStatus { Created, Shipped, Delivered }, type-safe and readable. [Flags] enums combine values with bitwise operations (powers of two), and HasFlag or bitwise checks test them.
i: Default underlying type is int; any int can be cast, so validate input (Enum.IsDefined).
Serialize as strings for APIs with JsonStringEnumConverter to keep contracts stable.
Store as strings or ints in the database deliberately; adding values in the middle changes numbers.
f: Why assign explicit values?
So reordering doesn't change stored or serialized values.
Enum vs smart enum class?
Classes can carry behaviour and data; enums are simple constants.
p4-35.y: An enum is a set of named constants, backed by numbers, like ShipmentStatus with Created, Dispatched and Delivered. It makes code readable and type-safe compared with magic numbers. With the Flags attribute, values can be combined. I always validate enums coming from APIs, because any number can be cast into an enum.

p4-36.q: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on a Task (.Result, .Wait()) while a SynchronizationContext (WinForms, WPF, classic ASP.NET) needs that same blocked thread to run the continuation: each waits for the other forever. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so it doesn't deadlock that way, but blocking still causes thread pool starvation.
i: Fix: async all the way; never block on async in request code.
Libraries use ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid capturing contexts.
If you must call async from sync (Main, legacy), GetAwaiter().GetResult() at the very top, knowing the risks.
Thread pool starvation symptoms: latency climbs, thread count grows slowly (about one thread per second injection beyond min).
f: Why does ASP.NET Core avoid the classic deadlock?
It has no request SynchronizationContext, so continuations run on any pool thread.
Is .Result ever fine?
After the task has completed (e.g. after WhenAll), it doesn't block.
p4-36.y: An async deadlock happens when code blocks on async work, like calling .Result or .Wait, in an environment with a synchronization context, such as old ASP.NET or a UI app. The blocked thread waits for the task, but the task needs that same thread to continue, so both wait forever. The fix is to use async all the way and never block on tasks.
p4-36.k: async deadlock, result, wait, synchronization context, async all the way

p4-37.q: ConfigureAwait(false) tells await not to resume on the captured SynchronizationContext or TaskScheduler, so the continuation runs on a thread pool thread. It matters in libraries and UI apps to avoid deadlocks and context-switch overhead; in ASP.NET Core app code it makes little difference because there's no context.
i: Library authors should still use it because their code may run under UI contexts.
.NET 8 added ConfigureAwaitOptions (e.g. SuppressThrowing, ForceYielding) for Task.
After ConfigureAwait(false), don't touch UI elements or context-bound state.
Rule of thumb: in app code (ASP.NET Core) skip it; in reusable libraries use ConfigureAwait(false) on every await.
f: Does ConfigureAwait(false) make code faster in ASP.NET Core?
Negligibly; it's mainly about correctness in libraries.
What does ForceYielding do?
Forces the continuation to be queued asynchronously even if the task already completed.
p4-37.y: ConfigureAwait false tells an await that it doesn't need to continue on the original synchronization context, so it can continue on any thread pool thread. It avoids deadlocks and is slightly faster. ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so in app code it doesn't matter, but in reusable libraries I still use ConfigureAwait false.

p4-38.q: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) gives one syntax to query collections, databases (EF Core) and XML using operators such as Where, Select, GroupBy, Join and OrderBy, in method or query syntax. Over IEnumerable it runs in memory with delegates; over IQueryable it builds expression trees that providers translate, e.g. to SQL.
i: Deferred execution: queries run when enumerated (foreach, ToList, Count).
Multiple enumeration re-executes the query; materialise once if reused.
.NET 9 added CountBy, AggregateBy and Index; .NET 6 added Chunk, MinBy, MaxBy, DistinctBy.
c:
var late = await db.Shipments
    .Where(s => s.Status == ShipmentStatus.InTransit && s.ExpectedAt < now)
    .OrderBy(s => s.ExpectedAt)
    .Select(s => new { s.Id, s.SiteId, s.ExpectedAt })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
f: Query vs method syntax?
Same result; query syntax compiles to method calls and can be clearer for joins.
What does CountBy do?
Groups by a key and returns counts without creating groups (.NET 9).
p4-38.y: LINQ is Language Integrated Query, a way to query collections and databases with C# methods like Where, Select, OrderBy and GroupBy. It works on in-memory collections and, through EF Core, gets translated into SQL. It makes data code short and readable. I use it every day, being careful about what runs in the database and what runs in memory.
p4-38.k: linq, query, where, select, ef core

p4-39.q: IEnumerable<T> gives forward-only iteration; ICollection<T> adds Count, Add, Remove and Contains; IList<T> adds index access and Insert. I accept the smallest interface a method needs and return read-only interfaces (IReadOnlyList, IReadOnlyCollection) to communicate intent.
i: IEnumerable may be lazy or infinite; Count() may enumerate everything.
IReadOnlyList<T> gives Count and indexing without mutation.
Arrays implement IList<T> but throw on Add.
Method parameters: accept IEnumerable<T> or IReadOnlyCollection<T>; return concrete or read-only interfaces based on what callers need.
f: Why return IReadOnlyList instead of List?
It prevents callers mutating internal state and documents intent.
Is IEnumerable always lazy?
No, it depends on the source; it's an abstraction, not a guarantee.
p4-39.y: IEnumerable only lets you loop over items. ICollection adds Count, Add and Remove. IList adds access by index, like item number five. So each one adds more abilities. For method parameters, I accept the simplest one I need, often IEnumerable or IReadOnlyCollection, which keeps the method flexible.

p4-40.q: First returns the first match and throws if none; FirstOrDefault returns default (null) instead. Single requires exactly one match and throws if none or more than one; SingleOrDefault returns default if none but still throws if more than one.
i: Use Single when duplicates indicate a data bug; First when order matters (with OrderBy).
In SQL, First becomes TOP(1); Single becomes TOP(2) to detect duplicates.
.NET 6 added FirstOrDefault(defaultValue) overloads.
FindAsync by key checks the change tracker first.
f: Which is faster in EF Core?
First (TOP 1) reads less than Single (TOP 2), but pick by meaning.
FirstOrDefault on value types?
Returns default (0 for int), which may be ambiguous.
p4-40.y: First returns the first match and throws if there's none, while FirstOrDefault returns null or default instead. Single expects exactly one match and throws if there are none or more than one, and SingleOrDefault allows zero but still throws for more than one. I use Single when duplicates would be a bug, like finding by a unique code, and FirstOrDefault when nothing found is normal.

p4-41.q: Any() stops at the first match and translates to EXISTS in SQL; Count() counts every matching row. Use Any() to check existence; on in-memory collections the Count property is already O(1), and LINQ Count() uses it when available.
i: Any() on IEnumerable without a predicate can use TryGetNonEnumeratedCount-like optimisations.
Count() > 0 is a common code smell (CA1827 analyzer).
In memory, LINQ Count() checks for ICollection<T> and uses .Count without enumerating.
For IQueryable, Count() becomes SELECT COUNT(*), which scans more rows than EXISTS.
f: What does EF Core generate for Any()?
SELECT CASE WHEN EXISTS (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END.
When use Count?
When you actually need the number.
p4-41.y: Any stops as soon as it finds one item, so it's the right way to check if something exists. Count goes through everything to count it, unless the collection already knows its count. In EF Core, Any becomes an EXISTS query, which is much cheaper than SELECT COUNT. So I use Any for existence checks.

p4-42.q: A closure is a lambda that captures variables from its outer scope; the compiler moves them into a hidden class so they live as long as the lambda. Pitfalls include capturing a loop variable in older for loops, accidentally keeping large objects alive, and hidden allocations on hot paths.
i: foreach variables are per-iteration since C# 5; for loop variables are shared.
static lambdas (C# 9) prevent capture and allocations.
Captured variables are shared: changing them later changes what the lambda sees.
f: Do closures allocate?
Yes, a display class instance and a delegate, unless the lambda is static or captures nothing.
Why can closures cause memory leaks?
Long-lived delegates (event handlers) keep captured objects alive.
p4-42.y: A closure is a lambda or function that captures variables from the surrounding code and keeps using them later. C# does this by moving those variables into a hidden class. A classic bug is capturing a loop variable in old for loops and all lambdas seeing the last value. I also watch for closures accidentally keeping large objects alive.

p4-43.q: Liskov Substitution says subtypes must work anywhere the base type is expected without breaking correct behaviour. Every ISftpClient provider honours the same contract (same exceptions, same semantics for overwrite), so callers never special-case one; the classic violation is Square inheriting Rectangle and breaking width/height expectations.
i: Violations: throwing NotSupportedException in overrides, stronger preconditions, weaker postconditions.
ReadOnlyCollection implementing IList and throwing on Add is a known framework compromise.
Contract tests run the same test suite against every implementation.
Our provider contract tests ran the same suite (upload, list, overwrite, error mapping) against Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, enforcing LSP.
f: How do you test LSP?
Shared contract tests for all implementations of an interface.
What smell suggests an LSP break?
Callers checking concrete types with is or casts.
p4-43.y: Liskov says a derived class must work anywhere the base class is expected, without surprises. The classic violation is a Square inheriting from Rectangle, where setting width also changes height. In my SFTP component, every provider passes the same contract tests for upload, list, overwrite and errors, so any library can replace another safely.

p4-44.q: Interface Segregation says clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Instead of one large IShipmentRepository, we use IShipmentReader for queries and IShipmentWriter for commands, so a reporting service only gets read access and tests mock less.
i: Small, role-based interfaces; one class can implement several.
Fits CQRS read/write split.
Fat interfaces force empty implementations and change ripple.
Microsoft's own example: IReadOnlyList<T> separated from IList<T> for consumers that only read.
f: Doesn't this create too many interfaces?
Only split where clients really differ.
Link to security?
Read-only interfaces make accidental writes impossible in reporting code.
p4-44.y: Interface segregation says don't force classes to depend on methods they don't use, so prefer small, focused interfaces over one big one. For example, a report service that only reads shipments should depend on a reader interface, not a full repository with update and delete. Microsoft does the same with IReadOnlyList separate from IList.

p4-45.q: Dependency Inversion says high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete classes, and abstractions are owned by the high-level side. VendorExchangeService depends on ISftpClient injected through ASP.NET Core DI, not on Rebex directly, so libraries can change without touching business logic.
i: DIP is the principle; DI is the technique; IoC containers are tooling.
Clean Architecture: interfaces in the domain/application layer, implementations in infrastructure.
Without DIP: VendorExchangeService news up RebexClient directly, so changing libraries means editing business code.
With DIP: the service owns the ISftpClient abstraction and infrastructure implements it.
f: DIP vs DI?
DIP is the design principle; DI is how dependencies are supplied.
Where should the interface live?
With the code that uses it, not with the implementation.
p4-45.y: Dependency inversion means high-level business code depends on abstractions, not on concrete classes. Without it, our vendor exchange service would create the Rebex client directly, so changing libraries means editing business code. With it, the service depends on ISftpClient, and the infrastructure layer provides the implementation through dependency injection. Changing the library becomes a configuration change.
p4-45.k: dependency inversion principle, dip, solid, abstractions

p4-46.q: I chose an interface to decouple callers from three SFTP implementations, enable DI and unit tests with Moq, and add providers without changing callers (open/closed). It also lets me map library-specific behaviour to one consistent contract.
i: Interfaces for seams: external systems, I/O, time (TimeProvider), randomness.
Don't create interfaces for every class "just because"; one implementation and no test need is a smell.
Interfaces also let you add decorators (logging, retry, metrics) around an implementation without changing it.
Consider an abstract base class when implementations share most code; we used both.
f: Interface vs abstract class here?
Interface for the contract plus an abstract base class for shared retry/logging.
How did it help testing?
Callers are tested with mocked ISftpClient, no real server needed.
p4-46.y: I chose an interface because I needed several interchangeable implementations, Rebex, SSH.NET and ComponentPro, behind one contract, and I wanted to mock it in unit tests. Interfaces also let me add decorators like retry and logging without changing the implementations. Where they shared a lot of code, I used an abstract base class as well.

p4-47.q: I avoid inheritance when the relationship isn't truly is-a, when behaviour varies independently (use strategy or composition), when hierarchies get deep, or across module boundaries where base changes ripple. Composition over inheritance keeps classes flexible.
i: Decorator pattern adds behaviour without subclassing (e.g. a logging ISftpClient wrapper).
Sealing classes by default prevents accidental hierarchies.
Example: a RetryingSftpClient decorator wraps any ISftpClient instead of a RetryingRebexClient subclass per library.
Inheritance across assemblies couples release cycles: a base class change can break consumers.
f: Example of composition in your code?
Providers receive a retry policy and logger rather than inheriting them in newer code.
When is inheritance right?
Stable is-a relationships with shared behaviour, like framework base classes (ControllerBase).
p4-47.y: I avoid inheritance when the relationship isn't really "is-a", or when I just want to reuse some code. Deep hierarchies become fragile, because changing a base class can break everything below it. I prefer composition. For example, I wrap any SFTP client in a retry decorator, instead of making a retrying subclass for each library.

p4-48.q: Garbage collections pause threads (briefly for Gen 0/1, longer for Gen 2 and LOH compaction) and high allocation rates trigger more collections, raising p99 latency and CPU. I reduce allocations on hot paths (pooling, Span, avoiding LINQ in tight loops, streaming), and measure with dotnet-counters and profilers.
i: Generational GC: Gen 0 (short-lived), Gen 1, Gen 2 (long-lived), LOH and POH.
Server GC for throughput (one heap per core); DATAS (default for Server GC since .NET 9) adapts heap count to reduce memory.
Background GC lets Gen 2 run concurrently.
ArrayPool<T>, RecyclableMemoryStream, object pooling for big buffers.
f: What is the POH?
Pinned Object Heap (.NET 5+) for objects that must not move, reducing fragmentation.
Should you call GC.Collect?
Almost never; it usually hurts performance.
p4-48.y: Garbage collection pauses or slows the app while it cleans up, so lots of allocations mean more frequent collections and higher latency. Generation 2 and large object collections are the expensive ones. So in hot paths, I reduce allocations with things like Span, pooling and avoiding unnecessary LINQ. For servers, .NET uses server GC, which is tuned for throughput.
p4-48.k: garbage collection, gc, performance, allocations, latency

p4-49.q: An exception in an async method is captured in the returned Task and rethrown at the await with its stack trace. If the Task is never awaited, the exception is unobserved (TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException) and silently lost; async void exceptions crash the process because there's no Task to hold them.
i: Await every task; avoid fire-and-forget without handling.
Task.WhenAll throws the first exception at await; inspect task.Exception for all.
async void only for event handlers.
Background work: BackgroundService or a queue with try/catch and logging.
f: How do you get all exceptions from WhenAll?
Keep the WhenAll task and read its Exception.InnerExceptions.
Do exceptions thrown before the first await behave differently?
They're still captured in the Task for async methods.
p4-49.y: The exception doesn't crash immediately, it's stored inside the returned Task. When I await the task, the exception is thrown again at that point, so normal try-catch works around the await. If nobody awaits the task, the exception can be lost. And with async void, it can crash the process, so I only use async void for event handlers.
p4-49.k: async exception, task, await, async void, error handling

p4-50.q: Dependency injection means an object receives its dependencies from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them. It gives loose coupling, easy testing with mocks, central lifetime management and configuration, and ASP.NET Core has a built-in container.
i: Lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped (per request), Transient.
Keyed services (.NET 8) for multiple named implementations.
ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild in Development catch lifetime and registration errors early.
c:
builder.Services.AddScoped<IShipmentService, ShipmentService>();
public class ShipmentsController(IShipmentService svc) : ControllerBase { }  // primary constructor
f: Is DI only for testing?
No, it also centralises configuration and lifetimes and decouples modules.
When would you use a third-party container?
For features like decorators, interception or assembly scanning (Autofac, Scrutor for scanning).
p4-50.y: Dependency injection means a class receives the objects it needs, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself. ASP.NET Core has a built-in container that creates and injects them. It makes code loosely coupled and easy to test, because in tests I can pass mocks. For example, our vendor exchange service gets its SFTP client factory and logger injected.
p4-50.k: dependency injection, di, ioc, constructor injection, loose coupling

p4-51.q: A dependency is any object a class needs to do its work, such as a repository, an HttpClient, a logger, configuration, a clock (TimeProvider) or an ISftpClient.
i: Hidden dependencies: static calls (DateTime.Now, File.ReadAllText) make code hard to test.
Make them explicit through constructor parameters.
Dependencies can be services, configuration (IOptions<T>), time (TimeProvider), randomness and the file system.
The fewer and more abstract the dependencies, the easier the class is to test and change.
f: Is DateTime.Now a dependency?
Yes, a hidden one; inject TimeProvider.
What are too many dependencies a sign of?
The class likely has too many responsibilities.
p4-51.y: A dependency is anything a class needs to do its job, like a repository, an HTTP client, a logger, configuration or even the current time. If a class creates these itself, it's tightly tied to them and hard to test. With dependency injection, they're passed in, so I can swap them, for example a fake time provider in tests.

p4-52.q: Inversion of Control means the framework, not your code, controls object creation and flow ("don't call us, we'll call you"); DI is one form. An IoC container registers services and lifetimes and builds object graphs automatically; ASP.NET Core's is Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.
i: Other IoC forms: events, template methods, middleware pipelines.
Container builds graphs recursively by constructor parameters.
ASP.NET Core itself is IoC: it calls your middleware, controllers and hosted services; you don't call them.
Containers also manage lifetimes and disposal, not just construction.
f: Does the built-in container support property injection?
No, only constructor injection (plus [FromServices] and [FromKeyedServices] in endpoints).
What is ActivatorUtilities?
A helper to create objects mixing container services and explicit arguments.
p4-52.y: Inversion of control means the framework controls the flow and calls my code, instead of my code controlling everything. ASP.NET Core calls my middleware, controllers and services. An IoC container is the part that creates objects, injects their dependencies, and manages their lifetimes and disposal. The built-in .NET container does this for us.
p4-52.k: inversion of control, ioc, ioc container, di

p4-53.q: Constructor injection makes dependencies required, immutable and explicit, and it's the default in ASP.NET Core; property injection sets optional dependencies after construction and is not supported by the built-in container. Method injection ([FromServices] on an action parameter) suits rarely used dependencies.
i: Primary constructors (C# 12) reduce boilerplate; parameters are captured, not readonly fields, so assign to readonly fields if immutability matters.
Too many constructor parameters signals a class doing too much.
Property injection hides required dependencies and allows half-initialised objects.
Method injection in minimal APIs: handler parameters are resolved from DI per request.
f: Why prefer constructor injection?
Objects are always valid after construction and dependencies are visible.
Are primary constructor parameters readonly?
No, they're mutable captured parameters unless assigned to readonly fields.
p4-53.y: Constructor injection passes dependencies through the constructor, so required dependencies are obvious and the object is always fully ready. Property injection sets them through public properties after creation, which hides what's required and allows half-ready objects. The built-in .NET container supports constructor injection, and that's what I always use.

p4-54.q: IServiceProvider is the built container that resolves services (GetService), created from IServiceCollection when the host is built. Scopes come from IServiceScopeFactory, and each request has its own scoped provider in HttpContext.RequestServices.
i: Root provider resolving scoped services is a bug (caught by ValidateScopes in Development).
IServiceProviderIsService checks registration without resolving.
Keyed lookup: GetRequiredKeyedService<T>(key).
Building the provider: builder.Build() creates the root provider; Development validates scopes and the graph when ValidateOnBuild is on.
f: Why not resolve scoped services from the root?
They'd live for the app's lifetime, becoming captive.
What is RequestServices?
The request-scoped provider used to create controllers and middleware dependencies.
p4-54.y: IServiceProvider is the interface of the built-in DI container. It's what actually resolves services, using GetService or GetRequiredService. The root provider is created when the app is built, and each request gets its own scoped provider. In normal code I don't use it directly, I just use constructor injection. I use it mainly in factories or when creating scopes.

p4-55.q: A service may depend on services that live at least as long as it does. Singleton on Scoped is a captive dependency bug (DbContext held forever, shared across threads); Singleton on Transient is allowed but the transient effectively becomes a singleton; Scoped on Singleton and Transient on anything are fine.
i: ValidateScopes (on in Development) throws for singleton-to-scoped.
Fix singletons needing scoped services: IServiceScopeFactory, create a scope per unit of work.
IDbContextFactory for singletons or background work needing DbContext.
Example captive bug: a singleton cache holding a scoped DbContext ends up sharing one context across threads and requests.
f: What is a captive dependency?
A shorter-lived service captured by a longer-lived one.
How do you catch it before production?
ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild, plus tests that build the host.
p4-55.y: The rule is that a service should only depend on services that live as long or longer. A singleton can depend only on singletons. A scoped service can depend on scoped and singleton services. A transient can depend on anything. A singleton depending on a scoped service, like DbContext, is a captive dependency bug, and ASP.NET Core catches it in development with scope validation.
p4-55.k: di lifetimes, captive dependency, singleton, scoped, transient

p4-56.q: GetService returns null if the service isn't registered; GetRequiredService throws InvalidOperationException. I prefer GetRequiredService to fail fast with a clear message, and use GetService only for truly optional services.
i: Both are service locator calls; prefer constructor injection.
IEnumerable<T> resolves to empty if none registered, never null.
GetRequiredService gives a clear error naming the missing type, much easier to debug than a NullReferenceException later.
Keyed versions: GetKeyedService / GetRequiredKeyedService.
f: When use GetService?
Optional plugins or features that may not be registered.
Is GetRequiredService an extension method?
Yes, in ServiceProviderServiceExtensions.
p4-56.y: GetService returns null if the service isn't registered, so it's for optional services. GetRequiredService throws a clear exception naming the missing type, so it's for services that must exist. I prefer GetRequiredService, because a clear error at startup is much easier to fix than a NullReferenceException later.

p4-57.q: Controllers declare dependencies in their constructor; for each request, the controller activator creates the controller from the request scope (HttpContext.RequestServices), so scoped services like DbContext are shared within that request and disposed when it ends. Controllers themselves aren't registered by default; AddControllersAsServices changes that.
i: Middleware constructors resolve once (singleton-like); request-scoped services go in InvokeAsync parameters.
Minimal API handlers get services as parameters, inferred from DI.
Constructor selection: the container picks the constructor with the most parameters it can satisfy.
Primary constructors (C# 12) work the same way for controllers.
f: Are controllers singletons?
No, a new instance per request.
What does AddControllersAsServices do?
Registers controllers in DI so the container (and features like decorators) creates them.
p4-57.y: When a request comes in, ASP.NET Core creates the controller through the DI container. The container looks at the constructor, picks the one with the most parameters it can satisfy, resolves each dependency, and their dependencies, in the request scope. Scoped services are shared within that request. At the end of the request, the scope disposes them.
p4-57.k: constructor injection, controller dependencies, di, request scope

p4-58.q: Register several implementations (AddTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>(), AddTransient<INotifier, SmsNotifier>()) and inject IEnumerable<INotifier> to get all; injecting INotifier gets the last registered. To pick one, use keyed services (.NET 8: AddKeyedSingleton<ISftpClient, RebexClient>("Rebex") with [FromKeyedServices]) or a factory.
i: TryAddEnumerable avoids duplicate registrations.
Keyed services fit our per-vendor SFTP provider choice from configuration.
Order matters: IEnumerable<T> preserves registration order, which can define a pipeline (e.g. validators).
f: Which one is resolved for a single INotifier?
The last registration.
Keyed services vs factory?
Keyed is built in and simple; factories allow custom logic.
p4-58.y: I can register several implementations of the same interface, then inject IEnumerable of that interface to get all of them, in registration order, which is good for things like a list of validators. If I need one specific implementation, I use keyed services from .NET 8 with the FromKeyedServices attribute, or a small factory. We use keyed services to pick an SFTP library per vendor.
p4-58.k: multiple implementations, keyed services, ienumerable, di

p4-59.q: Yes: using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope() and resolve from scope.ServiceProvider. I use IServiceScopeFactory in singletons and BackgroundServices that need scoped services like DbContext, creating one scope per unit of work (per message or per poll) so they're disposed properly.
i: CreateAsyncScope with await using for IAsyncDisposable services.
Never keep a scope for the whole app lifetime.
Scoped services resolved inside the scope are disposed when the scope is disposed, preventing leaks.
f: Why one scope per message?
So DbContext tracking and connections don't grow across messages.
CreateScope vs CreateAsyncScope?
The async version supports await using for async disposal.
p4-59.y: Yes. I inject IServiceScopeFactory and call CreateScope, then resolve services from that scope and dispose it when done. I use it in singletons like background services, where there's no request scope, but I need scoped services like DbContext. For example, our SFTP poller creates a new scope for each polling run.

p4-60.q: Service locator is pulling dependencies from IServiceProvider inside classes instead of declaring them in the constructor. It hides dependencies, makes tests harder and moves errors to runtime. It's acceptable at composition roots, factories and background scopes.
i: Smell: IServiceProvider in a business class constructor.
Testing requires a container or complex mocks.
Legitimate uses: factory classes, middleware InvokeAsync parameters are fine; static service locators (ServiceLocator.Current) are not.
Detect it in reviews: IServiceProvider injected into domain classes.
f: Is using IServiceScopeFactory a service locator?
Technically yes, but it's an accepted infrastructure exception.
How do you refactor away from it?
Move dependencies to constructor parameters or inject a typed factory.
p4-60.y: The service locator anti-pattern is when a class asks the container for its dependencies itself, by injecting IServiceProvider and calling GetService everywhere. It hides the real dependencies, so you can't see them in the constructor, and tests become harder. It's fine in factories or framework code, but in business classes I always use constructor injection.

p4-61.q: I don't use the container in unit tests: I construct the class directly with Moq mocks (or fakes) for its interfaces, call the method, and assert outcomes and key interactions. For wiring, I use integration tests with WebApplicationFactory and replace external services with ConfigureTestServices.
i: Prefer state-based assertions over verifying every call.
FakeTimeProvider, FakeLogger from Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing.
Integration example: WebApplicationFactory with ConfigureTestServices to replace ISftpClient with a fake.
f: Unit vs integration test?
Unit isolates one class; integration tests real wiring, often with a real database in containers.
What is Testcontainers?
A library that starts real dependencies (SQL Server, RabbitMQ) in Docker for tests.
p4-61.y: Because dependencies come through the constructor, I just create the class in the test and pass mocks or fakes, for example a mocked ISftpClient with Moq and a fake time provider. Then I test the behaviour, like which file was uploaded or which error was returned. For bigger tests, I use WebApplicationFactory and replace only the external services.
p4-61.k: unit testing, di, mocking, moq, testing

p4-62.q: VendorExchangeService receives ISftpClientFactory, IOptions<SftpOptions> and ILogger<T> through its constructor; the factory returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro client per vendor configuration. It's scoped, the factory is a singleton, and clients are created and disposed per transfer.
i: Registration via an AddSftpProviders extension method.
Options validated at startup.
Unit tests mock the factory and client.
Registration with keyed services: AddKeyedTransient<ISftpClient, RebexSftpClient>("Rebex"), resolved by vendor configuration.
f: Why is the factory a singleton?
It's stateless and cheap to share.
Why create clients per transfer?
SFTP sessions are stateful connections that should be disposed after use.
p4-62.y: Our vendor exchange service gets an SFTP client factory, its settings through IOptions, and a logger, all through the constructor. The factory returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro client based on each vendor's configuration. The service is scoped, the factory is a singleton, and the clients are created and disposed for each transfer.
p4-62.k: di example, real example, sftp, story

p4-63.q: Singletons are shared across threads and requests, so any state must be thread-safe, and holding scoped resources like DbContext causes captive dependency bugs. Everything transient creates many short-lived objects (GC pressure) and breaks sharing within a request, such as one DbContext per unit of work.
i: Choose by state: stateless and thread-safe → singleton; per-request state → scoped; lightweight, stateful per use → transient.
HttpClient handlers are pooled by IHttpClientFactory, not singleton HttpClients with stale DNS.
Transient disposables resolved from the root container are tracked until shutdown, effectively a memory leak.
Rule: singleton for stateless/thread-safe, scoped for per-request state, transient for lightweight stateless helpers.
f: Is DbContext thread-safe?
No, which is why it's scoped and never shared across concurrent operations.
Should a cache be singleton?
Yes, with thread-safe structures like IMemoryCache.
p4-63.y: Not everything should be singleton, because one shared instance must be thread-safe and must never hold per-request data, and it can't use scoped things like DbContext. Not everything should be transient either, because creating objects over and over wastes memory, and disposable transients can pile up. So I choose: singleton for stateless shared things, scoped for per-request, transient for light helpers.
p4-63.k: di lifetimes, singleton, transient, scoped, choosing lifetime

p4-64.q: When a request ends, its DI scope is disposed: every scoped and transient IDisposable created in it is disposed (DbContext closes its connection back to the pool), the HttpContext is returned for reuse, and response completion callbacks (OnCompleted) run.
i: Don't use HttpContext or scoped services after the request ends (e.g. in fire-and-forget tasks).
IHttpContextAccessor in background threads returns null or stale data.
The request's CancellationToken (RequestAborted) is signalled if the client disconnects earlier.
Scoped IAsyncDisposable services are disposed asynchronously.
f: What if you start a background task using DbContext from the request?
It may be disposed mid-use; create a new scope instead.
What is Response.OnCompleted?
A callback that runs after the response is sent, useful for metrics.
p4-64.y: When a request ends, the response is completed, and the request's DI scope is disposed, which disposes all scoped and transient services created in it, like DbContext, closing connections. If the client disconnected early, the request's cancellation token was already triggered, so well-written code stops work sooner. Then the HttpContext is released.
p4-64.k: request end, dispose, scope, request lifecycle

p4-65.q: The container disposes what it created: scoped and transient disposables when their scope ends, singletons when the root provider is disposed at shutdown. Instances you create yourself and register (AddSingleton(new X())) are not disposed by the container.
i: Transient disposables resolved from the root live until shutdown, a memory leak pattern.
IAsyncDisposable is supported; prefer async disposal at shutdown.
Factories like AddSingleton(sp => new X()) are disposed by the container because it created them via the factory.
IDisposable transients resolved repeatedly from the root are a classic leak; use scopes.
f: Why are transient disposables from the root a leak?
The root tracks them for disposal, so they stay referenced until the app stops.
Who disposes a singleton you constructed?
You do; the container won't.
p4-65.y: The container disposes what it creates. Scoped services, and transients resolved in a scope, are disposed when the scope ends, usually at the end of the request. Singletons are disposed when the application shuts down. If I create an object myself and register the instance, the container won't dispose it, so I must. And disposable transients resolved from the root stay alive until shutdown, which is a leak.

p4-66.q: ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's cross-platform, open-source, high-performance framework for web APIs, MVC, Razor Pages, Blazor and real-time apps (SignalR) on modern .NET, with built-in DI, configuration, logging, a middleware pipeline and the Kestrel server. It runs on Windows, Linux and containers.
i: Hosting: WebApplication builder (minimal hosting) since .NET 6.
Endpoints: controllers, minimal APIs, gRPC, SignalR hubs, health checks.
Performance features: Kestrel, System.Text.Json source generators, output caching, native AOT for minimal APIs.
.NET 10 additions: built-in validation for minimal APIs, OpenAPI 3.1 support, passkey support in Identity.
f: ASP.NET vs ASP.NET Core?
Classic ASP.NET runs only on .NET Framework/IIS; Core is a cross-platform rewrite.
Can ASP.NET Core run without IIS?
Yes, Kestrel serves directly or behind any reverse proxy.
p4-66.y: ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's modern, open-source and cross-platform framework for building web APIs, websites and real-time apps. It has built-in dependency injection, a middleware pipeline, configuration and logging, and it's one of the fastest web frameworks. It runs on Windows, Linux and in containers. All our IRT APIs are built on it.

p4-67.q: Kestrel is the cross-platform, async web server built into ASP.NET Core. It can serve traffic directly or sit behind a reverse proxy or load balancer (ALB, Nginx, IIS via the ASP.NET Core Module) that handles TLS termination, buffering and edge concerns.
i: Supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC).
Configurable limits: MaxRequestBodySize (default about 30 MB), header sizes, connection limits, timeouts.
Behind proxies, use ForwardedHeaders middleware to get the real client IP and scheme.
IIS in-process hosting runs the app inside w3wp without Kestrel.
f: Why use a reverse proxy?
TLS offload, load balancing, WAF and centralised edge security.
What header does ForwardedHeaders read?
X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, from trusted proxies only.
p4-67.y: Kestrel is the built-in, cross-platform web server in ASP.NET Core. It's very fast and supports HTTP 1, 2 and 3. It can face the internet directly, but often sits behind a reverse proxy or load balancer like an ALB, Nginx or IIS, which handles TLS and routing. Our containers run Kestrel behind an ALB.
p4-67.k: kestrel, web server, reverse proxy, asp.net core

p4-68.q: Middleware order is execution order, so mistakes break things quietly: UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication leaves users anonymous (401/403), UseCors after endpoints means no CORS headers, exception handling registered late misses earlier errors, and static files after auth either get protected unintentionally or bypass checks.
i: Recommended order: ExceptionHandler, HSTS, HttpsRedirection, StaticFiles, Routing, CORS, Authentication, Authorization, RateLimiter, custom, endpoints.
WebApplication adds UseRouting and endpoints automatically if you don't.
Part 10 Q1 has the full pipeline diagram.
Real example: putting app.UseCors() after app.MapControllers() means preflight responses miss headers and the browser blocks calls.
f: What happens if UseRateLimiter is before UseRouting?
Endpoint-specific policies can't be read; only global limiters apply.
Where does correlation-id middleware go?
Very early, so all later logs include it.
p4-68.y: Middleware runs in the order it's added, so wrong order causes real bugs. For example, if authorization is added before authentication, the user isn't known yet and every request fails. If the exception handler is added late, earlier errors aren't caught. And if CORS is added after the endpoints, preflight requests don't get the right headers and the browser blocks the call.
p4-68.k: middleware order, pipeline order, bugs, cors, authentication

p4-69.q: Use adds middleware that can do work and call next; Run adds terminal middleware that ends the pipeline; Map branches by path prefix and MapWhen by a predicate into a separate pipeline; UseWhen conditionally adds middleware and then rejoins the main pipeline.
i: Map strips the matched prefix from Request.Path and adds it to PathBase.
Prefer endpoint routing (MapGet, MapControllers) for routes; Map is for pipeline branches.
Map with nested pipelines can host separate branches, e.g. /admin with its own auth middleware.
c:
app.UseWhen(ctx => ctx.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/api"), a => a.UseMiddleware<AuditMiddleware>());
app.Map("/ping", a => a.Run(ctx => ctx.Response.WriteAsync("pong")));
f: MapWhen vs UseWhen?
MapWhen branches without rejoining; UseWhen rejoins the main pipeline.
What happens after Run?
Nothing; later middleware never executes.
p4-69.y: Use adds middleware that can do work and then call the next one. Run adds terminal middleware that ends the pipeline, so nothing after it runs. Map branches the pipeline based on the path, so requests to, say, /health go down a separate pipeline. For normal routes I use endpoint routing like MapGet or MapControllers.
p4-69.k: use, run, map, middleware, pipeline branching

p4-70.q: With endpoint routing, UseRouting matches the request to an endpoint early and stores it on HttpContext, so middleware in between (CORS, authentication, authorization, rate limiting) can read endpoint metadata like [Authorize] or policies; UseEndpoints (or the implicit endpoint middleware) then executes it.
i: ctx.GetEndpoint() returns the matched endpoint and its metadata.
Route constraints ({id:int}), route groups (MapGroup) for shared prefixes and policies.
LinkGenerator generates URLs from route names.
c:
var api = app.MapGroup("/api/shipments").RequireAuthorization().WithTags("Shipments");
api.MapGet("/{id:int}", (int id, IShipmentService s) => s.GetAsync(id));
f: Why was endpoint routing introduced?
So all frameworks share one routing system and middleware can see the chosen endpoint.
What is MapGroup?
A way to apply a prefix and conventions to many endpoints.
p4-70.y: With endpoint routing, the routing middleware matches the request to an endpoint early and stores it on the HttpContext. So middleware in between, like CORS, authentication, authorization and rate limiting, can read the endpoint's metadata, such as the Authorize attribute or a rate limit policy. Then the endpoint itself runs at the end.

p4-71.q: Since .NET 6 the minimal hosting model merges Startup's ConfigureServices and Configure into Program.cs (builder.Services... then app.Use...). A Startup class still works if you call it yourself, but new templates don't use it.
i: WebApplication.CreateBuilder configures configuration, logging, DI and Kestrel with sensible defaults.
Top-level statements; make Program partial or public for WebApplicationFactory tests (.NET 10 generates this automatically).
Extension methods keep Program.cs tidy (AddIrtServices()).
Testing: in .NET 10 a source generator makes Program public automatically for WebApplicationFactory.
f: How do integration tests find Program?
WebApplicationFactory<Program>; Program must be accessible (public partial class Program).
Is Startup deprecated?
Not removed, but no longer the default pattern.
p4-71.y: Since .NET 6, the separate Startup class and Program class were merged into one Program.cs using the minimal hosting model. Service registrations that were in ConfigureServices go on builder.Services, and the pipeline that was in Configure goes on the app object. Startup still works if you want it, but new projects don't use it.

p4-72.q: CORS doesn't protect the server: it relaxes the browser's same-origin policy and doesn't stop curl, Postman or server-to-server calls. Real security is authentication, authorization and validation; CORS only controls which browser origins can read responses.
i: Never combine AllowAnyOrigin with AllowCredentials (not allowed and unsafe).
Preflight OPTIONS requests for non-simple requests; cache with SetPreflightMaxAge.
Allow-list specific origins per environment.
f: What is a preflight?
An OPTIONS request the browser sends to ask permission for non-simple cross-origin requests.
Does CORS stop CSRF?
Not fully; simple form posts don't preflight, so use SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens.
p4-72.y: No, CORS is not a security feature for the API. It's a browser rule that relaxes the same-origin policy, telling the browser which other sites may read responses. Tools like Postman or a server can call the API regardless of CORS. So real security still comes from authentication and authorization. CORS only protects users in the browser.

p4-73.q: In production I use UseHttpsRedirection and UseHsts, with certificates either on Kestrel or, more commonly, TLS terminated at the ALB or API Gateway with ACM certificates and ForwardedHeaders so the app knows the original scheme. Internal traffic can be re-encrypted where policy requires.
i: HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a period; don't enable it in development.
TLS 1.2+ only; modern ciphers.
Certificate rotation automated by ACM.
dotnet dev-certs for local HTTPS.
f: Why ForwardedHeaders with TLS offload?
Otherwise the app sees HTTP and may redirect loop or generate wrong URLs.
What is HSTS preload?
Browsers ship a list of HTTPS-only domains so even the first visit uses HTTPS.
p4-73.y: In development I use the dev certificate. In production, HTTPS is usually terminated at the load balancer, like our ALB, with a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager. In the app I add UseHttpsRedirection and HSTS, and configure forwarded headers so the app knows the original request was HTTPS. Traffic between services is also encrypted.

p4-74.q: AddHealthChecks registers checks for the database, RabbitMQ and other dependencies, exposed with MapHealthChecks, typically /health/live (process only) and /health/ready (dependencies). Load balancers and orchestrators use them to route traffic and restart unhealthy instances.
i: Tags and predicates separate live and ready checks.
AspNetCore.HealthChecks.* packages provide checks for SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, URIs.
Custom IHealthCheck for business checks (e.g. SFTP reachable).
Don't expose detailed health output publicly; secure or minimise it.
f: Should liveness check the database?
No, or a DB blip restarts every instance.
What is Degraded used for?
Partial health that alerts without removing the instance.
p4-74.y: Health checks are endpoints that report if the app and its dependencies are healthy. In ASP.NET Core I add AddHealthChecks with checks for things like the database and the message broker, and map them to endpoints. I keep a simple liveness endpoint and a readiness endpoint that checks dependencies. The load balancer and ECS use them to route traffic only to healthy instances.
p4-74.k: health checks, liveness, readiness, monitoring, load balancer

p4-75.q: On SIGTERM the host stops accepting new requests, lets in-flight ones finish within the shutdown timeout (30 seconds by default since .NET 6; previously 5 seconds), signals ApplicationStopping and cancels BackgroundService tokens, then disposes services. Orchestrators must allow enough time (ECS stopTimeout, Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds) and load balancers should deregister first.
i: HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout configures the wait.
Background workers: stop taking new messages, finish or nack the current one.
ALB deregistration delay should be shorter than the stop timeout.
f: What happens if shutdown exceeds the timeout?
The orchestrator sends SIGKILL and work in progress is lost.
How do message consumers shut down safely?
Stop consuming, finish current messages and ack, or let unacked ones redeliver.
p4-75.y: When a container is stopped, it gets a SIGTERM signal. ASP.NET Core stops accepting new requests, lets current ones finish within the shutdown timeout, which is 30 seconds by default, and cancels the stopping token for background services. I make my background loops respect that token and finish or save their work. The load balancer also drains connections first.
p4-75.k: graceful shutdown, sigterm, shutdown timeout, stopping token

p4-76.q: I accept a CancellationToken in actions (bound to HttpContext.RequestAborted) and pass it through to EF Core, HttpClient, Task.Delay and other async calls, so abandoned requests stop work; in workers I use the stoppingToken. I check ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() in long loops and treat OperationCanceledException as normal, not an error.
i: Don't cancel after a point of no return (e.g. after committing); pass CancellationToken.None to cleanup.
CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource combines tokens; CancelAfter adds timeouts.
Log cancellations at lower levels to avoid noise.
f: What happens when a client disconnects?
RequestAborted is signalled, and awaiting cancellable calls throws OperationCanceledException.
Should writes be cancellable?
Be careful; partial work must be transactional or idempotent.
p4-76.y: I accept a CancellationToken in my async methods and pass it all the way down, to EF Core queries and HTTP calls. In APIs, ASP.NET Core gives a token that's cancelled if the client disconnects, so we stop wasting work. In background services I use the stopping token. I never ignore it, and I treat a cancellation exception as normal, not an error.

p4-77.q: PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent, so missing fields become defaults; PATCH applies a partial change (JSON Patch or JSON Merge Patch) and isn't guaranteed idempotent. I use PATCH for small updates like status changes and PUT when the client sends the full representation.
i: JSON Patch (RFC 6902): operations list; JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396): partial document.
.NET 10 adds JSON Patch support on System.Text.Json (previously required Newtonsoft).
Use ETags/If-Match for concurrency on both.
PATCH with JSON Merge Patch: send only changed fields; null means remove.
f: Can PUT create resources?
Yes, if the client chooses the id (PUT /items/42).
Is PATCH idempotent?
Can be, but not by definition (e.g. "add item" operations).
p4-77.y: PUT replaces the whole resource with what I send, so missing fields can be cleared, and it's idempotent. PATCH updates only the fields I send, which is better for small changes. For PATCH, I use JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch. In our APIs, we use PATCH for things like updating only a shipment's status.
p4-77.k: put, patch, http verbs, rest, partial update

p4-78.q: 200 OK means success with a body; 201 Created means a new resource was created, with a Location header pointing to it and usually the resource in the body. Others in the family: 202 Accepted (processing later) and 204 No Content (success without body).
i: CreatedAtAction / Results.Created set Location.
202 with a status URL suits long jobs like CSV import.
201 vs 202: 201 means created now; 202 means accepted for later processing.
c: return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = shipment.Id }, dto);
f: When 202?
When work is queued and finishes later.
204 vs 200 with empty body?
204 explicitly says no content; common for DELETE and PUT.
p4-78.y: 200 OK means the request succeeded and the result is in the body. 201 Created means a new resource was created, and the response should include a Location header pointing to it, usually with the created item. So for a POST that creates a shipment, I return 201 with the link to the new shipment.

p4-79.q: 400 Bad Request means invalid input; 401 Unauthorized means not authenticated (missing or invalid token, with a WWW-Authenticate header); 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not allowed.
i: Return ProblemDetails with validation errors for 400.
For resources the user may not know exist, 404 can hide existence instead of 403.
ASP.NET Core returns 401 via the authentication handler's challenge and 403 via forbid.
Return ProblemDetails consistently for all three.
f: Which code for an expired token?
What does WWW-Authenticate tell the client?
The scheme and error, e.g. Bearer error="invalid_token".
p4-79.y: 400 Bad Request means the request itself is wrong, like invalid JSON or failed validation. 401 Unauthorized actually means not authenticated: no token, or an invalid or expired one. 403 Forbidden means we know who you are, but you're not allowed to do this. So a logged-in user trying to open another study's data gets 403.

p4-80.q: 404 Not Found means the resource or route doesn't exist; 405 Method Not Allowed means the route exists but not for this HTTP verb (e.g. DELETE on a read-only endpoint), and the response should include an Allow header.
i: Endpoint routing returns 405 automatically when a route matches but the method doesn't.
Return 404 for missing ids, not 200 with null.
In ASP.NET Core, endpoint routing returns 405 when a route matches but no endpoint supports the method.
Use 404 for "no such resource id" rather than 200 with null.
f: 410 Gone means it existed and was permanently removed.
Why would you get 405 unexpectedly?
Missing [HttpPut] or a WebDAV module in IIS intercepting verbs.
p4-80.y: 404 Not Found means the resource or route doesn't exist, like asking for a shipment id that isn't there. 405 Method Not Allowed means the route exists, but not for that HTTP method, like sending DELETE to an endpoint that only supports GET. ASP.NET Core returns 405 automatically in that case.
p4-80.k: 404, 405, status codes, not found, method not allowed

p4-81.q: 409 Conflict means a valid request clashes with current state (duplicate, concurrency version mismatch); 422 Unprocessable Content means the request is well-formed but semantically invalid (business rule failed). Many APIs use 400 for validation; I use 422 for business rule failures when the team agrees.
i: 412 Precondition Failed for If-Match ETag mismatch.
Be consistent and document the choices.
409 example: inserting a site number that already exists in the study.
422 example: kit count exceeds depot stock, a valid request breaking a business rule.
f: Which for a duplicate import file?
409, with the existing import id.
Which for a concurrency conflict in EF Core?
409 (or 412 with ETags).
p4-81.y: 409 Conflict means the request conflicts with the current state, like creating a site number that already exists, or a concurrency conflict when someone else changed the record. 422 means the request is well-formed but breaks a business rule, like asking for more kits than the depot has. Both tell the client exactly what kind of problem to fix.

p4-82.q: 500 is an unhandled error in this server; 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or gateway got an invalid response from upstream; 503 Service Unavailable means overloaded or down for maintenance (often with Retry-After); 504 means the gateway timed out waiting for upstream.
i: ALB 502 often means the target closed the connection or returned malformed responses (keep-alive timeout mismatches).
ALB 504 means the target didn't respond within the idle timeout.
429 Too Many Requests for rate limiting.
503 should include Retry-After when planned maintenance or overload.
f: Why might ALB return 502 intermittently?
Target keep-alive timeout shorter than ALB idle timeout, so connections close unexpectedly.
What does 503 from ALB mean?
No healthy targets registered.
p4-82.y: 500 means something broke inside our service. 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer got an invalid response from the service behind it, for example the container crashed. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily overloaded or in maintenance, ideally with a Retry-After header. When I troubleshoot, these tell me which layer to look at first.

p4-83.q: DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) are simple classes or records that shape exactly what an API accepts or returns. They decouple the API contract from the database schema, prevent over-posting and data leaks, allow versioning, and let each endpoint carry only what it needs.
i: Records are ideal: immutable, value equality, concise.
Map with explicit code, Mapperly (source generated) or AutoMapper (now commercial for new versions).
Separate request and response DTOs.
c:
public sealed record CreateShipmentRequest(int SiteId, int KitCount, DateOnly ShipDate);
public sealed record ShipmentResponse(int Id, string Status, DateTimeOffset? DeliveredAt);
f: AutoMapper or manual mapping?
Manual or source-generated mapping is explicit and fast; AutoMapper hides errors until runtime.
Should DTOs have logic?
No, only data and validation attributes.
p4-83.y: A DTO, or data transfer object, is a simple class that defines exactly what the API sends or receives. It keeps the API contract separate from the database entities. So I can change the database without breaking clients, avoid exposing sensitive fields, and prevent over-posting. I use C# records for DTOs.
p4-83.k: dto, data transfer object, api contract, records

p4-84.q: Exposing EF entities directly leaks the schema and sensitive fields, couples clients to database changes, enables over-posting, and causes serialization cycles and lazy-loading surprises. DTOs give a stable, safe contract.
i: Navigation properties create cycles (JSON ReferenceHandler is a band-aid).
Lazy loading during serialization creates N+1 queries.
Projection with Select into DTOs also generates efficient SQL.
Security example: an entity with IsUnblinded or audit fields accidentally serialized to the client.
f: How do you return data efficiently?
Project to DTOs in the query so only needed columns are selected.
What is over-posting?
Clients setting fields they shouldn't by sending extra properties.
p4-84.y: Returning EF entities directly ties the API to the database design, so a schema change breaks clients. It can also leak sensitive or internal fields, create circular references when serializing, trigger lazy loading, and allow over-posting on input. In a clinical system, accidentally exposing an unblinding field would be serious, so we always map to DTOs.
p4-84.k: ef entities, dto, security, over-posting, api design

p4-85.q: A DTO is the transport shape between layers or services (API contracts); a ViewModel is shaped for one UI view and may include display-only data like dropdown options. In APIs we mostly use DTOs; ViewModels belong to MVC or front-end code.
i: BFF responses are close to view models for a specific screen.
Keep both free of business logic.
In our APIs, request DTOs (commands) and response DTOs (views) are separate records.
ViewModels belong to Razor/MVC; in React the client shapes its own view state.
f: Can a DTO be a ViewModel?
Sometimes, if the API is designed for one screen.
What is a command object?
An input DTO that represents an intent, as in CQRS.
p4-85.y: A DTO carries data across a boundary, like an API request or response, and has no behaviour. A ViewModel is shaped for a specific screen in server-rendered MVC or Razor pages, and can include display-specific data. With a React front end, our APIs return DTOs, and the client shapes its own view state.

p4-86.q: [ApiController] turns on API behaviours: attribute routing is required, invalid model state returns 400 ProblemDetails automatically, binding sources are inferred ([FromBody] for complex types, [FromRoute]/[FromQuery] for simple ones), multipart/form-data is inferred for IFormFile, and error status codes get ProblemDetails.
i: Can be applied at assembly level.
Customise the automatic 400 with InvalidModelStateResponseFactory or disable with SuppressModelStateInvalidFilter.
Services are inferred for parameters registered in DI (.NET 7+).
Since .NET 7, parameters registered in DI are inferred as services in [ApiController] actions without [FromServices].
f: Why do some actions not hit my breakpoint with bad input?
The automatic 400 filter returns before the action runs.
How do you customise the 400 response?
Configure ApiBehaviorOptions.InvalidModelStateResponseFactory.
p4-86.y: The ApiController attribute turns on API-friendly behaviours: it automatically returns a 400 with validation errors when the model is invalid, infers where parameters come from, like body or route, requires attribute routing, and returns errors as ProblemDetails. It removes a lot of repetitive code from every action.

p4-87.q: Routing maps URLs to endpoints. Attribute routing puts templates on controllers and actions ([Route("api/studies/{id}")]) and is the standard for APIs; conventional routing uses one template in Program.cs such as {controller}/{action}/{id?}, typical for MVC sites.
i: Route constraints ({id:int}, {date:datetime}) and tokens ([controller]).
Minimal APIs use MapGet/MapPost with the same routing engine.
Avoid ambiguous routes; route order and specificity resolve matches.
Route templates support optional parameters ({id?}), defaults and catch-all ({*path}).
f: What's a route constraint for?
Matching only valid formats; not for input validation.
Can you mix both?
Yes, but APIs usually stick to attribute routing.
p4-87.y: Routing maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to the code that handles it. Attribute routing puts the route on the controller or action, like Route api slash shipments, which is clear and flexible, and it's the standard for APIs. Conventional routing uses one central pattern, like controller slash action slash id, which is common in older MVC apps.
p4-87.k: routing, attribute routing, conventional routing, endpoints

p4-88.q: I accept query parameters such as ?status=Shipped&siteId=12&sortBy=shipDate&desc=true, apply them to IQueryable before paging so SQL does the work, and allow-list sortable and filterable fields to prevent injection and slow queries.
i: Build queries conditionally; never concatenate SQL.
Indexes to support common filters and sorts.
Stable sort with a tie-breaker (Id) for consistent paging.
f: Offset vs keyset paging?
Keyset (WHERE Id > last) is faster for deep pages; offset is simpler.
How do you stop huge page sizes?
Cap page size on the server.
p4-88.y: I accept filter and sort parameters in the query string, but only for a known list of fields, never raw SQL or any column name. I build the query step by step on IQueryable, adding Where clauses for each filter and an OrderBy for the sort, then apply paging. Everything runs in the database, and the most used filters have indexes.
p4-88.k: filtering, sorting, paging, iqueryable, query parameters
