p4-89.q: OpenAPI is the standard JSON/YAML description of an API; Swagger UI renders it interactively. In .NET 9+ the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi generates documents (Swashbuckle is no longer in templates), with XML comments, examples and auth settings; Scalar or Swagger UI can render it.
i: .NET 10 supports OpenAPI 3.1 and XML doc comments in generated docs.
Generate clients (NSwag, Kiota) from the spec.
Contract-first or code-first; version documents per API version.
f: Why did templates drop Swashbuckle?
Microsoft moved to a built-in, maintained OpenAPI generator.
How do you keep docs accurate?
Generate from code and test the spec in CI.
p4-89.y: OpenAPI is a standard way to describe an API: endpoints, parameters, request and response models and status codes. Swagger is the tooling around it, like the interactive Swagger UI. In .NET, I generate the document from the code, and since .NET 9 it's built in. We share it with front-end and vendor teams and generate clients from it.
p4-89.k: swagger, openapi, api documentation, swagger ui

p4-90.q: HTTPS only; authentication with JWTs from OIDC/SSO; authorization policies and resource-level checks; input validation; rate limiting; restricted CORS; security headers; no secrets or PHI in logs; dependency scanning; and least-privilege access to data and cloud resources.
i: OWASP API Top 10 as the checklist (Part 2 Q51).
Secrets in Secrets Manager; managed identities/roles.
WAF at the edge, request size limits.
Audit logs for sensitive actions.
f: Most common API security bug?
Broken object level authorization (missing per-resource checks).
How do you test API security?
Automated authz tests, DAST scans and penetration tests.
p4-90.y: I secure an API in layers: HTTPS everywhere, authentication with JWT from our identity provider, authorization with policies and per-record checks, input validation, and DTOs so we don't leak data. Then rate limiting, secure headers, secrets in Secrets Manager, logging without sensitive data, and regular dependency and security scans.
p4-90.k: api security, authentication, authorization, jwt, owasp

p4-91.q: The access token is short-lived (e.g. [15 minutes]) and sent on every API call; the refresh token is long-lived, stored securely and sent only to the identity provider to get new access tokens, and it can be revoked. This limits exposure if an access token leaks.
i: Refresh token rotation: each use returns a new one; reuse of an old one signals theft.
Store refresh tokens server-side (BFF) or in secure HttpOnly cookies.
Our logout fix revokes refresh tokens and denylists access token jti.
Access tokens are validated locally by APIs; refresh tokens are validated only by the identity provider.
f: Why not long-lived access tokens?
They can't easily be revoked and increase damage if stolen.
Where should refresh tokens never be stored?
localStorage or anywhere JavaScript can read.
p4-91.y: An access token is short-lived, maybe [15 minutes], and is sent with every API call to prove who you are. A refresh token lives longer and is used only to get a new access token from the identity provider, without logging in again. If an access token leaks, it expires soon, and refresh tokens can be revoked. That's how we fixed our logout issue.
p4-91.k: access token, refresh token, jwt, oauth, token lifetime

p4-92.q: Role-based authorization ([Authorize(Roles = "StudyManager")]) is simple but coarse; policy-based uses named policies with requirements and handlers registered in AddAuthorization, plus resource-based checks via IAuthorizationService for rules like "this user can access this study".
i: Requirements + handlers keep rules testable.
RequireAssertion for quick inline rules.
Resource-based: pass the resource to AuthorizeAsync.
f: How do you apply a policy?
[Authorize(Policy = "CanUnblind")] or RequireAuthorization("CanUnblind").
Fallback policy?
A default policy applied to endpoints without attributes, e.g. require authenticated users.
p4-92.y: Role-based authorization checks if the user is in a role, like Admin. Policy-based authorization is more flexible: a policy is a set of requirements, like a claim, a role, or custom logic, written in a handler. I register policies with AddAuthorization, then use them on endpoints. We use policies for things like checking the user has access to a specific study.
p4-92.k: role-based authorization, policy-based authorization, policies, authorization handler

p4-93.q: Over-posting is when clients send extra fields that bind to properties they shouldn't set (IsAdmin, Status). I prevent it with input DTOs containing only allowed fields and never binding entities directly; [Bind] or [BindNever] are weaker alternatives.
i: Mass assignment is the same issue (OWASP API3: broken object property level authorization).
Response DTOs prevent the reverse: excessive data exposure.
Integration test sending {"status":"Delivered","isAdmin":true} to verify extra fields are ignored.
System.Text.Json UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow (.NET 8) can reject unknown fields entirely.
f: Is [Bind] enough?
It works but is easy to forget; DTOs are clearer.
How do you test for it?
Send extra fields and assert they're ignored.
p4-93.y: Over-posting is when a client sends extra fields, like isAdmin, and the server saves them because it binds directly to the entity. I prevent it by binding only to request DTOs that contain just the allowed fields, then mapping them to entities myself. I also have tests that send extra fields and check they're ignored.

p4-94.q: I limit size (Kestrel MaxRequestBodySize, [RequestSizeLimit]), stream instead of buffering, compress, paginate responses, and send big files through presigned S3 uploads or chunked uploads rather than JSON bodies.
i: Defaults: Kestrel about 30 MB request body; IIS has its own limit.
Form limits: FormOptions.MultipartBodyLengthLimit.
Response compression with Brotli/Gzip (careful with secrets and BREACH).
Streaming request bodies: read Request.Body directly or use MultipartReader instead of buffering IFormFile.
f: What happens over the limit?
Kestrel returns 413 Payload Too Large.
How do you stream JSON responses?
Return IAsyncEnumerable<T>, which System.Text.Json serializes as it goes.
p4-94.y: First I set sensible size limits, in Kestrel and per endpoint, so huge requests are rejected early. For large data, I don't buffer everything in memory, I stream the request body. For really large files, the client uploads directly to S3 with a presigned URL, and the API only receives a reference. For big imports, I process them in the background.
p4-94.k: large payloads, request size limit, streaming, s3, upload

p4-95.q: I use IFormFile for small files and streaming (MultipartReader) for large ones; validate size, extension and content (magic bytes), scan for malware, store outside the web root (S3) with random names, and process asynchronously. Our CSV import used a [5 MB] limit, streamed parsing and a file hash for duplicate detection.
i: Never trust the client's file name or content type.
IFormFile buffers to disk above 64 KB, so huge files still cost disk.
Antiforgery is required for form uploads in minimal APIs (.NET 8+) unless disabled.
Large files: disable form value model binding and stream sections with MultipartReader to avoid buffering.
f: How do you check file type?
Read the first bytes (magic numbers) and validate parsing, not just extension.
Why random names?
To prevent path traversal and overwriting.
p4-95.y: For small files, I accept IFormFile with a size limit, check the extension and the actual content, and never trust the file name. I store files outside the web root, like S3, and scan them if needed. For large files, I use presigned S3 uploads or stream the multipart body. Our CSV import checks size, format and content before processing.
p4-95.k: file upload, iformfile, multipart, s3, validation

p4-96.q: Contract: OpenAPI, versioning, DTOs, validation and ProblemDetails errors. Security: authentication, authorization, rate limits and HTTPS. Resilience: timeouts, retries, idempotency keys and health checks. Observability: structured logs, correlation ids, metrics and alerts. Operations: config validation at startup, graceful shutdown, CI/CD and documentation.
i: Performance: pagination, caching, async I/O, efficient queries.
Backward compatibility: additive changes, deprecation policy.
Tests: unit, integration, contract and load tests.
Startup checks: ValidateOnStart for options, health checks for dependencies, and fail fast on misconfiguration.
f: What's often forgotten?
Timeouts on outbound calls and config validation at startup.
How do you version?
URL segment or header via Asp.Versioning, keeping old versions for a deprecation period.
p4-96.y: A production-ready API needs clear contracts with DTOs and OpenAPI, validation and consistent ProblemDetails errors, and security with authentication, authorization and rate limits. It needs logging with correlation ids, metrics and health checks, resilience with timeouts and retries, and paging for lists. Plus startup checks for configuration, versioning, and automated tests in the pipeline.
p4-96.k: production ready api, api design, best practices, checklist

p4-97.q: At every boundary for its purpose: shape and format at the API (model validation, FluentValidation or .NET 10 built-in minimal API validation), business rules in the service/domain layer, and constraints in the database (keys, unique, check constraints) as the last defence. UI validation is only for user experience.
i: Validate early, fail fast with clear messages.
Domain invariants enforced in entities (encapsulation).
Database constraints catch race conditions that app checks miss.
Example: API checks the CSV format, the service checks "site belongs to an active country/depot", and the database's unique index stops duplicate site numbers.
f: Why also in the database?
Concurrent requests can pass app checks simultaneously; unique constraints stop duplicates.
FluentValidation vs data annotations?
FluentValidation handles complex, conditional rules better and is easier to test.
p4-97.y: Validation happens at several layers, each with its own job. The API checks the shape and format of the request. The service layer checks business rules, like a site must belong to an active depot. The database enforces constraints, like unique site numbers, as the final safety net. That way bad data is stopped as early as possible, but nothing slips through.

p4-98.q: Clients send an idempotency key header; the server stores the key with the result and on a repeat returns the stored result instead of executing again. I back it with natural keys and unique constraints, optimistic concurrency, and disabling double-submit in the UI.
i: Store key, request hash and response; reject same key with different payload (422).
Expire keys after a window (24 hours).
Race: insert the key first with a unique constraint to claim it.
f: What if two identical requests arrive together?
The unique constraint lets one win; the other waits or gets 409.
Is this needed for GET?
No, GET is already safe and idempotent.
p4-98.y: For requests that create something, I use an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key, and the server stores it with the result, so a repeated request returns the same result instead of creating a duplicate. I also add unique constraints in the database. Our CSV import uses a file hash to block importing the same file twice.
p4-98.k: duplicate requests, idempotency key, idempotency, unique constraint

p5-1.q: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's open-source ORM for .NET: it maps classes to tables, translates LINQ to SQL, tracks changes to entities and writes them back in SaveChanges, and manages schema through migrations. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Cosmos DB and more through providers.
i: Core pieces: DbContext (unit of work), DbSet (tables), change tracker, model built from conventions, attributes and Fluent API.
EF Core 8: complex types, raw SQL for unmapped types, JSON columns; EF Core 9/10: better LINQ translation, named query filters (10), LeftJoin operator (10), vector search for SQL Server.
Performance tools: AsNoTracking, compiled models, compiled queries, ExecuteUpdate/Delete, DbContext pooling.
In IRT: EF Core for most CRUD and domain writes, Dapper or raw SQL for heavy reporting.
f: Is EF Core slow?
Not inherently; most problems come from query shape (N+1, over-fetching, tracking).
What's new in EF Core 10?
LeftJoin/RightJoin LINQ operators, named query filters, JSON and vector improvements.
p5-1.y: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's ORM for .NET. It lets me work with the database using C# classes and LINQ, and it translates my queries into SQL, tracks changes to objects, and saves them back. It also handles migrations for schema changes. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL and others. Most of our IRT services use EF Core with SQL Server.
p5-1.k: ef core, entity framework, orm, database

p5-2.q: ADO.NET gives raw connections, commands and data readers: fastest and full control, but manual SQL and mapping. EF Core adds LINQ, change tracking, migrations and relationships for productivity, with some overhead. Dapper sits between: you write SQL, it maps results fast.
i: EF Core itself uses ADO.NET underneath.
Choose EF Core for domain writes and typical queries; Dapper/raw SQL for complex reports or bulk paths.
SqlBulkCopy for very large inserts.
Both must use parameters to avoid SQL injection.
f: Can you mix EF Core and Dapper?
Yes, even sharing the same connection and transaction.
When is raw ADO.NET justified?
Extreme performance paths, streaming large results, or special features like table-valued parameters.
p5-2.y: ADO.NET is the low-level way: I open connections, write SQL, and read rows manually, which gives full control and top speed but more code. EF Core sits on top of ADO.NET and does the mapping, change tracking and SQL generation for me, so I'm much more productive. I use EF Core by default, and Dapper or raw SQL for a few performance-critical or reporting queries.
p5-2.k: ef core, ado.net, dapper, orm, comparison

p5-3.q: DbContext is a session with the database combining unit of work, change tracker and connection management; the model is configured in OnModelCreating. DbSet<T> represents a table you query with LINQ and add or remove entities from.
i: DbContext is not thread-safe and is registered as scoped; one per request or unit of work.
AddDbContextPool reuses instances for performance; IDbContextFactory for background or Blazor.
Configurations split into IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> classes and ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly.
f: What happens if two threads use one DbContext?
EF throws "A second operation was started on this context"; use separate contexts.
Context pooling caveat?
State must be reset; don't store per-request data in context fields.
p5-3.y: DbContext is the main EF Core class. It represents a session with the database: it manages the connection, tracks changes, and saves them in a transaction. A DbSet is a property on the DbContext for one entity type, like Shipments, which I query with LINQ and add or remove from. DbContext is short-lived, one per request.

p5-4.q: Include loads a navigation of the root entity; ThenInclude loads the next level from that navigation, e.g. Studies.Include(s => s.Sites).ThenInclude(site => site.Shipments). Filtered includes (EF Core 5+) restrict loaded children with Where, OrderBy and Take.
i: Multiple collection includes can cause a cartesian explosion; AsSplitQuery runs separate queries.
Projection with Select is often better than Include for read-only views.
Include is ignored if you project to a non-entity type.
f: What is a cartesian explosion?
Joining several collections multiplies rows, sending huge duplicate data.
Split query downside?
Multiple round-trips and possible inconsistency without a transaction.
p5-4.y: Include loads a related entity together with the main one, like shipments with their site. ThenInclude goes one level deeper from that related entity, like the site's country. Both turn into joins in a single query. I use them carefully, because including too much can load a lot of data. For read screens, I often use a Select projection instead.
p5-4.k: include, theninclude, eager loading, ef core

p5-5.q: dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentIndex generates Up and Down code from model changes, which I review like any code; then I generate an idempotent SQL script (dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent) or a migration bundle for the pipeline, so DBAs and the regulated release process can review and run it.
i: Don't call Database.Migrate() at app startup in production with multiple instances (race conditions); run migrations as a pipeline step.
Migration bundles (efbundle) are self-contained executables.
Data migrations and expand/contract for zero-downtime.
Model snapshot file must be committed and merged carefully.
f: Why idempotent scripts?
They can run against any environment state safely, checking applied migrations.
How do you resolve migration conflicts between branches?
Remove and re-create the later migration after merging, or merge snapshots carefully.
p5-5.y: I change my entity classes or configuration, then run dotnet ef migrations add with a clear name. EF Core compares the model with the last snapshot and generates a migration with Up and Down methods. I review the generated code. For deployment, we generate an idempotent SQL script, review it, and apply it as a controlled step in the release, not automatically at startup.
p5-5.k: ef core migrations, dotnet ef, schema changes, database

p5-6.q: In Code First the C# model is the source of truth and migrations create and evolve the schema; in Database First you scaffold entities from an existing database (dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold) and the database stays the source of truth. IRT uses [Code First for newer services and scaffolding for legacy schemas].
i: Code First suits greenfield services owning their data.
Database First suits shared or DBA-owned databases.
EF Core Power Tools helps with reverse engineering.
Hybrid: scaffold once from an existing database (dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold), then continue Code First with migrations.
f: Can you switch later?
Yes, by creating a baseline migration from the existing schema.
How do you keep scaffolded code customisable?
Partial classes and templates (T4) so re-scaffolding doesn't overwrite custom code.
p5-6.y: Code First means I write the C# entity classes first and EF Core creates and updates the database with migrations. Database First means the database already exists and I generate the classes from it with scaffolding. For new services I use Code First, and for an existing database I scaffold once and can then continue with Code First.
p5-6.k: code first, database first, scaffolding, ef core

p5-7.q: LINQ-to-Entities is LINQ over DbSet/IQueryable that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; only translatable methods are allowed in filters (Where, Select, OrderBy, string Contains/StartsWith, EF.Functions). The query is an expression tree until enumerated.
i: ToQueryString() shows the SQL without running it.
EF.Functions.Like, DateDiffDay and others map to SQL functions.
Final Select projections can call client code (top-level only).
The provider translates expression trees to SQL; ToQueryString() shows the SQL without executing it.
f: What triggers execution?
Enumeration: ToList, First, Count, foreach, await ToListAsync.
How do you see generated SQL quickly?
query.ToQueryString() or logging.
p5-7.y: LINQ to Entities is LINQ used against EF Core. Instead of running in memory, my LINQ query becomes an expression tree that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database. So Where, Select and OrderBy happen in SQL Server. I can see the generated SQL with ToQueryString, which helps when tuning.
p5-7.k: linq to entities, ef core, iqueryable, sql translation

p5-8.q: Client-side evaluation happens when you use methods EF can't translate (custom C# functions, some string or date operations) inside a filter. Since EF Core 3, it throws instead of silently loading everything into memory; only the final projection may run client code.
i: Fixes: rewrite with translatable methods, EF.Functions, computed columns, or map a database function with HasDbFunction.
AsEnumerable() explicitly switches to in-memory after filtering in SQL.
Since EF Core 3.0, untranslatable expressions in Where throw instead of silently evaluating on the client; only the final Select projection may run client-side.
Common causes: calling your own C# methods in Where, string.Format, or unsupported overloads; fix with translatable expressions or a mapped DB function.
f: Why did EF Core 3 change this?
Silent client evaluation loaded whole tables and caused serious performance issues.
Is AsEnumerable dangerous?
Only if used before filtering, which loads too much data.
p5-8.y: Client-side evaluation happens when part of a query can't be translated into SQL, like calling my own C# method inside a Where. Since EF Core 3, that throws an error instead of quietly loading all rows into memory, which was a big performance trap. Only the final Select can run in C#. I fix it by rewriting the query with translatable expressions.
p5-8.k: client-side evaluation, ef core, query translation, performance

p5-9.q: I use AsNoTracking for reads, project to DTOs with Select, filter and page in SQL, avoid N+1 with Include or projections, use AsSplitQuery for multiple collections, add the right indexes, batch writes, use ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete for set-based changes, and measure with logged SQL and execution plans.
i: DbContext pooling and compiled models reduce startup and per-request overhead.
Avoid lazy loading in APIs.
Check for implicit conversions and non-SARGable predicates in generated SQL.
The shipment-list fix: index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE plus projection took [9 s to under 300 ms].
f: How do you detect N+1?
Log SQL and look for repeated similar queries per row, or use MiniProfiler.
AsNoTracking vs AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution?
The latter de-duplicates entity instances without tracking.
p5-9.y: First I look at the generated SQL and the execution plan. Then the usual fixes: use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, project only the columns I need with Select, avoid N+1 queries, add paging, and make sure the right indexes exist. For big updates I use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. That's how our shipment list went from [9 seconds to under 300 milliseconds].
p5-9.k: ef core performance, optimization, asnotracking, projection, n+1

p5-10.q: SaveChanges detects changes in tracked entities and writes all pending INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements in one transaction, batching them where possible. SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking a thread during I/O, which is what I use in ASP.NET Core.
i: Returns the number of affected rows; throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException or DbUpdateException.
Interceptors (SaveChangesInterceptor) for auditing and soft delete.
ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled can be turned off for bulk adds.
SaveChanges wraps all changes in one transaction by default and batches statements (SQL Server batching).
f: Is SaveChanges transactional?
Yes, each call is one transaction unless you've started an explicit one.
Why call SaveChanges once per unit of work?
Fewer round-trips and all-or-nothing behaviour.
p5-10.y: SaveChanges looks at all the tracked changes and writes them to the database as inserts, updates and deletes, inside one transaction by default. SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking the thread while waiting for the database. In ASP.NET Core I always use SaveChangesAsync, so the server can handle other requests meanwhile.

p5-11.q: EF Core 7+ ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete run set-based SQL without loading entities; AddRange with batching handles moderate inserts. For very large loads I use SqlBulkCopy (or a library like EFCore.BulkExtensions) into a staging table, then MERGE set-based.
i: ExecuteUpdate bypasses the change tracker and interceptors; handle auditing separately.
Batch size (MaxBatchSize) affects round-trips.
Wrap staging plus merge in a transaction.
c:
await db.Shipments.Where(s => s.Status == ShipmentStatus.Pending && s.CreatedAt < cutoff)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(u => u.SetProperty(s => s.Status, ShipmentStatus.Expired), ct);
f: Downside of ExecuteUpdate?
Tracked entities in memory aren't updated, and SaveChanges interceptors don't run.
How fast is SqlBulkCopy?
Hundreds of thousands of rows per second, depending on table and indexes.
p5-11.y: For large updates or deletes, I use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run one SQL statement without loading entities into memory. For large inserts, I batch them, or use SqlBulkCopy or a bulk extension library, which is much faster than adding thousands of entities one by one. Our CSV import saves rows in batches inside one transaction.
p5-11.k: bulk operations, executeupdate, executedelete, sqlbulkcopy, ef core

p5-12.q: EF.CompileAsyncQuery caches the LINQ-to-SQL translation of a query shape so very hot paths skip translation cost. EF already caches translations internally, so compiled queries give only small gains; compiled models (dotnet ef dbcontext optimize) help startup for large models.
i: EF Core 9+ supports precompiled queries for native AOT (experimental).
Use only after profiling shows translation cost matters.
EF Core already caches query plans; compiled queries mainly save the expression-tree compare and translation cost on very hot paths.
c:
static readonly Func<IrtDbContext, int, Task<Shipment?>> ById =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((IrtDbContext db, int id) => db.Shipments.FirstOrDefault(s => s.Id == id));
f: When are compiled queries worth it?
Extremely hot, simple queries in high-throughput services.
What is a compiled model?
A generated model that avoids building the model at startup.
p5-12.y: A compiled query is a LINQ query that EF Core translates once and then reuses, using EF.CompileAsyncQuery. EF Core already caches query plans, so this only saves the small cost of processing the query each time. I'd use it only for very hot queries that run thousands of times per second, after measuring.

p5-13.q: Use LogTo(Console.WriteLine) on the options builder, or the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command log category at Information, which logs SQL and timing. EnableSensitiveDataLogging shows parameter values, for development only.
i: ToQueryString() for one query.
Interceptors (DbCommandInterceptor) can log slow queries or add query tags.
TagWith("ShipmentList") adds comments to SQL to find it in Query Store.
In tests or dev: optionsBuilder.LogTo(Console.WriteLine, LogLevel.Information); never EnableSensitiveDataLogging in production.
f: Why not enable sensitive data logging in production?
It logs parameter values that may contain personal data.
How do you find which code issued a slow query?
TagWith or TagWithCallSite to add identifying comments.
p5-13.y: I set the log level for the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command category to Information, and EF Core logs every SQL command it runs, with timings. For a single query, ToQueryString shows the SQL without running it. I never turn on sensitive data logging in production, because it would log parameter values.
p5-13.k: log sql, ef core logging, toquerystring, debugging

p5-14.q: Relationships are configured with navigations and foreign keys by convention or Fluent API (HasOne/WithMany, HasMany/WithMany). One-to-one: Subject and Consent; one-to-many: Study and Sites; many-to-many: Users and Studies, with EF Core 5+ creating the join table automatically or using an explicit join entity with extra data.
i: Delete behaviour: Cascade, Restrict, SetNull, configured per relationship.
Required vs optional by FK nullability.
Explicit join entities when the join has data (role, assigned date).
c:
b.Entity<Site>().HasOne(s => s.Study).WithMany(st => st.Sites).HasForeignKey(s => s.StudyId).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);
b.Entity<User>().HasMany(u => u.Studies).WithMany(s => s.Users).UsingEntity<StudyAssignment>();
f: Why Restrict on delete?
To avoid accidental cascades deleting regulated data.
What are multiple cascade paths?
SQL Server rejects schemas where deletes can cascade by more than one path.
p5-14.y: In EF Core, I define relationships with navigation properties and configure them with the Fluent API. One-to-many is the most common, like a site with many shipments, using a foreign key on the shipment. One-to-one uses a foreign key with a unique constraint. Many-to-many can be automatic with a hidden join table, or an explicit join entity if it needs extra columns.
p5-14.k: relationships, one-to-many, many-to-many, one-to-one, ef core, fluent api

p5-15.q: Shadow properties exist in the EF model and table but not in the C# class, such as LastModifiedBy or a foreign key; they're accessed with EF.Property<T>(entity, "Name") in queries and through the change tracker. They keep infrastructure concerns like audit columns out of domain classes.
i: Set them in a SaveChanges interceptor.
Query filters can use them (soft delete IsDeleted).
Common use: audit columns (CreatedAt, UpdatedBy) set in SaveChanges via ChangeTracker without polluting the domain model.
f: When would EF create a shadow FK?
When a navigation exists without an FK property in the class.
Downside?
Less discoverable in code.
p5-15.y: A shadow property is a column that EF Core knows about but that isn't a property on my C# class. I access it through the change tracker or EF.Property. It's handy for things like audit columns, such as created date or updated by, which I set in SaveChanges without cluttering my domain classes.
p5-15.k: shadow properties, ef core, audit columns

p5-16.q: Owned entities map value objects as part of their owner with OwnsOne/OwnsMany, e.g. an Address inside Site stored in the Site table's columns; they have no identity of their own. EF Core 8 complex types (ComplexProperty) are a newer option for value objects with value semantics, and owned types can be mapped to JSON columns.
i: Value objects: immutable, compared by value (Money, Address, TemperatureRange).
OwnsMany can map to a separate table or JSON.
Owned types can map to the same table (columns prefixed) or a separate table; in EF Core 8, complex types are an alternative for value objects.
c:
b.Entity<Site>().OwnsOne(s => s.Address);   // Address_City, Address_Country columns
b.Entity<Site>().ComplexProperty(s => s.StorageRange);  // EF Core 8 complex type
f: Owned type vs complex type?
Owned types are entity types with hidden keys; complex types are true value types without identity.
Why JSON columns?
Flexible nested data queried with JSON functions without extra tables.
p5-16.y: An owned entity is a type that has no identity of its own and belongs to its owner, like an Address inside a Site. By default its columns are stored in the owner's table, with prefixed names. It's a nice way to model value objects. In EF Core 8 there are also complex types for the same idea.
p5-16.k: owned entity, value object, ef core, complex types

p5-17.q: Fluent API HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status }) with IsUnique, HasFilter or IncludeProperties (SQL Server), or the [Index] attribute on the class; migrations then create the index. I base indexes on real query patterns and verify with execution plans.
i: Unique indexes enforce business rules (one kit number per study).
Filtered indexes for hot subsets.
Name indexes explicitly for stable migrations.
c:
b.Entity<Shipment>().HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status, s.ShipmentDate })
 .IncludeProperties(s => new { s.SiteId, s.KitCount }).HasDatabaseName("IX_Shipments_Study_Status_Date");
f: What does IncludeProperties do?
Adds INCLUDE columns so the index covers the query.
Unique index vs unique constraint?
Functionally similar in SQL Server; a constraint expresses intent and is backed by an index.
p5-17.y: I configure indexes in OnModelCreating with HasIndex, or with the Index attribute on the class. I can make them unique, combine several columns, add a filter, and include extra columns for SQL Server. Then a migration creates them. For example, a unique index on study and site number stops duplicate sites.
p5-17.k: indexes, hasindex, ef core, unique index

p5-18.q: A primary key uniquely identifies each row, can't be null, and there's one per table (clustered by default in SQL Server). A foreign key is a column referencing another table's primary or unique key, enforcing referential integrity so you can't have orphan rows.
i: Surrogate keys (identity, sequence, GUID) vs natural keys (kit number).
GUID PKs: use sequential GUIDs (NEWSEQUENTIALID, or Guid.CreateVersion7 in .NET 9) to avoid fragmentation.
Index foreign key columns; SQL Server doesn't do it automatically.
Choose surrogate keys (int/bigint identity or sequential GUID) for stability; natural keys can change.
f: Should every FK be indexed?
Usually, for joins and to avoid locking scans on deletes of the parent.
What is Guid.CreateVersion7?
A .NET 9 API creating time-ordered UUIDv7 values, better for index locality.
p5-18.y: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, it can't be null, and there's only one per table. A foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table, which keeps the relationship valid, so a shipment can't point to a site that doesn't exist.
p5-18.k: primary key, foreign key, relational database, constraints

p5-19.q: A unique constraint forbids duplicate values and is backed by a unique index. A table has one primary key but can have many unique keys; the PK can't be null, while a unique key in SQL Server allows one NULL (use a filtered unique index to allow many).
i: Unique constraints enforce business rules regardless of app bugs or races.
Composite unique keys (StudyId, KitNumber).
A unique constraint allows one NULL in SQL Server; use a filtered unique index (WHERE col IS NOT NULL) to allow many NULLs.
c: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Users_Email ON dbo.Users(Email) WHERE Email IS NOT NULL;
f: Why enforce uniqueness in the database too?
Concurrent requests can both pass an app check.
Can a FK reference a unique key?
Yes, not only primary keys.
p5-19.y: A unique constraint makes sure no two rows have the same value in a column or set of columns. Compared with a primary key, a table can have many unique keys but only one primary key, and a unique key allows a null in SQL Server. I use unique constraints for business rules, like no duplicate site numbers in a study.
p5-19.k: unique constraint, unique key, primary key, constraints

p5-20.q: A composite index covers several columns, such as (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate). Column order matters: it supports seeks on the leading column(s), so put equality-filtered columns first and range or sort columns after. It can serve queries on StudyId alone or StudyId plus Status, but not Status alone.
i: Leftmost prefix rule.
INCLUDE columns make it covering without widening the key.
Our shipment fix used exactly (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE, cutting reads from [400,000 to 2,000].
Our shipment index (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) INCLUDE (...) served the main list query: equality columns first, the range/sort column last.
f: Why equality before range?
After a range column, later key columns can't be used for seeking.
Can SQL Server use a skip scan?
Not generally; it would scan instead.
p5-20.y: A composite index covers more than one column. The order of columns matters: SQL Server can seek on the first column, or the first and second, but not the second alone. I put equality filters first and range or sort columns last. Our shipment list used an index on StudyId, Status, then ShipmentDate, with display columns included.
p5-20.k: composite index, multi-column index, column order, sql server

p5-21.q: A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (e.g. only Pending shipments): smaller, cheaper to maintain and faster for queries on a hot subset. The query predicate must match the filter, and parameterised queries may not use it unless the optimizer can prove the match.
i: Great for status columns where few rows are "active".
Filtered unique indexes allow uniqueness only among non-null or active rows.
Requires specific SET options (QUOTED_IDENTIFIER, ANSI_NULLS).
Parameterized queries may not use a filtered index if the plan can't prove the filter matches; use literals or OPTION(RECOMPILE) when needed.
f: Why might a parameterised query ignore it?
The plan must be valid for any parameter value, so it can't rely on the filter.
Fix?
Use a literal for the filtered value or OPTION (RECOMPILE).
p5-21.y: A filtered index only covers rows that match a condition, like only active shipments. It's smaller, faster to maintain, and great when most queries look at a small part of the table. A common use is a unique index that ignores nulls. The query needs to match the filter, otherwise SQL Server can't use it.
p5-21.k: filtered index, partial index, sql server

p5-22.q: Indexes help because the B-tree lets SQL Server seek rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning, cover queries without lookups, and avoid sorts. They hurt when there are too many: every insert, update and delete must maintain them, they use storage and memory, and unused or duplicate indexes add cost without benefit.
i: Check sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats for unused indexes.
Key lookups on many rows can make a seek slower than a scan.
Fragmentation matters less on SSDs; statistics freshness matters more.
Monitor with sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats: indexes with many updates and no seeks are candidates to drop.
f: How many indexes are too many?
There's no fixed number; judge by write workload and usage stats.
What is a key lookup?
Fetching extra columns from the clustered index for each row found in a non-clustered index.
p5-22.y: An index is like a book's index: SQL Server finds rows directly instead of scanning the whole table, which makes reads much faster. But every insert, update and delete must also update the indexes, and they take storage. So too many or unused indexes slow down writes. I add indexes for the main queries and remove ones that are never used.
p5-22.k: indexes, performance, write overhead, sql server

p5-23.q: An execution plan is the optimizer's recipe for a query: operators (seeks, scans, join types, sorts), estimated vs actual row counts and costs. I read the actual plan to find scans, key lookups, bad estimates, spills and implicit conversions, and use Query Store to see plan history and regressions.
i: Read right to left, top to bottom; thick arrows mean many rows.
Warnings: implicit conversion, missing index, tempdb spills.
Join types: nested loops (small inputs), hash (large unsorted), merge (sorted inputs).
Query Store can force a known good plan.
f: Estimated vs actual plan?
Estimated shows the plan without running; actual adds real row counts.
What does a big estimate vs actual gap mean?
Stale statistics or parameter sniffing; investigate cardinality.
p5-23.y: An execution plan shows how SQL Server will run, or actually ran, a query: which indexes it uses, the join types, and the estimated versus actual row counts. It's the main tool for tuning. I look for scans on large tables, key lookups, and big gaps between estimated and actual rows. That's how I found the problems in our slow shipment query.
p5-23.k: execution plan, query plan, sql server, tuning

p5-24.q: A table scan reads every row of a heap; an index scan reads all or a large range of an index (clustered index scan reads the whole table); an index seek navigates the B-tree directly to matching rows. Seeks are best for selective queries; scans can be fine for large portions of data.
i: Non-SARGable predicates (functions on columns, leading wildcards, implicit conversions) force scans.
Range scans are seeks with a range predicate.
Key lookups after a nonclustered seek can dominate cost; covering indexes with INCLUDE remove them.
c:
-- Non-SARGable: WHERE YEAR(ShipmentDate) = 2025
-- SARGable:    WHERE ShipmentDate >= '2025-01-01' AND ShipmentDate < '2026-01-01'
f: Is a scan always bad?
No, reading most of a small table is cheaper by scan.
What is SARGable?
A predicate that can use an index seek (Search ARGument able).
p5-24.y: A table scan reads every row of a table with no clustered index. An index scan reads the whole index, which is still a lot. An index seek jumps directly to the matching rows using the index, which is what we want for selective queries. When I see a scan on a big table, I check for a missing index or a non-SARGable condition.
p5-24.k: table scan, index scan, index seek, sql server, performance

p5-25.q: A cardinality estimate is how many rows the optimizer expects at each plan step; statistics are histograms of column value distributions (up to 200 steps) used to make those estimates. Bad estimates from stale or missing statistics lead to bad plans, like nested loops over millions of rows.
i: Auto update statistics triggers after a threshold of changes (dynamic threshold since SQL Server 2016).
UPDATE STATISTICS ... WITH FULLSCAN for skewed data.
Table variables historically estimated 1 row (improved with deferred compilation in SQL 2019).
Auto-update statistics triggers after a percentage of changes; large tables may need manual UPDATE STATISTICS after bulk loads.
f: Why did a plan change overnight in your incident?
A statistics update caused recompilation with an unrepresentative parameter value.
What is the cardinality estimator version?
The model tied to compatibility level; changes can shift plans after upgrades.
p5-25.y: Cardinality is the number of rows SQL Server expects at each step of a query. Statistics are the data distribution information it uses to make that estimate. If statistics are outdated, the estimate is wrong, and SQL Server may choose a bad plan. So after big data loads, I make sure statistics are updated.
p5-25.k: cardinality, statistics, query optimizer, sql server

p5-26.q: UNION removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you truly need de-duplication.
i: Column count and types must match; names come from the first query.
ORDER BY applies to the whole result, at the end.
UNION adds a sort or hash distinct, which costs CPU and memory on large sets.
Use UNION ALL by default when sets can't overlap or duplicates are fine.
f: When is UNION needed?
When overlapping sources may return the same row and duplicates are wrong.
UNION vs JOIN?
UNION stacks rows vertically; JOIN combines columns horizontally.
p5-26.y: Both combine the results of two queries. UNION removes duplicate rows, which needs extra sorting work. UNION ALL keeps all rows, including duplicates, so it's faster. I use UNION ALL by default, unless I actually need duplicates removed.

p5-27.q: EXISTS stops at the first match; IN compares against a list or subquery. Modern optimizers often produce the same semi-join plan for both, but NOT IN with NULLs in the subquery returns no rows, so I prefer NOT EXISTS for anti-joins.
i: Large IN lists from apps create plan cache bloat; use table-valued parameters or JSON (OPENJSON).
EF Core 8+ translates Contains on lists using OPENJSON parameters.
NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns no rows; NOT EXISTS behaves as expected, so prefer it.
c: SELECT s.* FROM Sites s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id);
f: Why does NOT IN fail with NULL?
Comparison with NULL is unknown, so the whole predicate isn't true.
How did EF Core 8 change Contains?
It sends the list as a JSON parameter, keeping one cached plan.
p5-27.y: IN checks if a value is in a list or subquery, and EXISTS checks if a subquery returns any row. For most queries, SQL Server builds the same plan. The big difference is NOT IN: if the subquery contains a null, it returns nothing, which surprises people. So I use NOT EXISTS for that case.
p5-27.k: exists, in, not exists, not in, sql

p5-28.q: A CTE is a named query for one statement: not materialised, readable, and supports recursion. A temp table (#t) is materialised in tempdb, can be indexed, has statistics and can be reused across statements in the session. Use CTEs for readability, temp tables for large intermediate results reused or needing indexes.
i: Table variables (@t) have limited statistics; good for small sets.
CTE referenced twice is evaluated twice.
Recursive CTEs for hierarchies (MAXRECURSION default 100).
Table variables have limited statistics (improved by deferred compilation in SQL Server 2019+); temp tables have full stats.
f: Is a CTE faster than a subquery?
No, it's the same; it's about readability.
Temp table vs table variable?
Temp tables have statistics and are better for larger data.
p5-28.y: A CTE is a named query that exists only for one statement, which makes complex queries readable, and it can be recursive. A temporary table is stored in tempdb, lasts for the session, can have indexes and statistics, and can be reused across several statements. For large intermediate results used more than once, I use a temp table.
p5-28.k: cte, temporary table, temp table, sql

p5-29.q: ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence even for ties; RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps (1,1,2). All need OVER (ORDER BY ...), optionally PARTITION BY.
i: Deterministic ROW_NUMBER needs a unique ORDER BY (add a tie-breaker).
NTILE splits into buckets; LAG/LEAD access neighbouring rows.
Use ROW_NUMBER for pagination and dedup; DENSE_RANK for "nth highest" when ties count once.
c:
SELECT SiteId, KitCount,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) rn,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY KitCount DESC) drnk
FROM SiteStock;
f: Which for nth-highest distinct value?
DENSE_RANK.
Can you filter on a window function in WHERE?
No, wrap it in a CTE or subquery first.
p5-29.y: All three number rows in order. ROW_NUMBER gives unique numbers, 1, 2, 3, even for ties. RANK gives ties the same number and then skips, like 1, 1, 3. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps, like 1, 1, 2. I use ROW_NUMBER for paging and removing duplicates, and DENSE_RANK for nth highest.
p5-29.k: row_number, rank, dense_rank, window functions, sql

p5-30.q: Group and count: SELECT KitNumber, COUNT(*) FROM Kits GROUP BY KitNumber HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. To see or delete the duplicate rows themselves, use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id) and keep rn = 1.
i: Delete duplicates via a CTE where rn > 1, then add a unique constraint to prevent recurrence.
Delete duplicates keeping one: WITH d AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY Id) rn FROM Users) DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1.
Prevent recurrence with a unique index after cleanup.
c:
WITH d AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY StudyId, KitNumber ORDER BY Id) rn FROM Kits)
DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1;
f: Why can you delete from a CTE?
SQL Server allows DML through a CTE over a single base table.
What prevents new duplicates?
A unique constraint or index.
p5-30.y: I group by the columns that should be unique and use HAVING COUNT greater than one, which lists the duplicate values. To see or delete the extra rows, I use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by those columns and keep only row number one. After cleaning up, I add a unique constraint so it can't happen again.
p5-30.k: duplicate records, group by, having, row_number, sql

p5-31.q: SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Emp ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET N-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY; or DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) in a CTE and filter on rank = N, which handles ties correctly.
i: The classic MAX with subquery works for second highest only.
Return NULL when there's no nth value if required.
OFFSET/FETCH alternative: SELECT DISTINCT Salary ... ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET n-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY.
c:
WITH r AS (SELECT Salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) dr FROM Emp)
SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM r WHERE dr = @N;
f: Why DENSE_RANK not ROW_NUMBER?
Ties would otherwise count as separate positions.
Per department?
Add PARTITION BY DepartmentId.
p5-31.y: The cleanest way is DENSE_RANK ordered by salary descending, then pick the rows where the rank equals N, which also handles ties correctly. Another option is OFFSET N minus 1 rows and fetch next one row on distinct salaries. For the second highest only, a simple MAX of salaries less than the overall max also works.
p5-31.k: nth highest salary, second highest, dense_rank, sql

p5-32.q: Use ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY: WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) rn FROM Shipments) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn <= 3. CROSS APPLY with TOP is an alternative that can be faster with a good index.
i: Index (SiteId, ShipDate DESC) supports both.
CROSS APPLY with TOP (N) ... ORDER BY can be faster than ROW_NUMBER when an index supports the per-group ordering.
Ties: use RANK or WITH TIES if equal values should all appear.
c:
SELECT s.Id, x.* FROM Sites s
CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP (3) Id, ShipDate FROM Shipments sh WHERE sh.SiteId = s.Id ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) x;
f: When is CROSS APPLY better?
When there are few groups and an index allows a seek per group.
Ties?
Use RANK or DENSE_RANK if ties should all be included.
p5-32.y: I use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the group and ordered by the ranking column, inside a CTE, then keep rows where the number is less than or equal to N. For example, the latest three shipments per site. If an index supports it, CROSS APPLY with TOP N can be even faster.
p5-32.k: top n per group, row_number, partition by, cross apply, sql

p5-33.q: A dirty read reads uncommitted data that may be rolled back; a non-repeatable read gets different values for the same row within a transaction because another transaction updated it; a phantom read finds new rows on re-running a range query because another transaction inserted them.
i: Read Uncommitted (NOLOCK) allows dirty reads; Read Committed prevents them; Repeatable Read prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents phantoms; Snapshot gives a consistent versioned view.
NOLOCK can also skip or double-read rows, not just read dirty data.
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) avoids readers blocking writers by reading row versions from tempdb.
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted allows all three; Repeatable Read stops non-repeatable reads; Serializable stops phantoms.
f: Why avoid NOLOCK?
It can return wrong results, including missing or duplicated rows.
Which isolation does RCSI give?
Read Committed using row versions, so readers don't block writers.
p5-33.y: A dirty read is reading data another transaction hasn't committed yet, which might be rolled back. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in a transaction and getting different values, because someone updated it. A phantom read is running the same query twice and getting new rows. Higher isolation levels prevent each of these.
p5-33.k: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, isolation levels

p5-34.q: ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules and constraints hold after each transaction), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere beyond the isolation level) and Durability (committed data survives crashes, via the transaction log).
i: Write-ahead logging gives durability and rollback.
Distributed systems trade some ACID across services (sagas, eventual consistency).
Durability in SQL Server comes from write-ahead logging: the log record is hardened before commit returns.
Distributed services can't have ACID across databases cheaply, so we used outbox plus eventual consistency.
f: How does SQL Server guarantee durability?
Log records are hardened to disk before commit returns.
ACID vs BASE?
BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) describes many NoSQL systems.
p5-34.y: ACID describes reliable transactions. Atomicity means all or nothing. Consistency means the data always follows the rules and constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other. Durability means once committed, the data survives a crash. Our CSV import relies on atomicity: everything saves, or nothing does.
p5-34.k: acid, atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, transactions

p5-35.q: Optimistic locking takes no locks; it detects conflicts at write time with a rowversion and fails the second writer, best for low contention (EF Core concurrency tokens). Pessimistic locking locks the row while working (SELECT ... WITH (UPDLOCK)), best for high contention like allocating the next randomization slot.
i: EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException; reload and retry or show a conflict.
APIs expose the version as an ETag with If-Match.
EF Core: a rowversion column marked IsRowVersion() gives optimistic concurrency; catch DbUpdateConcurrencyException and return 409.
c: public class Shipment { public int Id { get; set; } [Timestamp] public byte[] RowVersion { get; set; } = []; }
f: What does EF do with [Timestamp]?
Adds the version to the UPDATE WHERE clause and checks rows affected.
Risk of pessimistic locking?
Blocking and deadlocks if transactions are long.
p5-35.y: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: there's no lock, but a version column is checked when saving, and if someone else changed the row, the save fails. Pessimistic locking locks the row while working on it, so others wait. I use optimistic locking with a rowversion column for user edits, and pessimistic locks only for short critical sections.
p5-35.k: optimistic locking, pessimistic locking, concurrency, rowversion

p5-36.q: Measure first (Query Store, wait stats, slow query logs), then fix the top queries (indexes, SARGable predicates, less data fetched, better joins), keep statistics fresh, shorten transactions, consider RCSI, cache hot reads, and scale hardware only after.
i: Wait stats tell where time goes (PAGEIOLATCH = I/O, LCK = blocking, CXPACKET = parallelism).
Batch and set-based operations instead of row by row.
Archive old data, partition very large tables.
Measure first: Query Store top resource consumers, wait stats, and actual execution plans before changing anything.
f: What do you check first?
Top queries by total CPU and duration in Query Store.
When would you partition?
Very large tables where sliding windows or maintenance per partition help.
p5-36.y: First I measure, using Query Store to find the most expensive queries, wait statistics, and execution plans. Then I fix the biggest problems: missing or wrong indexes, non-SARGable queries, N+1 calls from the app, and loading too much data. I also keep transactions short and statistics updated. Measuring before and after proves the fix worked.
p5-36.k: database performance, optimization, query store, indexes, tuning

p5-37.q: Start from real query patterns. The clustered key should be narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing; add non-clustered indexes on foreign keys and frequent filters with equality columns first, INCLUDE columns to cover hot queries, filtered indexes for hot subsets, and remove unused or duplicate indexes. Verify with execution plans.
i: Avoid wide clustered keys: they're copied into every non-clustered index.
Consider write cost on busy tables.
Review missing index DMVs critically; they often over-suggest.
Design from queries: list the top queries' WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY columns, then build the fewest indexes covering most of them.
f: Why ever-increasing clustered keys?
Inserts go to the end, reducing page splits and fragmentation.
Are missing index suggestions reliable?
They're hints; combine and validate them.
p5-37.y: I design indexes from the real queries. I list the main queries' WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY columns, and build composite indexes with equality columns first and range columns last, adding INCLUDE columns to avoid lookups. I aim for the fewest indexes that cover the most important queries, then check the plans and usage over time.
p5-37.k: index design, composite index, covering index, sql server

p5-38.q: Microservices are small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its data, communicating over APIs or messages. Teams can build, deploy and scale them separately.
i: Characteristics: database per service, decentralised governance, automated deployment, design for failure.
Size by business capability, not lines of code.
IRT services: randomization, supply, shipments, notifications.
Each service owns its data; sharing a database between services recreates a monolith.
f: Must each service have its own database?
Logically its own data, at least separate schemas with no cross-service access.
Microservices vs SOA?
Microservices are finer-grained, with smart endpoints and dumb pipes rather than an ESB.
p5-38.y: Microservices is an architecture where the system is split into small, independent services, each owning one business area and its own data, deployed on its own and talking over APIs or messages. In IRT, we have separate services for things like randomization, supply and shipments.

p5-39.q: Advantages: independent deploys and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy and technology choice per service. Disadvantages: distributed-system complexity (network failures, eventual consistency), harder testing and debugging, operational overhead (many pipelines, monitoring, tracing) and data consistency challenges.
i: Needs mature DevOps and observability.
Latency from network hops.
Advantages: independent deploys, scaling per service, fault isolation, team autonomy.
Disadvantages: network failures, distributed data consistency, more ops (observability, CI/CD per service).
f: Biggest hidden cost?
Operational complexity and data consistency across services.
How do you mitigate it?
Platform automation, templates, tracing and clear contracts.
p5-39.y: The advantages are independent deployments, scaling each service separately, fault isolation, and teams owning their own services. The disadvantages are the complexity of a distributed system: network failures, keeping data consistent across services, and much more work on monitoring, testing and deployment. So the benefits must be worth that cost.

p5-40.q: I wouldn't use microservices for a small team or early product, unclear domain boundaries, low scale, no DevOps maturity (CI/CD, monitoring), or when strong transactional consistency across the whole domain matters. A modular monolith is the better default.
i: Premature splitting creates a distributed monolith.
Extract services later along proven boundaries.
Small teams, unclear domains, or early products: start with a modular monolith and split on proven boundaries.
If services must always deploy together, they are a distributed monolith.
f: What is a modular monolith?
One deployable with strongly separated modules and boundaries.
Signal it's time to split?
Teams blocking each other or different scaling needs.
p5-40.y: I wouldn't use microservices for a small team, an early product, or a domain that isn't well understood yet, because the overhead is high and the boundaries will likely be wrong. If services always have to be deployed together, it's just a distributed monolith. In those cases, a well-structured modular monolith is better, and you split later where needed.
p5-40.k: when not to use microservices, monolith, modular monolith

p5-41.q: I use Domain-Driven Design: split by business capability and bounded context, the area where one model and its language are consistent (Randomization, Supply, Shipments). Signals include different data ownership, change frequency, team ownership and scaling needs; Event Storming workshops help find them.
i: A "Kit" means different things in Supply vs Dispensing: separate models.
Context maps describe relationships (customer-supplier, anti-corruption layer).
Avoid splitting by technical layer (a "data service").
Event storming with domain experts finds boundaries where language and data ownership change.
f: What is an anti-corruption layer?
A translation layer protecting your model from another system's model.
What is ubiquitous language?
Shared terms between developers and domain experts within a context.
p5-41.y: I find service boundaries around business capabilities, not technical layers. A bounded context, from domain-driven design, is an area where terms have one clear meaning and one team owns the data. For example, a shipment means something specific in the shipment context. Talking with domain experts, through event storming, helps find where these boundaries are.
p5-41.k: service boundaries, bounded context, ddd, domain driven design

p5-42.q: Synchronous REST or gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer; asynchronous events or commands (Kafka, RabbitMQ) when it doesn't, to decouple services and absorb load. Prefer async for state changes others react to, and keep synchronous chains short.
i: gRPC for internal high-performance calls with contracts (Protobuf).
Events carry facts ("ShipmentDelivered"); commands request actions.
Always with timeouts, retries and idempotency.
Rule of thumb: sync for queries needing an immediate answer, async events for state changes others react to.
f: Why avoid long synchronous chains?
Latency adds up and one failure breaks the whole chain.
Events vs commands?
Events notify many about something that happened; commands tell one handler to do something.
p5-42.y: They should use synchronous calls, like REST or gRPC, when the caller needs an immediate answer, like fetching data for a screen. They should use asynchronous messaging, like Kafka or RabbitMQ, when other services just need to react to something that happened, like a shipment status change. Async messaging keeps services more independent and resilient.
p5-42.k: microservices communication, rest, grpc, messaging, async

p5-43.q: Synchronous (REST/gRPC) is simple with an immediate result but creates temporal coupling: a slow or down callee affects the caller. Asynchronous messaging decouples in time and absorbs spikes, enabling independent scaling, but adds eventual consistency, duplicate handling and harder debugging.
i: Request/reply over messaging exists but adds complexity.
Choose per interaction, not per system.
Sync chains multiply latency and failure probability: three services at 99.9% each give about 99.7% combined.
Async decouples availability but needs idempotency, ordering decisions and monitoring of lag.
f: Example of each in IRT?
REST to randomize a subject (needs an answer); Kafka events for shipment status changes.
How do you debug async flows?
Correlation ids, tracing and message logs.
p5-43.y: With REST, which is synchronous, the caller waits for the answer, which is simple but couples availability: if the other service is down, the call fails. With messaging, which is asynchronous, the sender publishes and moves on, so services stay independent and can absorb spikes. But then we need idempotency and must accept eventual consistency.
p5-43.k: rest vs messaging, synchronous, asynchronous, communication

p5-44.q: Service discovery is how services find each other's current addresses: DNS-based (Kubernetes Services, ECS Service Connect / Cloud Map) or registry-based (Consul, Eureka), often behind load balancers. Clients call a stable name instead of IPs that change with scaling.
i: Client-side vs server-side discovery.
.NET Aspire provides service discovery for HttpClient (Microsoft.Extensions.ServiceDiscovery).
On ECS: Cloud Map or Service Connect; on Kubernetes: Services and DNS; behind an ALB, the ALB is the stable endpoint.
Client-side vs server-side discovery: client picks an instance from a registry vs a load balancer picks.
f: Why not hardcode IPs?
Containers come and go with changing IPs.
ECS Service Connect?
Managed service discovery and proxy for ECS services with metrics.
p5-44.y: Service discovery is how a service finds the network address of another service, since instances come and go. On Kubernetes, services get DNS names. On ECS, we use Cloud Map, Service Connect, or a load balancer as a stable address. That way services call a name, and the platform routes to healthy instances.
p5-44.k: service discovery, dns, cloud map, service connect, kubernetes

p5-45.q: Retrying non-idempotent operations duplicates side effects; retrying permanent errors (400, 401, validation) wastes resources; and retry storms from many clients amplify an outage. So I retry only transient errors (timeouts, 408, 429, 5xx), with exponential backoff and jitter, limited attempts, idempotency keys, and a circuit breaker.
i: Retry budgets limit total retries.
Respect Retry-After headers.
Retries at multiple layers multiply (3 × 3 × 3 = 27).
Retry only transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429 with Retry-After) and idempotent operations; use exponential backoff with jitter.
f: Why jitter?
To spread retries so clients don't retry in sync.
Example?
The Copilot retry suggestion that would have duplicated release creation (Part 3 Q35).
p5-45.y: Retrying everything can make things worse. Retrying a non-idempotent call, like creating a payment, can create duplicates. Retrying permanent errors, like a 400 or a bad password, never helps. And many clients retrying at once can overload a struggling service. So I retry only temporary errors on safe operations, with backoff, jitter and a limit.
p5-45.k: retries, retry storm, idempotency, backoff, resilience

p5-46.q: Bulkhead isolation uses separate resource pools per dependency (connection pools, concurrency limits, queues) so one slow dependency can't exhaust all threads or connections and take the whole service down. The name comes from ship compartments that contain flooding.
i: Polly concurrency limiter or ASP.NET Core rate limiting per dependency.
Separate HttpClients with their own handlers per downstream.
Separate worker pools or queues per workload type.
Polly v8 / Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience: the concurrency limiter strategy acts as a bulkhead.
f: Bulkhead vs circuit breaker?
Bulkhead limits resources used; circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency.
Example in IRT?
[Separate consumer pools for vendor file processing and notifications].
p5-46.y: Bulkhead isolation is like the compartments in a ship: if one floods, the ship still floats. In software, I limit the resources, like concurrent calls or threads, given to each dependency, so one slow dependency can't use up everything and bring down the whole service. Polly has a concurrency limiter for this.

p5-47.q: Distributed tracing follows one request across services with a trace id and spans (timing per hop), using OpenTelemetry and W3C traceparent headers, visualised in X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo. It shows where latency and errors occur in a multi-service flow.
i: .NET has built-in Activity/ActivitySource; HttpClient and ASP.NET Core propagate context automatically.
Propagate through messages by putting traceparent in headers.
Sampling controls cost.
f: Trace id vs correlation id?
Similar purpose; trace ids are standardised and include parent-child spans.
How do you trace through RabbitMQ?
Inject traceparent into message headers and start a consumer span from it.
p5-47.y: Distributed tracing follows one request as it moves through many services. Each service adds a span with its timing, and they're linked by a trace id passed in headers. So I can see the whole journey and exactly where it was slow or failed. We use OpenTelemetry for this, together with our correlation ids in logs.
p5-47.k: distributed tracing, opentelemetry, trace id, spans, observability

p5-48.q: Eventual consistency means data across services becomes consistent after a short delay rather than instantly, accepted for availability and decoupling. Design for it with idempotent consumers, clear UI states (Pending), versioning and reconciliation jobs.
i: Read-your-writes can be provided for the user who made the change.
Monitoring lag between services.
Users must see something sensible meanwhile, e.g. "Processing" status, not stale success.
Reconciliation jobs catch messages that went missing despite the outbox.
f: Where is it unacceptable in IRT?
Randomization slot allocation and kit assignment within a transaction.
How do you show it in a UI?
Status like "Processing" and refresh or push updates.
p5-48.y: Eventual consistency means that after a change, different services may briefly show different data, but they all catch up after a short time. It's the trade-off for decoupled services that talk through events. The user interface should show something sensible meanwhile, like a processing status, and we use reconciliation to catch anything missed.

p5-49.q: Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and fallbacks for synchronous calls; asynchronous messaging with durable queues and DLQs; idempotent handlers; sagas with compensation for multi-step workflows; and health checks with alerts.
i: Graceful degradation: show cached data when a dependency is down.
.NET 8 standard resilience handler bundles these for HttpClient.
Timeouts on every call, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks, and DLQs for async work.
Idempotent consumers so retries don't double-apply.
f: What is a fallback?
An alternative response when the call fails, like cached or default data.
What timeout values?
Based on the dependency's p99 plus margin, always less than the caller's own timeout.
p5-49.y: I assume calls will fail. Every call has a timeout, temporary errors are retried with backoff, and a circuit breaker stops calling a service that's down. I provide fallbacks where possible. For async work, messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue, and consumers are idempotent so retries are safe.
p5-49.k: failure handling, resilience, timeout, retry, circuit breaker, dlq

p5-50.q: Version APIs (URL segment or header) and message contracts (additive changes, a schema version field), stay backward compatible, use consumer-driven contract tests, and deprecate old versions with notice. Prefer additive, non-breaking changes so versions rarely change.
i: Tolerant reader: consumers ignore unknown fields.
Asp.Versioning library for ASP.NET Core.
Schema registry for Kafka (Avro/Protobuf compatibility rules).
Prefer backward-compatible changes (additive fields); version URLs (/v2) only for breaking changes, with a deprecation window.
f: What's a breaking change?
Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings, new required inputs.
How long do you keep old versions?
Per agreement with consumers, with monitoring of usage.
p5-50.y: I version the contracts, both APIs and events. I prefer backward-compatible changes, like adding optional fields, so consumers don't break. For breaking changes, I add a new version, like v2 in the URL or a new event version, run both for a while, and remove the old one after consumers move. Each service is deployed independently with its own version.
p5-50.k: microservices versioning, api versioning, backward compatibility

p5-51.q: Each service has its own pipeline: build, test, image, IaC; deployments are independent to ECS or Kubernetes with rolling or blue-green strategies, health checks and automatic rollback, with configuration per environment and the same image promoted everywhere.
i: Shared pipeline templates for consistency.
Feature flags decouple release from deploy.
Contract tests prevent breaking consumers.
Each service has its own pipeline and artifact; rolling or blue/green deployments with health checks gate traffic.
f: How do you deploy a change spanning two services?
Make it backward compatible and deploy in order (provider first).
ECS deployment circuit breaker?
Stops and rolls back a deployment when tasks fail to become healthy.
p5-51.y: Each service has its own pipeline that builds, tests and produces a versioned Docker image. We deploy it to ECS with rolling updates and health checks, so traffic only goes to healthy tasks, and a deployment circuit breaker rolls back automatically if it fails. The same image is promoted through all environments.
p5-51.k: microservices deployment, ci/cd, ecs, rolling deployment

p5-52.q: Golden signals per service, centralised structured logs with correlation ids, distributed tracing, Grafana or CloudWatch dashboards, SLOs with alerts, and business metrics such as shipments processed.
i: Same telemetry conventions across services (OpenTelemetry semantic conventions).
Dependency maps from traces.
Synthetic checks for critical flows.
Correlation ids across services (our [2024] middleware) let you follow one request through logs and traces.
f: What's an SLO?
A target like 99.9 percent of requests under 500 ms over 30 days.
Synthetic monitoring?
Scripted checks simulating user flows on a schedule (CloudWatch Synthetics).
p5-52.y: I monitor each service with metrics for the golden signals, structured logs with correlation ids, and distributed traces. Dashboards in Grafana show health in one place, and alerts fire on user impact, like error rate or latency. The correlation id lets me follow one request through all services.
p5-52.k: microservices monitoring, observability, metrics, logs, tracing

p5-53.q: Private networking (VPC, security groups) plus mTLS where required; service identities (OAuth client credentials tokens or IAM roles) with authorization per call; secrets from a vault; and zero trust: never assume the internal network is safe.
i: Validate tokens audience-scoped per service.
Service mesh can provide mTLS automatically.
Least-privilege security group rules.
On AWS: IAM roles per task, security groups allowing only required ports, and TLS; JWT client-credentials for app-level identity.
f: Client credentials flow?
A service authenticates with its own credentials to get an access token for another API.
Why not trust internal traffic?
A compromised service could otherwise reach everything.
p5-53.y: All traffic is encrypted with TLS. Each service has its own identity, using IAM roles on AWS or OAuth client credentials tokens for app-level calls, and the receiving service checks permissions. Network rules, like security groups, only allow the traffic that's needed. Secrets are kept in Secrets Manager, never in code.
p5-53.k: service-to-service security, mtls, client credentials, iam, zero trust

p5-54.q: Timeouts everywhere, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting and load shedding, async queues to absorb spikes, graceful degradation and fallbacks, and avoiding deep synchronous call chains.
i: Retry with backoff and budgets to avoid amplification.
Health checks shouldn't call dependencies deeply (avoid cascading restarts).
Timeouts shorter than the caller's, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding (429) and caches for read paths.
Avoid retry storms: retry budgets and jitter.
f: What is load shedding?
Rejecting excess requests early (503/429) to protect the system.
How do circuit breakers help?
They stop calls to a failing dependency, giving it time to recover and failing fast.
p5-54.y: A cascading failure is when one slow service makes its callers slow, and it spreads. I prevent it with timeouts that are shorter than the caller's, circuit breakers, bulkheads to limit resources per dependency, and rejecting extra load early with a 429. I also avoid retry storms with backoff and jitter.
p5-54.k: cascading failure, circuit breaker, timeout, bulkhead, resilience

p5-55.q: Unit tests; integration tests with a real database and broker in containers (Testcontainers); consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) between services; a few end-to-end tests on critical flows; plus performance and resilience tests.
i: Test pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, few E2E.
WebApplicationFactory for in-memory API tests.
.NET Aspire testing for distributed app tests.
Consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) catch breaking API changes before deploy.
f: Why contract tests?
They catch breaking API changes without full end-to-end environments.
Why not EF Core InMemory provider?
It behaves differently from real databases; use SQLite or Testcontainers.
p5-55.y: I test at several levels: unit tests for logic, integration tests for each service with real dependencies in containers, and contract tests so a service doesn't break its consumers. Then a few end-to-end tests for the critical journeys. Monitoring after release is part of testing too.
p5-55.k: microservices testing, contract testing, integration tests

p5-56.q: Environment variables plus central stores (AWS Parameter Store / Secrets Manager, Azure App Configuration), per-environment values, validation at startup (ValidateOnStart), no secrets in code, and feature flags for runtime toggles.
i: Configuration providers layered in .NET: appsettings, environment, secrets, command line.
IOptionsMonitor for reload without restart.
Version and review config changes like code.
Parameter Store/Secrets Manager plus appsettings per environment; options validated on start.
f: How do you change config without redeploying?
Central store with reload (IOptionsMonitor) or feature flags.
Why validate at startup?
Missing config fails the deployment, not live requests (the UAT lesson).
p5-56.y: Each service reads configuration from appsettings files plus environment-specific values from Parameter Store, and secrets from Secrets Manager. The values are injected into the containers at startup and bound with the Options pattern. Options are validated on start, so a missing value stops the deployment instead of breaking at runtime.
p5-56.k: configuration management, parameter store, secrets manager, options pattern

p5-57.q: Structured JSON logs with correlation ids shipped to one place (CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, Loki), common fields (service, environment, version, trace id), retention policies, no PHI or secrets, and queries and alerts on top.
i: Serilog or built-in JSON console logger.
Log levels set per category; avoid noisy debug in production.
Source-generated logging ([LoggerMessage]) for performance.
Structured JSON logs with correlation id, service name and environment fields make cross-service queries possible.
f: Why structured logs?
Fields can be queried and aggregated instead of parsing text.
How do you avoid logging PHI?
Redaction (Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance), reviewed log templates, and tests.
p5-57.y: All services write structured JSON logs with the same fields: service name, environment and correlation id. They're shipped to CloudWatch Logs, and we query them with Logs Insights. Because the fields are consistent, one query can follow a request across all services. We never log sensitive data.
p5-57.k: centralized logging, cloudwatch, structured logging, correlation id

p5-58.q: An API gateway in front of stateless services on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling; database per service with Redis caching; async messaging for events; observability (logs, metrics, traces); CI/CD per service; resilience patterns; and multi-AZ deployment.
i: Start with clear bounded contexts.
Platform templates for new services.
Security: identity provider, mTLS or tokens between services.
Stateless services behind load balancers, autoscaling on CPU or queue depth, caching, and async processing for spikes.
f: What's the first bottleneck usually?
The database; plan indexing, caching and read replicas.
How do you handle cross-service queries?
API composition or read models built from events (CQRS).
p5-58.y: I'd keep services stateless behind load balancers so they can scale out, with autoscaling on CPU or queue depth.
